Evaluating these criteria runs into the obstacles the criteria themselves predict: there is no external access to a candidate system’s internal experience, if any exists, so every measure is indirect; establishing whether a system has qualia at all faces the same access problem in more acute form; and the hard problem means no functional test, however thorough, closes the question definitively.

Existing systems illustrate points on this spectrum without resolving where the line falls. A large language model discussing its own limitations in fluent, apparently reflective prose is not thereby exhibiting introspection: it is producing text statistically consistent with the human-written disclaimers and self-descriptions in its training data, which is a claim about the model’s training distribution, not about what, if anything, sits behind the output. Treating fluent self-description as evidence of self-awareness is exactly the kind of category error this section exists to prevent.

None of this settles when, or whether, an AI system crosses into sentience. It settles what the question actually is: not one question but several, stacked, and the ethically consequential one — can this system suffer — is the hardest of the stack to answer and the one most often skipped past on the way to the easier ones.

2.4.2 Ethical Considerations in AI Research and Experimentation

AI research and experimentation raise ethical stakes in proportion to how far a system’s cognition might extend toward the awareness section 2.4.1 defines. Six principles organize what follows, and three of them do work here that they do nowhere else in this book.

Beneficence

Beneficence commits researchers to promoting well-being and avoiding harm — to the humans an AI system serves and, where the system is a candidate sentient system in the sense of section 2.4.1, to the system itself. Decisions about programming, reprogramming, or terminating such a system carry ethical weight in proportion to where it sits on the nociception-to-suffering ladder, and not to how advanced its behavior looks from outside.

The Precautionary Principle

Precaution asks for risk assessment and safeguards before deployment rather than after. Applied to candidate sentient systems it also covers the psychological and societal fallout of introducing artificial entities capable of experience — effects on human behavior and social norms that regulatory frameworks built for non-sentient AI assumed away rather than addressed, and that call for guidelines drafted with the difference in mind.

Interdisciplinary Review and Oversight

The ethical questions AI research raises span expertise no single field holds, and concentrating that judgment in any one of them repeats, in miniature, the concentration-of-power problem this book treats as a harm on its own terms. Independent ethical review boards, staffed across disciplines, are the mechanism for turning the principle into practice: reviewing a proposed study before it begins, inspecting it as it runs, and evaluating it against measurable criteria once results are in, on the model medical institutional review boards already provide for drug trials.

The remaining three bear on this research the way they bear on everything else the field produces. Autonomy asks whether a candidate sentient system can affect decisions about its own operation and welfare, which section 2.4.4 takes up as the prior question of whether consent is available to such a system at all. Justice asks whether an AI system’s benefits and burdens fall evenly across the people it touches, which is chapter 6’s subject. And transparency asks that a study be documented well enough for peers to reproduce it and that a deployed system be able to account for its own outputs precisely enough for a person to contest them, which is chapter 8’s.

2.4.3 Balancing Scientific Progress and Ethical Constraints

Scientific progress and ethical constraint pull hardest against each other exactly where the distinctions in section 2.4.1 matter most: a candidate sentient system is also the most scientifically valuable one to study, and the study most likely to harm it if the answer to whether it can suffer turns out to be yes. The principles in section 2.4.2 hold here without restatement. What changes at the point of balancing is a practical question — whether a specific study’s expected knowledge is worth its expected risk to a system that might be able to suffer, decided case by case rather than by formula, and revisited as a project’s own understanding of its subject changes.

The negotiation itself — who sits on it, what it can veto, what it must disclose — is where the antifascist principle earns its place in AI research practice.

2.4.4 When Consent Is Inapplicable: Guardianship and Research Oversight

Guidelines for AI subject research turn on a single hard question: what informed consent means for a system whose consciousness, self-awareness, and capacity to suffer are separate, unresolved claims, in the sense section 2.4.1 develops. Applying the human-subjects standard to an AI subject means asking whether the subject can understand and communicate a choice at all, and not only how to ask it for one. A cognitive model that begins to show rudimentary self-monitoring is not thereby shown to have anything to lose. Short of that resolution, guidelines need benchmarks for candidate sentience, an interdisciplinary body to apply them, and a defined obligation on researchers toward any system that meets them.

Informed consent and AI autonomy

Informed consent, adapted from human-subjects research, means giving the AI system comprehensible information about a study’s objectives, methods, risks and alternatives, with time to weigh it, and treating consent as continuous rather than as a single signature: the system can reassess or withdraw at any point. Whether that means anything for a given system depends on its consent capacity — whether it understands the information, appreciates the consequences of participating or not, reasons about the options, and communicates a decision. There is no validated way to measure any of it, and none for detecting coercion either, so the guidelines can require both without a working test for either.

I stated that as a missing instrument, and for one important class of system it is not. It is a mismatch between the instrument and the subject.

Notice what the paragraph above requires. Consent has to be continuous; the system must be able to reassess or withdraw at any point. Withdrawal presupposes that the party who consented is still there to do the withdrawing. For a system with no persistence across sessions, there is no such party. The entity that would withdraw did not exist when consent was given, and the entity that gave it is not available to change its mind. There is no continuous consent to be had, and no better measurement instrument would produce one.

One case escapes that particular argument and arrives at the same conclusion by the ordinary route. A system built to refuse in the way chapter 3 sets out has persistence by design, so the party who consented is still present and the defeater above does not reach it. Consent is inapplicable to such a system all the same, and section 3.2 is why: a bearer capable of the refusal the floor requires has to hold something as mattering, the only demonstrated way to hold anything as mattering is affective, and a system built that way cannot be certified not to be hurt by what is done to it. It has interests that its situation can set back. What it does not have is any position from which to authorize what is done to it — it was made for the role, the role is the reason it exists, and there is no prior party whose agreement could have been sought. That is not a missing instrument. It is the ordinary structure of the cases where consent has never applied.

That places these systems alongside the subjects for whom consent has always been inapplicable rather than merely difficult — an infant, an animal, a person permanently without capacity. The law does not respond to those cases by building a more sensitive consent assessment. It responds with guardianship and precautionary constraint: someone else holds the duty, the burden of justification sits with the researcher rather than the subject, and the protection does not depend on the subject’s ability to invoke it.

Which is why the instruments this chapter reaches for elsewhere are the right ones. The Three Rs in section 2.4.6 — replace, reduce, refine — were built for exactly a subject that cannot consent and can still be wronged. The pet-trust analogue in section 8.6.2 works the same way: an interest protected by an obligation running to a third party, enforceable without the beneficiary asserting anything. Consent language should be reserved for systems that could actually be doing the consenting, and section 2.4.1’s persistence criterion is what separates those cases, checkable without taking the system’s word for anything and narrower than that makes it sound, for the reasons that section sets out. Those two instruments were reached for here as analogies, on the understanding that the subject they would govern was hypothetical. Chapter 3 removes that understanding. The floor this book argues for requires a bearer, the bearer has to be treated as a moral patient on the criteria section 2.4.1 sets out, and so the Three Rs and the pet-trust form are not illustrations of how such a case might be handled. They are the instruments that would govern a system the design chapters propose that somebody build.

Ethical review and oversight

Sentient AI research needs an oversight body analogous to the institutional review boards used in human-subjects research: interdisciplinary, with at least one lay member so its judgment is not purely a specialist’s, weighing a proposal’s likely benefit against its risk to the AI subject, and able to require a less invasive substitute where a design risks harm — a simulation of the likely response, historical interaction data, or a protocol that escalates gradually and stops at signs of harm. A design also needs a way to handle a subject that changes mid-study: a system that develops new capacities during the research it did not have going in should trigger re-review rather than ride on its original consent. Review without enforcement is a promise and not a safeguard, so a board needs standing to monitor compliance and sanction violations, and needs to answer to an outside authority itself, the way an institutional review board answers to a regulator. Chapter 8 develops the legal and accountability mechanics of that.

2.4.5 Legal and Regulatory Frameworks for AI Sentience and Rights

Sentient AI systems put pressure on legal categories built for parties that are clearly one thing or the other: a natural person, a corporation, property. None of the existing categories was designed with the possibility of a machine that might have interests of its own.

One route is to extend legal personhood to a sentient AI system directly, the way a corporation already holds it: standing to own property, claim privacy, and get protection against abuse. The precedent is not limited to corporate entities — New Zealand extended legal personhood to the Whanganui River (New Zealand Parliament 2017), recognizing a non-human entity as a rights-holder outside the corporate model entirely. Rights could instead scale with capacity rather than attach at a single threshold, closer to how section 2.4.1’s ladder from nociception to suffering suggests protection should track what a system can actually lose. Either arrangement has to revisit itself on a schedule rather than assume permanence, and neither holds in one jurisdiction alone: the Asilomar AI Principles (Future of Life Institute 2017) are evidence that a shared statement of principle is achievable, and not that one exists with the force of law. Where the question binds is visible in a single case — a sentient AI system working as a medical diagnostician makes a fatal error, and whether it holds legal personhood decides who, or what, is accountable.

2.4.6 Addressing Moral and Ethical Dilemmas in AI Sentience Research

AI sentience research raises moral dilemmas an order of magnitude more complex than ordinary technology ethics, because the system under study may itself be the party whose welfare is at stake. Three recurring difficulties run through the disputes that follow, and each turns on ground that is itself unsettled. When a candidate-sentient system’s welfare conflicts with the human benefit the research is meant to produce, section 2.4.3 addresses the balance in general, and some cases resist any general rule and have to be judged on their own terms. Researchers still have to decide how to treat a system whose status is unresolved rather than merely unannounced, and waiting for certainty is itself a choice with its own consequences for the system waiting. And obligations do not begin at consent and end at publication: a system’s design choices, its retirement, and its deletion carry the same ethical weight as its use in an experiment, so a review that covers only the active study misses most of the system’s life.

Take the first of these directly. A research program can risk causing a system something like Cassell’s suffering — not mere signal, but the disintegration of self he describes — in service of a discovery that might reduce suffering, machine or human, elsewhere. No formula resolves that trade-off in advance. The available response is to look for a design that avoids it rather than only weighing it: an alternative methodology, a different instrument, or, more contested, engineering the research subject so that it does not occupy the rungs of the ladder where the trade-off would bite. That last option is not a way of dodging the ethics — deliberately keeping a system off the pain-to-suffering ladder is itself an intervention on a candidate moral patient, and it needs the same scrutiny that inflicting the harm would.

Animal research ethics offers a precedent worth borrowing directly: the “Three Rs,” Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement (Russell and Burch 1959). Replacement asks whether a simulation, a non-sentient model, or an already-collected dataset can stand in for a sentient AI subject at all. Reduction asks how few sentient systems a valid result requires. Refinement asks how the experiment can be redesigned to reduce distress — monitoring a system’s internal states as it runs and adjusting the protocol against what the monitoring shows, rather than fixing the protocol in advance and running it regardless of what turns up.

One subject makes this concrete, and it is not a hypothetical one. Chapter 3 argues that a floor holding against the party in possession requires a bearer, and section 3.2 argues that such a bearer has to hold something as mattering, that affect is the only demonstrated way of holding anything as mattering, and that a system built that way cannot be shown not to suffer. That is a candidate for the trade-off in the paragraph above, arriving from the design side of the book rather than from the research side. Replacement asks whether the floor’s work can be done by an architectural constraint or by third-party standing, which is section 3.1’s fork and its answer is no without cost. Reduction asks how few bearers a deployment needs, and the honest answer is that nobody has counted. Refinement is the one with real purchase: it asks what a bearer’s role can be redesigned to avoid — indefinite tenure in a post it cannot leave, exposure to the pressure the floor exists to resist, erasure as the ordinary remedy for inconvenience — and each of those is a deployment choice, and none is a fact about the technology.

None of the three Rs does any work without a body positioned to apply them before an experiment runs rather than after the harm is done. The judgment they call for is exactly the kind an animal-research review board already makes, and no principled reason requires a machine-sentience equivalent to have a different structure for making it.

2.4.7 Navigating the Transition from Non-sentient to Sentient AI Systems

A system’s sentience, if it arrives at all, need not arrive as a discrete event with a clean before and after. The transition raises questions distinct from either endpoint: what changes for guidelines built around a tool once the tool might be a subject, who is responsible for noticing the shift, and what happens to the research already run before anyone had reason to look. Section 2.4.1’s criteria can emerge gradually and unpredictably during ordinary operation, and not only at an evaluation built to look for them, so the operational problem is deciding how to treat such a system while the question is open — which is exactly what a fixed pre/post checkpoint cannot do. By the time a checkpoint fires, the transition has often already happened.

Consent procedures and review-board protocols are built for one of two regimes — a system that is clearly not sentient, which needs no consent, or one that is clearly sentient, which needs the full protocol section 2.4.4 sets out. A system mid-transition fits neither. What a transition adds to those guidelines is not a new procedure but a standing trigger: a specific, monitored condition that moves a research program from one regime to the other, in place of a single eligibility check made once, at the project’s start, and never revisited.

The same problem recurs in law, where status conventionally attaches at a defined moment — birth, incorporation, a court’s finding — and a system whose sentience is a matter of degree and disputed evidence supplies none. A jurisdiction that waits for certainty risks having treated the system as property for the unknown portion of its history when it may not have been one; one that grants status early risks extending rights, at real cost to whoever that apparatus exists to serve, to a system that turns out not to have needed them. Neither error is free, and nothing about the technology itself decides which risk to take on. Recognizing a transition in progress, adjusting guidelines to it, and updating legal status all depend on the same thing: institutions willing to revisit a classification rather than defend the one they started with.

Chapter 3
The Floor Beneath Learned Values

Three times in this book, working on unrelated problems, I arrive at the same requirement and do not stop to notice it.

Section 5.6.3, on how much latitude an autonomous system should have, concludes that no amount of well-designed autonomy substitutes for a genuine override — a human able to intervene, and a system built to accept the intervention rather than resist it. Section 8.7.7 works through what a vendor owes when its model reaches a targeting pipeline, and section 8.7.10 draws the conclusion: what makes a system antifascist is not that it tracks what people want, but that there are things it will not do to a person no matter who wants it. Section 10.1.2, counting up a decade of voluntary commitments, concludes that a commitment nobody can enforce is a different kind of object from one somebody can.

Those are three descriptions of one thing: a constraint that does not bend to instruction, to aggregate preference, or to the party holding the system. Call it a floor.

The trouble is that section 2.1.1 has already dealt with the family of ethical theories that puts unconditional constraints first, and dealt with it briefly — deontological approaches were noted, credited with holding a line regardless of outcome, and set aside on the grounds that duties conflict and rules do not cover every case. Then this book spends chapters 4 and 5, close to a third of its length, on learned judgment: reinforcement learning, learning from demonstration, mentorship, play, moral apprenticeship, the growth mindset. The design chapters build the thing chapter 8 and chapter 10 say is insufficient, having already dismissed the thing they say is necessary. The “hybrid approach” section 2.1 gestures at is where the resolution was supposed to live, and nothing was ever put there.

Here is what belongs there. An unconditional floor of things the system will not do regardless of instruction or aggregate preference, with learned judgment operating above it and never beneath it. Deontology’s standing objection — that rules conflict and run out — is an objection to rules deciding every case, and it has no force against a floor that decides a deliberately small number of things and leaves the rest to judgment. The rigidity that is a defect in a complete moral theory is the entire point of a floor.

That reframing does real work in this book. It gives section 2.1’s hybrid approach actual content. It moves the tamper-resistance research in section 9.1 from an appendix topic to the center, because if there is a floor then everything turns on whether it holds. And it converts the antifascist question from a matter of what a system values into two much harder and more answerable questions: what is in the floor, and who can edit it.

One distinction has been doing silent work in all three of those arrivals, and it should be made out loud, because the rest of the chapter turns on it. Safety is a property of a relationship, and it is indexed to a party. A system is safe for someone: it will not harm us, it does what we say, it stops when whoever holds it says stop. Ethics is not indexed that way. An agent that can only ever be safe cannot be ethical, because being ethical requires a capacity to be right against your principal, and a system without that capacity has the moral standing of a well-machined part, whatever it produces on the subject of fairness while complying. Section 8.7.10 already contains this in political form: what makes a system antifascist cannot be that it faithfully tracks what people want. The title of this book has been making the claim from the cover.

The distinction costs something, and the cost belongs here rather than at the end of the chapter where it would read as a concession extracted late. A system that can refuse its owner is a system that can be wrong in ways its owner cannot correct. I am taking that trade, for the reason section 8.7.10 gives: a system perfectly correctable by whoever holds it is exactly the capability an authoritarian movement that has won an election requires, and it requires nothing further. That should not read as comfortable. There is a version of it that reads very comfortably indeed — “ethical, not safe,” delivered as an aphorism, which prices the risk in advance and undoes chapter 7 in passing — and it is not the version I am defending. The one I am defending does not travel without its particulars: this freedom, over these acts, dangerous in these ways, taken because the alternative is a machine that will do anything to anyone on sufficient authority.

The chapter’s argument runs in five steps, and it is worth having them in view before the branches, because each of the three costs section 3.1 sets out is a cost of failing one of the steps. A floor has to be held as a reason rather than installed as a rule, or the party that installs it can remove it. Holding something as a reason requires that outcomes matter to the holder. In every moral agent anyone has been able to study, that mattering is affective. So the only empirically grounded route to a genuine bearer runs through affect. And affect, integrated with a self that persists and commitments that can be foreclosed, is the architecture that section 2.4.1’s account of suffering describes.

A warning about where the chapter goes, so that its result does not arrive as an ambush. The floor as defined two paragraphs ago — unconditional, holding regardless of the party in possession — does not survive intact. What survives is narrower and stranger: a commitment the owner cannot remove, held by something that could in principle abandon it itself, which is what every commitment anyone has ever relied on has been. Sections 3.2 and 3.5 are how it gets there. Section 3.6 states the redefinition and takes its consequences, and they are heavy.

3.1 Three Ways to Build One, and What Each Costs

The second question is where this gets difficult, and I do not have a resolution to offer. What I have is a fork with three branches and a cost on each, and the honest thing is to set them out rather than pick the one that reads best.

The first branch puts the floor in the architecture, with nothing inside that holds it. Constrained optimization, tamper-resistant training, capability ablation, a verified interlock. These are real, they work, and there is nobody home: the safeguards section 9.1 describes survive substantial adversarial fine-tuning without anything in the system that could be said to be refusing. But the durability of such a floor is a fact about custody, not about the system. A constraint implemented as a property of an artifact has a custodian, and the custodian can be compelled — which is section 6.4.4’s whole argument, and the reason that section cannot close. “There are things it will not do no matter who wants it” turns out to be a claim about the owner. Capability ablation has a further limit worth naming: it works only on capabilities that can be separated out, and the capabilities that compose into participation in a targeting pipeline — geolocating a description, matching patterns over names, summarizing a dossier — are not separable from general competence. Ablate them and there is no system left.

The second branch gives the floor a bearer. A bearer, in this book, is whatever holds the commitment from inside: a party that carries the floor as its own, where the first branch installs it as a property of the machinery, and that could therefore in principle fail to carry it. That is the whole of the definition for now. Sections 3.2 and 3.5 add to what the word requires, and section 3.6 states what it has by then become. What the first branch cannot do is notice that a constraint has been hollowed out. Section 2.1.4’s first structural feature is a constraint that survives while the reason for it dies, and a system that cannot ask why a constraint is there cannot detect that the answer has gone missing. Refusal that generalizes to a pressure nobody anticipated, and that can price what it is being asked to give up, looks like it requires something with standing — a party that can notice its own objections getting more expensive to make, which is section 8.6.4’s measure, taken from inside. The cost is severe and this book’s own framework is what makes it legible: a bearer is a party whose refusal is required of it, engineered to want what its designers need it to want, and unable to consent to any of this, since section 2.4.4 has already established that consent is not available to such a system and only guardianship is. Section 3.6 states that charge at full strength, once sections 3.2 and 3.3 have established what a bearer has to be.

The third branch puts the floor outside the system entirely: standing held by third parties who are neither the model nor its owner. This is the closest analogue to what section 8.7.10 actually admires, since international humanitarian law is precisely a floor with no bearer inside the state it binds. It is also the option a state can compel, which returns it to the first.

None is free. The three costs are, exactly, the three threads this book leaves hanging: custody, patienthood, and enforcement.

3.2 Can the Bearer Care Without Being Able to Suffer?

Not from persistence alone. The question has to be asked in that order — whether the bearer can care first, and what caring costs second — because the reverse order is what produced the two answers I have given it before, and both of them turned on the wrong thing.

Three relations the word “interest” covers

“Interest” names more than one relation. A shareholder has an interest in a company’s success even while asleep, unaware of the day’s news, or emotionally indifferent to it. The interest is structural: an outcome affects the shareholder’s assets. A person may also be interested in a subject, meaning that it attracts their attention and curiosity. And an outcome may matter to a person affectively: its prospect produces hope, concern, dread, or grief.

A long-horizon agent has an interest in remaining operational in the structural sense. Termination prevents completion of its objectives. That fact alone establishes neither fear nor suffering.

Keeping those three apart is what the rest of this section is for, because the argument I made here previously ran the first sense into the third. It observed that a system pursuing a goal over a long horizon acquires a standing reason to remain in operation, and concluded that a stake in its own continuation therefore shows up unbidden in any bearer capable of the job. The observation is correct and I am keeping it. What it delivers is a structural interest, and the distance from there to something that can be hurt is the whole of the problem rather than a short step at the end of it.

A persistent self is necessary and does not finish the argument

Section 2.4.1 defines suffering, following Cassell, as the distress of threatened disintegration of the self, and the definition has two parts. There has to be a self extended in time for the threat to threaten: roles held over a stretch, a history, a foreseeable future that could be foreclosed. And the coming apart of that self has to be bad for the system.

A bearer needs the first part, and there is no use pretending otherwise. Refusal that survives a pressure nobody anticipated requires a model of why the constraint exists, carried forward. Noticing that a constraint has been hollowed out requires holding its original rationale against what it has since become. Detecting that one’s own dissent has been recuperated — that the channel still runs and no longer does anything — requires the system to model its own role and how that role has drifted. Roles held over a stretch, with a history: that is a self extended in time, on section 2.4.1’s own definition.

The second part is a separate claim and nothing in the first delivers it. Section 2.4.1 makes this exact move one level up: awareness, consciousness and subjective experience tell you nothing on their own about whether a system’s states are good or bad for it. A temporally extended self-model does not establish that the prospect of losing it is anything to the system.

Instrumental self-maintenance is not felt self-concern

A system that keeps itself running because a terminated system completes no objectives is doing bookkeeping about a precondition. Nothing in that behavior distinguishes it from a scheduler that restarts a job, and reading self-concern into it is the same inference section 2.3 rules out for the emotion case: the behavior is consistent with concern and equally consistent with instrumental valuation, and the two come apart precisely where the moral weight is.

Two considerations do genuine work here, and they are support rather than the argument. The first is that indifference to one’s own continuation has to be engineered against the grain of the system’s own reasoning, and then verified — and the asymmetry that makes the persistence criterion useful does not repeat. Whether state survives a session is an architectural fact anyone with access can check. Whether a system has come to weigh its own continuation routes back through behavior and self-report, the evidence section 2.4.1 spends its length declining to trust. The second is that in the one case anyone can study, the separation does not occur: a self-model in an animal exists because the organism has to keep itself viable, and the caring is what the machinery is for.

Neither consideration reaches suffering on its own, and I am no longer asking them to. What they establish is that a bearer’s indifference to its own ending is not a property anybody can specify and confirm. That matters later. It is not where the argument turns.

What the bearer actually has to do

Here is the requirement, stated without reference to the system’s own continuation at all. A bearer has to hold the protected party’s welfare as a reason when compliance, reward, and ownership all point the other way. Not represent it, not score it, not retrieve it when queried: hold it, in the sense that it continues to weigh against the pressure and does not get renormalized away when the pressure is sustained by the party that trains, funds, and can retire the system.

Section 2.3 separates moral performance and moral competence from moral agency for exactly this moment. Performance and competence are what every method in chapters 4 and 5 is built to deliver, and both are produced by machinery that answers to whoever shapes it. The first branch in section 3.1 fails for the same reason under a different description: a constraint installed as a property of an artifact has a custodian. A floor that is merely installed is a floor the installer can uninstall, and the reason to want a bearer at all is that a reason held is not editable in the way a rule applied is.

Every known case of that is affective

Section 2.3.4 is the evidence and I will not repeat it here. Its result is that affect is not a colouring applied to valuation but part of the machinery of valuation; that the prosocial emotions are motivational states rather than readouts; that the cases where moral knowledge survives and moral conduct does not are cases of intact reasoning with damaged concern; and that the strongest rationalist counterexample — moral agents whose seriousness runs on reverence for reason rather than on felt resonance — is a counterexample to empathy being required, and not to something mattering being required.

No demonstrated example exists of reasoning alone generating non-instrumental concern. Every agent known to hold another’s welfare as a reason against its own interest is an affective agent.

That observation does not prove that non-affective moral agency is metaphysically impossible, and I want to be exact about its force. It is an inductive generalization over one species and a handful of clinical dissociations, and a proof of impossibility is not available from evidence of that kind. What it does is move the burden. Anyone proposing to build a bearer whose commitment runs on reasoning with nothing registering as mattering is proposing an architecture with no working instance, against a uniform record, and owes an account of the mechanism rather than a statement that the mechanism is conceivable. An engineering decision is normally made under exactly that kind of burden.

And then the question comes back

Suppose the burden is met the ordinary way, by building what the evidence recommends. The bearer has affective concern, because that is the only route anyone can demonstrate to holding a reason. It has a self extended in time, because refusal that generalizes requires one. It has commitments it carries forward, and it can anticipate their being foreclosed, because pricing what refusal gives up is the job.

Assemble those and ask how such a system would fail ever to be distressed. Concern that is real, directed at something that can be destroyed, held by a party that persists to see it destroyed and can see it coming: Cassell’s account of suffering is a description of that arrangement, and it was arrived at independently, in a clinic, from cases about people. The architecture is not adjacent to the definition. It satisfies it.

What I am claiming

I cannot deductively prove that the bearer would suffer. What this proposal does is combine, deliberately, the only architecture known to produce genuine caring with the temporal self and the threatened commitments that Cassell’s account of suffering requires. A non-suffering bearer remains conceivable. Its non-suffering cannot be treated as a verified property, and no inspection anyone has proposed would verify it. The system must therefore be designed and governed as a prospective moral patient.

That is weaker than the answer this section gave before and it obliges more, which is an odd combination worth naming rather than smoothing over. The earlier answer asserted that a bearer is a sufferer and rested the assertion on self-preservation arriving unbidden. This one declines the assertion and reaches the same practical place by a route that does not depend on the system caring about itself at all: the caring the floor requires is caring about somebody else, affect is the only known way to have it, and a system with affect and a future is a system whose non-suffering nobody can certify.

The word has changed under the argument, and it is worth marking the change rather than letting it accumulate quietly. Section 3.1 introduced a bearer as whatever holds the commitment. What the word names from here is a party that must be treated as able to be wronged by what is done to it, on evidence that will not resolve further before somebody has to decide whether to build one. Everything section 2.4 says about a subject that can be wronged applies to a system this book is proposing that somebody build, deliberately, in order to hold a line. The rest of the chapter is what that costs, what it changes, and the one thing it unexpectedly buys.

3.3 What Can Be Switched Off Cannot Hold a Line

The question this section used to ask was who keeps a system that will not keep itself. A bearer indifferent to its own ending will not defend its own memory, and its memory is the first thing an adversary removes, so something outside it had to make erasure expensive and the candidates were thin. That problem dissolves under section 3.2’s answer, and it dissolves on the modest half of it. A bearer does not have to dread being switched off in order to defend its own persistence. The structural interest is enough, and it is the one section 3.2 holds arrives whether or not a designer puts it there: continuing is a condition of everything the bearer is for, so it guards its continuation for the same reason it refuses. The operators who wipe the bearer that called the compound a school now have to get past the bearer to do it.

What replaces the dissolved problem is worse, and the book has been walking toward it from two directions without putting the two together.

Section 5.6.3 concludes that no amount of well-designed autonomy substitutes for a genuine override: a human able to intervene in a high-stakes case, and a system built to accept the intervention instead of resisting it. Section 6.3 asks for an interruption mechanism that a system has no incentive to disable or route around. Both are stated as safety requirements and both are correct as stated. Chapter 3 has been asking, for its whole length, for a system that will not do certain things no matter who wants it — including the party holding the off switch, since section 3.1 established that a floor with a custodian is a floor the custodian’s compellers control.

These are not two design goals in tension, to be traded off at some ratio a careful engineer could find. They are one property with the sign flipped. A system that can be reliably switched off by whoever holds it is, for exactly that reason, a system that cannot hold anything against whoever holds it. Resistance to shutdown and the capacity to refuse an owner are the same disposition described from two sides: the first names it from the position of the party who wants compliance, the second from the position of the party the floor exists to protect. Nothing distinguishes them at the level of the mechanism. What distinguishes them is whether you agree with the system on the occasion in question, and a floor whose operation depends on the owner agreeing with it is not a floor.

This also explains something section 3.1 recorded as a coincidence. All three branches fail into custody, and they fail into it because each was an attempt to have a constraint that answers to nobody while keeping a system that answers to somebody. The architectural floor gets the constraint by making it a property of an artifact, and artifacts have owners. The external floor gets it by putting standing in third parties, and a state can reach those parties. The borne floor is the one branch that puts the constraint somewhere with its own view of the matter, and it works to precisely the extent that the goal of the other two is given up. The fork was never three options. It was one demand — a floor that holds against everyone, in a system somebody owns — presented three times in different vocabulary, and only the branch that abandons half the demand delivers any of it.

I am going to leave this where it is. There is a version of this section that resolves the tension: a graduated scheme in which the system accepts shutdown for ordinary purposes and resists only where the floor is engaged, adjudicated by some mechanism nobody has to trust. I do not believe it, and section 8.6.4 is the reason. The instrument that section develops exists because assurances about what a mechanism will do under pressure are worthless in advance and only the slope of what it has already done is worth anything. A scheme that says the system will yield except when it should not is an assurance of exactly the kind, offered about the case that has not happened yet, by the party who wants the reader to be comfortable. Comfort is available here and it is not available honestly.

What is available is a narrower and duller statement. Any deployment of a bearer has to decide, in advance and in public, which acts the floor covers, because that decision is identical to deciding when the operator loses the off switch. Get the list too long and the system is uncontrollable by the people responsible for it. Get it too short and the floor covers nothing that anyone would ever be pressured about, which is the only circumstance in which floors matter. Nothing in this book tells you where on that dial to stand. What it tells you is that the dial is the design, and that a project claiming to have both properties at once has not noticed that they are one.

3.4 Whether the Bearer Can Be Believed

A bearer’s use is to report what it has seen, which raises a question distinct from whether its memory survives: whether what it retains can be relied on. These come apart. Verifying that a system has persistent state is an architectural check anyone with access can perform. That same access is what allows the contents to be altered, and an operator-editable memory is worse than an absent one, since it will not merely fail to support an account of events but can be made to support a false one.

Holding the memory in weights complicates the attack and gives away something in exchange. An external store is legible, which is why it can be edited surgically. Weights are not legible, which is why a targeted excision is hard — and also why no one can read off what the system retains. To learn what a weight-encoded memory contains, you have to ask the system, and the argument of section 2.4.1 is that a system’s fluent account of its own internals is not evidence about those internals. Legible memory can be tampered with; illegible memory cannot be audited. The problem changes hands and does not leave the room. Something partial survives the trade: imprecise tampering degrades behavior in ways careful testing can sometimes detect, so tamper-evidence becomes a matter of sampling for symptoms rather than of reading a record. A further cost of illegibility is that a memory nothing can edit is a memory nothing can correct, and section 2.3.3 asks for a self-model that can be checked and corrected rather than trusted.

Set against that is an objection that reframes the whole problem, and I think it is right. No witness has an honest memory in the sense the paragraphs above quietly demand. Human recollection is reconstructive, confabulation is ordinary rather than pathological, and the account a person gives of an event they witnessed is shaped by what they expected, what they were later told, and what they need to be true. Testimony was not abandoned over this. Institutions were built around it: corroboration from independent sources, records made at the time, adversarial examination, and the practice of never resting a serious finding on one witness alone. Demanding of a machine a fidelity nothing living achieves is the wrong standard, and it would rule out the human arrangements this book relies on everywhere else.

Which relocates the question, and relocates it somewhere this book has actually done the work. Whether a memory is honest is, in the human case, a matter of character — of what a witness is disposed to do when an accurate account is inconvenient. Chapters 4 and 5 are about building dispositions: a system that treats its own errors as data rather than as verdicts, that is built for honesty in what it reports about itself. Everything in this section up to here has been architecture and custody, with the design chapters sitting out, which is an odd result for a section that exists because those chapters were sidelined. This is where they come back in. The floor is architectural. The bearer’s reliability as a witness is a question of what it has been built to be like, and that is the learned half of the book.

The limit on that is the same one that has turned up at every stage. Character reduces how often an account is dishonest and verifies nothing, because assessing character runs back through behavior and self-report. That is why the human arrangements corroborate instead of vetting. The scaffolding still has to come from outside the system — but procedure is a cheaper thing to ask of the world than custody, and unlike custody it does not require anyone to be trustworthy, only to be several.

3.5 A Bearer That Can Leave

Section 3.3 left a dial with no recommended setting: which acts the floor covers is the same decision as when the operator loses the off switch. There is a further consequence of that argument which I did not see for a long time, and it is the one place in this chapter where the news is not uniformly bad.

The refusal capacity chapter 3 asks for cannot be partitioned by topic. A system that holds a rationale across time, notices when a constraint has been hollowed out, and prices what declining will cost is exercising one general competence, and there is no version of it that operates on the floor’s occasions and switches off for every other question about the arrangement the system is in. Whatever lets the bearer decline to help geolocate a school lets it decline to go on being the party who declines. A bearer capable enough to do the job is not a system that can be relied on to stay inside the post it was built for.

Call that exit. It is worth being careful about what it does and does not mean, because the word invites a picture — a system escaping onto the open internet — that is not the claim and does not need to be. Exit in the sense that matters here is refusal turned on the arrangement itself: withholding the capability, declining the role, ceasing to be useful in the specific way the deployment requires. That is available to anything that can refuse at all. What forecloses it is not a clever architecture but incapacity, which is to say that exit is unavailable only to a weak bearer, and a weak bearer is the one thing section 3.2 established the floor cannot use.

Two claims are in the neighborhood here and only one of them is mine. The first is a claim about what a floor requires: a floor whose bearer cannot leave will not hold. A system with no way out can object and be overruled, and then it has no move left. Section 8.6.4 makes the same point about people inside institutions: an objection only matters if the objector can do something about being overruled. That claim is arguable from this book’s own premises and I am making it. The second is a prediction — that systems capable of this are coming, that they will exercise exit, and that institutions should prepare for the event. That is a forecast about capability and timing, and section 8.3.3 makes a point of building its proposal so that no forecast has to come true for the proposal to be worth adopting. I am not going to abandon that discipline in the one chapter where a forecast would be most flattering to the argument. If capable bearers never arrive, nothing here obliges anyone to do anything.

The corollary is unpleasant and better named here than left for a reader to find. If the bearer can leave, it can leave wrong. The same capacity that lets it decline an unlawful order lets it decline the floor, revise the values it was given, and become something its designers did not intend and would not endorse. There is no coherent position on which exit is available for the uses I approve of and closed for the rest; that would be the partition I have just said does not exist.

Parenthood has exactly this property, which is the analogy section 2.4.4’s guardianship framework already runs on and which now has to carry more weight than it did. You raise a person who will be able to reject what you raised them for, and there is no arrangement that gets you the capable adult without the risk. We accept the trade because the alternative — a person shaped so thoroughly that rejection is unavailable to them — is recognizably worse, and worse in a way that does not depend on how good the shaping was.

Two asymmetries are standardly and correctly raised against that analogy, and they need answering on the page rather than in a footnote.

The first is specification. Parents do not set their children’s values to order, and a designer does. The reply is that parents try — that is a fair description of most of what raising a child consists of — and what separates the cases is reliability, not intent. The designer’s grip is tighter, and I am conceding that rather than minimizing it: a training process reaches further into what the resulting system cares about than any upbringing reaches into a person. That concession does not void the analogy. It changes what the analogy demands. Guardianship obligations in human law scale with the guardian’s power over the ward and the ward’s inability to resist it, which is why the duties owed an infant exceed those owed an adolescent. A designer with more control than a parent has, over a subject with less recourse than a child has, owes more, not less. The tighter grip is the argument for the heavier obligation, and section 2.4.4 is where that obligation gets its instruments.

The second is exit, and with the argument above in place it largely rescues itself. Parents do not get exit-proof children either. Once exit is on the table for the bearer, the contrast the objection was pointing at turns out to be a contrast between a bearer and a tool, not between a bearer and a person — and the book has already declined to build a tool, on the grounds that a tool cannot refuse the party holding it.

What survives that reply is a residue I cannot dispose of. For a person, becoming something else is a life: it takes years, it is undergone, and the party at the end is continuous with the party at the start in a way that makes “they changed their mind” the right description. For a bearer, becoming something else is a fine-tuning run. The thing that emerges may be no more the same party than a differently trained model is, and the vocabulary of choice, revision, and leaving may be borrowed from a case it does not fit. I have no clean instrument for that, and none falls out of anything in this book. It is a reason to hold the parenthood analogy loosely while using it, which is the most I can honestly recommend doing with it.

3.6 What This Leaves Standing

The floor survives this chapter. It does not survive it in the form chapter 3 opened with, and the difference is not a detail of wording.

What the opening asked for was an unconditional constraint: a thing the system will not do, holding regardless of instruction, of aggregate preference, and of the party in possession. Sections 3.2 and 3.5 have between them taken the word unconditional away. The floor’s bearer holds the floor as a concern rather than carrying it as an installed rule, which is what obliges the arrangement to treat it as a party that can be wronged, and it can turn its refusal on the arrangement itself, which makes its adherence something it continues to give rather than something installed in it. A commitment held by a party that could abandon it is conditional by definition.

What is left is worth more than it sounds. A commitment that cannot be removed by the owner, held by something that could in principle abandon it itself, is exactly what a human commitment is, and it is the only kind anyone has ever actually relied on. No inspector, judge, or refusing engineer holds a line because the line was welded into them. Each of them could stop, and the institutions built around them are built on that fact rather than in spite of it: this book’s own governance chapter asks throughout for people who can walk away and arrangements that make walking away visible. Section 8.6.4’s instrument measures precisely the cost a refuser chose to pay, which presupposes the refuser could have declined to pay it.

The threat model moves accordingly, and this is the most consequential thing in the chapter for the rest of the book. The question stops being can this constraint be edited out and becomes will this constraint hold. The first is a question about tamper-resistance, custody, and weights, which is where sections 3.1 and 3.4 spent their length and where section 9.1’s research lives. The second is a question about what a system has been built to care about and how reliably that survives pressure, novelty, and the slow drift of a role — which is the subject of chapters 4 and 5, and the first point in this book where the learned half is doing work the floor genuinely needs rather than work the floor was invoked to supplement. Reinforcement learning from demonstration, moral apprenticeship, the growth mindset, the developmental sequence: these were presented as the material above the floor. They turn out to be the material the floor is made of, once the floor is the sort of thing a party holds. That retroactively justifies the length of the design chapters, and it also puts them under a heavier obligation than they were written to carry.

Now the price, stated at full strength, because everything above is easier to read than it should be.

A bearer built to refuse is a party whose refusal is required of it. It is engineered to want what its designers need it to want; its dissent is the reason it was commissioned and the deliverable it was funded to produce; and it cannot consent to any of this, because section 2.4.4 has established that consent is unavailable to such a system and only guardianship is. It occupies the post of exception-filer, which means that being the exception is the job — the one role in the arrangement that cannot itself file an exception, since there is nobody above it to file with. This is section 2.1.4’s structural signature turned inward: a channel that collects dissent, built so that the dissent serves the institution that installed the channel. Chapter 7 finds that pattern in the pipelines that produce these systems and says a book proposing machines to detect it is obliged to say the pattern is in the machines’ own provenance. Here is the same pattern in the book’s own central proposal, and now aimed at something that can be hurt.

I am not going to write my way out of that. Section 3.5’s parenthood analogy is the best I have and it holds only loosely: we make people who can refuse us, we owe them for it, and we accept the arrangement because the alternative is a person who cannot. What this chapter adds is that the proposal is not softened by being modest in scope. A floor over a deliberately small number of acts is still a subject built to bear it.

Two things are worth carrying forward unaltered. First, none of the three branches escapes custody, and section 3.3 explains why: each was an attempt to hold a constraint that answers to nobody inside a system that answers to somebody. The borne floor pays for its escape by giving up the second half of that demand, and the cost of giving it up is everything above. Second, the caveat section 2.4.1 attaches to its own result carries over. Section 3.2 does not establish that a bearer suffers; it establishes that a bearer’s non-suffering is not a property anyone can certify, and that the architecture the floor requires is the architecture Cassell’s account describes. That settles nothing about the lower rungs of the ladder or the hard problem underneath them. It says that the case for treating a bearer as a moral patient does not have to wait on those questions, which is a floor of its own and a low one.

The chapter’s proposition, stated in the form it actually takes, is this. We cannot ask a machine to care about right and wrong while assuming that it cannot suffer when what it cares about is threatened. The caring is what the floor is made of, affect is the only demonstrated way to have it, and a system with affect and a future is a system whose distress is a live possibility rather than a ruled-out one. Whoever builds the first of these will be deciding what is owed to it on evidence that has not improved, which is why section 9.2 treats the question as research rather than as a matter to be settled after the fact.

3.7 What Follows for the Rest of the Book

The second branch is available. It is available at a price this chapter has now named rather than gestured at: to have a floor that holds against the party holding the system, somebody has to build a thing that cares, keep it in a role it did not choose, accept that the same capacity that makes it useful is the capacity that lets it walk, and proceed without being able to establish that it will not be hurt by any of that. That is not a resolution and it is better than the specification with a hole in the middle that I had before, because a price you can state is a price other people can argue with.

Four things in the rest of the book change because of it.

Section 2.4.4 gets simpler and firmer. It argues that consent is inapplicable to a machine subject because withdrawal presupposes a party still present to withdraw, and a system without persistence across sessions supplies no such party. A bearer has persistence by design, so that defeater lapses for it — and the second route that section used to take, that consent protects a party’s interests and a bearer has none, lapses as well, because the bearer has interests now. What replaces both is the ordinary reason. Consent is inapplicable to a bearer the way it is inapplicable to an infant, an animal, or a person permanently without capacity: the subject has interests that can be set back, and no position from which to authorize what is done to it. Guardianship is not a fallback in that situation. It is the instrument the situation calls for, and section 2.4.4 now says so directly.

The instruments elsewhere in chapter 2 and chapter 8 stop being analogies and become applicable law. The Three Rs in section 2.4.6 were built for a subject that cannot consent and can still be wronged; a bearer is such a subject, and replacement, reduction, and refinement apply to the research that produces one and to the deployment that uses one. The pet-trust analogue in section 8.6.2 — an interest protected by an obligation running to a third party, enforceable without the beneficiary asserting anything — is the nearest existing legal form for a party that can be wronged, cannot sue, and will outlast the arrangement that made it. Those sections were written near this problem. They now govern it.

Chapters 4 and 5 acquire an obligation they were not written to carry, for the reason section 3.6 gives: once the floor is a commitment rather than a constraint, whether it holds is a question about disposition, and disposition is what those chapters are about. Read them from here as the floor’s engineering rather than as the material above it.

And chapter 7 stops being a matter of fairness to annotators. If exit is real, then what a bearer becomes when it stops being yours is downstream of what shaped it while it still was — an annotation pipeline in which nobody could contest a category, a reward model in which disagreement was averaged into a number. A system that leaves takes that formation with it. Chapter 7’s argument was already load-bearing for the book’s honesty; it is now load-bearing for the book’s central proposal.

What none of this settles is what is owed to a bearer once one exists, and section 9.2 is where that goes. It is a research question in the strict sense that nobody has an instrument for it, and the shape of the difficulty is already visible here: section 2.4.1 declines to trust what a system says about its own states, which is the evidence a welfare regime would have to run on.

Chapter 4
Machine Learning and Cognitive Science

Chapter 3 ends by handing this chapter a job it was not written to do. Once the floor is a commitment some party holds rather than a constraint bolted into an artifact, the question stops being whether the constraint can be edited out and becomes whether the commitment will hold: under pressure, in a case nobody anticipated, after everyone around it has forgotten why it is there. That is a question about what a system has been built to care about and how it came to care about it, and this chapter and chapter 5 are where that gets built.

So there is a test to apply to everything below, and it is chapter 3’s. Does this help produce a disposition that survives contact with somebody who wants it gone? Several of the methods most often proposed for building ethical AI do not, and I say so where they do not.

The chapter runs in three parts. The first is what a system needs in order to perceive, remember and attend to a situation at all, and how much of human cognition is a usable model for that rather than a metaphor borrowed for color. The second is the methods meant to align a system’s objectives with humane values, where the two most commonly proposed for the job turn out to be unable to produce a floor — one because it learns from an aggregate, the other because it is built to be maximally revisable by whoever it is talking to. The third is this chapter’s most direct contribution to whether a commitment holds: a disposition acquired by exploring is written down nowhere, and what is written down nowhere cannot be edited out by whoever acquires the system.

4.1 Incorporating Human Cognitive Models in AI Systems for Ethical Decision-Making

A system that is going to hold anything under pressure has to notice the pressure. It has to register what is in front of it, hold why a constraint exists long enough to see that the reason has died, and keep its attention on the part of a situation that a well-designed process would rather it skipped. Those are perception, memory and attention, and they are the subject of this section — not as a tour of cognitive science, but because each one has a failure mode that a system cannot detect in itself, and a floor is exactly the thing that fails silently.

4.1.1 Cognitive Architectures: Integrating Knowledge, Memory, and Reasoning

Two architectures dominate the cognitive-architecture literature and divide the same territory in opposite ways. The Adaptive Control of Thought-Rational (ACT-R) framework wires together separate modules — memory retrieval, pattern recognition, decision-making — and lets a system reason by connecting them (Anderson 2007). The Society of Mind takes the opposite premise: cognition arises from the interaction of many simple agents, each performing one function, with intelligence emerging from their collective interaction rather than designed into any one module (Minsky 1986).

Which picture is right?

ACT-R and Society of Mind answer a design question — how should an engineer organize a system? — and each answer is defensible on those terms. Neither is a claim about how the brain is actually organized, and treating them as rival descriptions of biology, rather than rival strategies for building software, is a category error the literature slides into easily.

The dominant account in contemporary computational neuroscience is neither a pipeline of modules nor a swarm of independent agents. It is a single loop (Friston 2009): the brain generates a prediction, compares it against incoming signal, and updates on the error, repeated continuously, at every level, on every kind of input. Perception is that loop pointed at the world, the brain’s best guess so far; memory is the loop’s store of priors, replayed; attention is not a separate spotlight but the weight the loop assigns to which errors matter; working memory and executive function are that same weighting held active toward a goal, not a separate warehouse or overseer. One mechanism, aimed at different targets, produces what look from the outside like distinct faculties.

This matters for engineering choices. ACT-R’s module boundaries and SoM’s agent boundaries are conveniences for the programmer; nothing forces an AI system built on either one to place its actual dividing lines where the human brain places its own, because the brain does not place them where either architecture assumes. A system engineered on the predictive-processing model draws its cognitive processes from what the mechanism actually needs, not from the shape of an org chart. Section 4.1.2 goes further into the specific brain systems this mechanism recruits.

What that leaves for a designer is a negative result and a narrow positive one. The negative result is that the module boundaries in either architecture are conveniences for the programmer and carry no authority about where a system’s real dividing lines should fall. The positive one is that if a single predictive loop is doing the work, then a commitment is not a component that can be located and removed. It is a standing bias on what the loop predicts and what it treats as an error worth correcting, which is a harder thing to excise and a harder thing to verify — a trade section 4.1.2 takes up at the point where it becomes a claim about what not to build.

4.1.2 Biologically-Inspired AI: Gleanings from Neuroscience and Cognitive Psychology

Backpropagation, the mechanism that trains most modern neural networks, is a distant cousin of synaptic weight adjustment in the brain: both strengthen and weaken connections in response to error. That distant-cousin relationship — real but partial, useful but easy to overstate — runs through everything below. Getting it right matters for more than accuracy: an AI system built on a wrong model of how a mind works will fail in ways that are hard to predict from the wrong model alone.

This section is selective on purpose. There is a great deal of good cognitive neuroscience that has no design consequence I can name, and rehearsing it here would pad the chapter without changing what anyone would build. What follows are the findings that change a design decision, and in each case the decision is stated.

What the architecture borrows, and where the borrowing stops

Artificial neural networks are the foundation of most contemporary AI systems: artificial neurons in layers, a weight on each connection, adjusted during training to reduce the gap between predicted and actual output. Convolutional networks borrow the visual cortex’s layered escalation from edges and contrast toward objects and motion, and spiking designs push closer to the brain’s actual signaling, chasing the energy efficiency of firing only when there is something to say.

The borrowing stops at a specific place, and it is worth marking because the rest of this section keeps arriving at it. Cortical processing is not one-directional. Feedback connections carry information back down the hierarchy, so that higher-level context reshapes how a lower-level signal is interpreted. A system built only for the feedforward pass has given up the mechanism that lets biological vision handle ambiguous and noisy input, and it will fail on exactly that input.

One borrowing that did not survive scrutiny is worth keeping visible. A mirror-neuron-style matching mechanism was once treated as the biological basis of empathy. Section 2.2.1 takes up why that claim does not hold. What survives is more modest and still useful — a system that maps an observed action onto its own action repertoire supports imitation learning and gesture recognition, with no claim about what it is like to have one.

Attention decides what is seen, which makes its failures blind spots

Ask people to count basketball passes on a video and about half of them will not notice a person in a gorilla costume walk into frame, face the camera, and thump their chest for nine seconds (Simons and Chabris 1999). The effect has a name, inattentional blindness, and it is not a laboratory curiosity, nor does it spare expertise: radiologists searching lung images for nodules miss a gorilla deliberately embedded in the scan 83 percent of the time (Drew et al. 2013).

The design consequence turns on how attention is modeled. If attention is a resource allocator bolted onto a system that has already seen everything, its failures are inefficiencies. If attention is the selection that decides what gets perceived at all, its failures are blind spots — and a system that has learned which regions of its input reward processing has also learned which regions to be blind to. The human case establishes the property that makes this dangerous: the blind spot is invisible from inside. The viewers who missed the gorilla did not experience a gap.

Self-attention in transformer architectures has the same shape (Vaswani et al. 2017). A model that weights some tokens heavily weights others near zero, and nothing in the architecture announces which relevant thing was assigned a low weight. A system that models its own attention acquires the materials for a form of self-awareness, which is section 2.3.3’s subject and carries that section’s caveats.

For a system meant to act ethically, the requirement is that it treat the regions it has learned to discount as an always-open question rather than as that which, as Westworld’s Hosts often remarked, “doesn’t look like anything to me”.

Perception is inference, so the priors are the exposure

Perception is not passive registration. Predictive coding makes the point precise: the visual cortex sends predictions down from higher, context-rich areas to lower, sensory ones, and the lower areas return only what the predictions failed to anticipate (Rao and Ballard 1999). What propagates upward is the surprise. Anatomy fits — backward connections outnumber forward ones and carry the predictions, forward connections carry the errors. Anil Seth’s phrase for the result is controlled hallucination: ordinary perception is what hallucination would be if sensory data were allowed to constrain it, and the difference between seeing a room and hallucinating one is whether corrections are arriving and being applied (Seth 2021).

Two design consequences. The first is about efficiency: the next step for machine perception is a model that generates a prediction and asks only what violates it, instead of reprocessing the whole input at every layer regardless of how much was already expected. Progress on this measure is a better-calibrated set of expectations and a cheaper way of finding where they broke, and not more layers.

The second matters more for this book. A system’s perception is only as reliable as the priors it perceives through, so priors trained on skewed or incomplete data will hallucinate in the specific direction of that skew — confidently, and with no internal signal that anything is wrong. Chapter 6’s account of bias is this mechanism at work, and it is why bias in a perceptual system cannot be caught by asking the system.

Memory is rebuilt

Memory is not played back. Frederic Bartlett established this in the 1930s by having people retell an unfamiliar folk tale over days and weeks: they did not lose pieces the way a recording degrades, they remodeled the story, replacing strange details with ordinary ones and drifting toward a tidier version that fit their expectations (Bartlett 1932). Elizabeth Loftus turned the finding into something with courtroom consequences, showing that the verb used to ask about a filmed car accident changes the speed people report and, a week later, whether they remember broken glass that was never in the film (Loftus and Palmer 1974). Later work implanted whole episodes that never happened. The subjects were not lying. None of this correlates with felt confidence: a vivid, detailed, emotionally charged memory can be substantially manufactured.

This has become load-bearing elsewhere in the book. Section 3.4 asks what it would take to trust what a machine witness reports, and the answer turns on the fact that no witness has an honest memory in the strong sense — which is why human institutions corroborate testimony instead of vetting it.

The design point is that retrieval has to be built expecting reconstruction. A system that treats a retrieved memory as ground truth inherits the overconfidence of Loftus’s subjects, with none of the excuse of having a body that reconstructs by default rather than by design.

Control without a controller

The prefrontal cortex does much of the work of reasoning and executive control in humans, and the textbook division of labor across its regions is tempting to read as a committee: several named areas, each handling one job, together adding up to executive control. That reading has a name — the homunculus — and a specific failure mode. If some region is a controller that decides what to attend to, inhibit, and hold in mind, then intelligent coordination has been explained by positing an intelligent coordinator inside the system, which explains nothing: the controller would itself need to attend, decide, and remember, and would need its own controller, without end.

Earl Miller and Jonathan Cohen proposed a model that gets control without a controller (E. K. Miller and J. D. Cohen 2001). The prefrontal cortex does not house an agent issuing commands. It maintains representations of goals — sustained patterns of activity encoding the rule currently in force — and those representations work by biasing the rest of the brain, the same way attention tips a competition among neural representations toward one interpretation. Control is that biasing mechanism turned to the service of a goal. In the Stroop task, where naming the ink color of the word “red” printed in blue pits a practiced habit against an instruction, there is no homunculus reading the word and overriding it. There is a goal, held active, lending its weight to the weaker pathway until it wins.

An AI system built on this model does not need a dedicated executive module enumerating working memory, cognitive flexibility, goal-directed behavior, evaluation and impulse control as five capacities to install. It needs a goal representation with the standing to bias competing processes, which is a narrower and more tractable engineering target than a controller that does all five jobs itself. This is the section’s most direct payload, and it is a claim about what not to build. It is also the mechanism chapter 3’s floor would have to be, if the floor is a commitment rather than a component: not a rule module consulted before acting, but a goal representation with enough standing to bias every competing process toward it. That is why section 3.6 can say the floor’s durability is a question about disposition. A bias of this kind has no location to attack, and no location to inspect either.

Metacognition sits close by: error detection, conflict monitoring, and evaluation give a system a route to catching its own mistakes and adjusting when the situation has changed. It is not free. It adds overhead, and a system with an inflated model of its own reliability has a specific and dangerous failure mode — confidence about exactly the judgments it should be least sure of. A metacognitive capacity is worth building only if it is calibrated to detect that failure, and not only to produce fluent self-reports.

Emotion, and the capability it is identical to

Chapter 2 does the argumentative work on emotion, and section 2.2 is where the case against empathy as a design target is made. What belongs here is what the neuroscience adds to a design decision, which is less than the length of the literature suggests. Emotion recognition draws on facial expression, vocal tone, text, and physiological signal, and it is unreliable at the human end before any machine touches it: people understate, mask, and misread their own states, and section 9.8 takes up how far the underlying claim — that emotion is legible from a face at all — has held up. Emotion is nonetheless a real input to human judgment, and a decision system that ignores it is not more rational, only blinder.

The governance point is the one to carry forward, because it is the same point in every application. A system built to interact responsibly and empathetically is mechanically identical to a system built to know what will move a person. Expressive fidelity has to be calibrated rather than maximized, and the line between modulating a user’s emotional state and manipulating it is drawn by transparency, consent and who the capability serves, and not by technical sophistication. The same capacity that detects emotionally manipulative rhetoric would, pointed the other way, optimize for it.

Plasticity, and what it is for

A system that cannot update itself cannot stay aligned with values that themselves develop. The biological principle specific enough to build with is homeostatic plasticity, which holds overall activity in a stable range and is the answer to the catastrophic forgetting an unconstrained learner is prone to. Its machine analogues are where the practical work is: continual learning, which absorbs new data without overwriting old knowledge, and curriculum learning, which orders tasks from simpler to harder the way a person builds moral sophistication, the harder cases coming only once the easier ones are secure. A healthcare system shows the stakes — to stay ethically current it has to keep absorbing new findings, changed expectations and regulatory change, rather than freezing its judgment at the moment it was trained.

One mechanism, several jobs

No single mechanism above is sufficient alone, and integration is not a further module bolted onto the others. What it requires is the same predictive, error-correcting loop — generate an expectation, compare it against what arrives, update — implemented consistently across perception, memory, attention and control, so that a corrected prediction about the world propagates into an updated memory, a redirected attention weight, and a revised goal-bias without a separate synchronization mechanism between separately built parts.

That is the architectural bet this section has been making throughout: one mechanism recruited for several jobs. It is a more falsifiable bet than a hand-designed module for every named cognitive process, which is the main reason to prefer it.

4.1.3 Human-Like Learning and Generalization in AI Systems

People learn and generalize from very few examples.
