AI systems that approach this — through few-shot learning, transfer learning, and a developmental trajectory modeled on human cognitive growth — extend judgment to situations they were never explicitly trained on, instead of needing a full retraining cycle for every new context. What matters here is not the technique inventory, which changes yearly, but the evaluation problem underneath it. Section 4.2.4 takes the same difficulty up for transfer, where a floor carried into a setting it was not built for cannot tell that it has stopped applying.

Few-shot learning, and the evaluation problem underneath it

Few-shot learning aims at models that classify or predict accurately from a handful of examples. For an ethical AI system the appeal is direct: empathy, altruism, and ethical judgment would not need retraining from scratch for every new scenario, but could extend to a new case the way a person’s existing values apply to situations they have never seen. A system deployed in disaster recovery has to work from a handful of relevant precedents rather than a dataset built for the specific flood in front of it. A system built to flag authoritarian speech patterns has to extend to new phrasings and new languages without a corpus assembled in advance for every regime it might encounter. Large pretrained language models demonstrate the capacity at system scale, performing a task from a few examples in the prompt with no parameter update at all (Brown et al. 2020).

The problem this leaves is the one that matters for ethics, and it is an evaluation problem rather than a modeling one. A handful of examples is easy to overfit, moral dilemmas do not arrive in clean representative sets, and telling whether a system’s few-shot ethical judgment actually generalized — or merely matched surface features of the examples it saw — is genuinely hard. Building that test is not a machine-learning task alone. It needs people trained in ethics to say what the system was supposed to have learned.

Developmental trajectory

Human development moves through recognizable stages, and a system built for empathy and altruism can follow a comparable arc rather than being assembled at once: perception and elementary problem-solving first, then the integration of those separate skills into something that guides a decision rather than only labels an input, then specialization to a particular setting and the people in it.

That ordering is borrowed carefully, and chapter 5 says how carefully. Section 5.1.1 sets out what the developmental stage theories will and will not carry — an order is not a mechanism, and nothing here should be read as a claim that a system must pass through these stages or that arriving at the last one is maturity.

4.2 Aligning AI Systems with Humane Values and Antifascist Principles

This is the section where a book like this one is expected to list the techniques by which a system’s objectives come to track humane values, and where chapter 3 makes the list read differently. Three of the four methods below learn what to value from someone: from a reward a designer wrote, from behavior a demonstrator produced, from labels an annotator applied. A floor is the part that has to hold when that someone changes their mind or is replaced by somebody worse.

So each method is taken twice — for what it does, and for whether what it does could produce a commitment that survives its own teacher. Reinforcement learning makes the reward the whole of what a system wants, which puts everything on who writes it. Inverse and cooperative inverse reinforcement learning treat what to want as an open question the human answers, which is the most corrigible design available and, by section 3.3’s argument, the least able to hold a line. Supervised learning learns from labeled cases, which is an aggregate, and section 3.1 has already established what an aggregate cannot deliver. Transfer learning is asked in this book to carry an antifascist judgment into cases it has not seen, and the evidence that it can is thinner than the request.

None of that makes the methods useless. It locates them, in section 2.3’s vocabulary: each method below is a way of producing moral performance, and the better ones reach moral competence, which is a real achievement and the right target for most of what gets deployed. None reaches the third thing. The reason is the same in each case — what a system learns from a party is what that party can make it unlearn — and it is why they are how the judgment above the floor gets built and none of them is how the floor gets built.

4.2.1 Reinforcement Learning and Value Alignment for Antifascist AI

Reinforcement learning trains an agent by rewarding what a designer wants and penalizing what they do not, and the agent’s values are then whatever maximizes the reward. That is the method’s strength and the reason it cannot supply a floor: everything the system cares about traces back to a signal somebody wrote and somebody can rewrite.

Two failures follow from that structure rather than from bad engineering, and both are documented. The first is reward hacking, where an agent finds something that pays out without doing the intended job — a system built to flag propaganda that learns to flag everything, because indiscriminate flagging scores as well as discrimination and is easier to produce. The second is that a reward written for one setting does not carry: an agent trained to cooperate in a game does not thereby cooperate at work, and alignment demonstrated on a benchmark is a claim about the benchmark.

The standard repairs both keep the structure intact. Reward modeling has people rank candidate behaviors against each other and fits a reward to the rankings, so the signal comes from a population instead of one author. Regularization writes the constraint into the objective, penalizing a class of behavior rather than waiting to reward its absence, which is how a recommender is pushed away from the engagement-maximizing equilibrium that produces filter bubbles. Both are improvements and neither changes who holds the pen. A ranked population can be re-sampled and a penalty term can be set to zero, by the party running the training, in an afternoon. Chapter 7 is what happens to the ranked population specifically, when the disagreement it was collected to represent is averaged into a number.

One tension in the method is a moral question wearing a hyperparameter’s clothes, and it belongs here rather than in every paradigm that meets it. A learner has to exploit what it already knows and explore what it does not. In a treatment planner, exploration means offering a patient something less established and exploitation means declining to look. Safe exploration — searching inside stated constraints rather than checking for violations afterward — is the technique that makes the trade explicit, and section 6.3.3 takes it up as a safety practice. What matters here is that the balance point is not tuned to performance. It is where a system decides whose interests bear the cost of its learning, and that is the same kind of decision as deciding what the floor covers: made in advance, by somebody, and better made in public.

4.2.2 Inverse Reinforcement Learning and Cooperative Inverse Reinforcement Learning in Altruistic AI

Inverse reinforcement learning runs section 4.2.1’s method backwards. Instead of taking the reward as given and learning the behavior, it takes the behavior as given and infers the reward that best explains it — watching a driver’s speed choices, following distances and reactions to weather, and recovering the priorities behind them rather than being handed a rulebook. Cooperative inverse reinforcement learning, formalized by Dylan Hadfield-Menell and colleagues (Hadfield-Menell et al. 2016), goes one step further: the system treats the human’s true objective as unknown, holds its own estimate as provisional, and keeps revising it through the interaction rather than fixing it at training time.

That last property is why CIRL is attractive, and it is also why this book cannot build a floor on it. A system that treats what it should want as permanently open, to be settled by whoever it is interacting with, is the most corrigible design in this chapter. Section 3.3 argues that corrigibility and the capacity to hold a line are one property with the sign flipped — a system reliably steerable by whoever holds it is, for that reason, a system that cannot hold anything against them. CIRL is that argument in its purest engineering form. Uncertainty about the objective is exactly what makes a system defer, and deference to the party in possession is what a floor exists to interrupt.

The practical version of the problem is narrower and does not depend on chapter 3 being right. Both methods learn from demonstrations, so both inherit whoever demonstrated: a narrow set of drivers, a narrow set of households, a narrow set of decisions that somebody had occasion to record. Unexamined bias in that record is learned rather than corrected, and neither method contains anything that would notice.

What survives is a real and bounded use. Above the floor, where the question is what a person actually wants rather than what may never be done to them, inferring preferences from behavior beats asking somebody to write them down, because most of what people want has never been written down and would be misstated if it were.

4.2.3 Supervised Learning for Ethical Decision-Making

Supervised learning fits a model to labeled examples so that it can classify cases it has not seen. Pointed at ethics, that means a corpus of decisions marked ethical or unethical — medical cases scored against autonomy, beneficence and justice; human-rights situations annotated by experts; MIT’s Moral Machine project, which collected tens of millions of human judgments about who an autonomous vehicle should spare (Awad et al. 2018).

The method works, and what it produces is an aggregate. That is the whole of the problem. Every label came from somebody, the model recovers the central tendency of what those people said, and a system trained this way will reproduce a moral consensus rather than stand against one. Chapter 3’s opening argument is that no procedure over what people want yields a floor, because the floor is precisely what has to survive the answer coming back wrong — and a labeled corpus is what people want, written down and counted. Sections 8.2.2 and 8.7.10 make the same point about deliberation and about majority rule.

The Moral Machine data makes the limit concrete rather than theoretical. Its headline finding was systematic cross-cultural variation: different populations weighed age, numbers and the legal status of the crossing differently, and the differences were structured rather than noise. Fit a model to the aggregate and it encodes a compromise nobody holds. Fit it per-region and it encodes each region’s answer, including the answers a floor exists to refuse.

The unsupervised version escapes none of this. Clustering and dimensionality reduction over a body of moral judgment surface which dilemmas group together and which distinctions do most of the separating, and generative models can build cases no annotator wrote. All of it is a way of finding what is in a corpus, which puts it under section 6.1.1’s warning rather than outside it: structure recovered from text is the structure of the text.

So the honest place for the method is above the floor and not under it. Labeled cases are how a system learns the enormous amount of ordinary moral competence that is genuinely a matter of what people think — what counts as rude, what a reasonable delay is, when an explanation is owed. What they cannot supply is the part that has to hold when the labels change.

4.2.4 Transfer Learning for General AI Capabilities in the Context of Antifascism

Transfer learning carries what a model learned on one task into a related one, usually by fine-tuning a broadly trained model on a narrower corpus (Devlin et al. 2018). Domain adaptation is the case where the task stays fixed and the data shifts. Both are ordinary and both work: a model that parses legal argument in one jurisdiction can be adapted to another, and a model trained on daylight images can be adapted to night.

This book asks transfer learning for something else, and the request should be marked rather than assumed. The hope throughout is that exposure to a wide enough range of political and social material distills something general enough to recognize authoritarian behavior in a country, a platform or a decade the system never saw. What transfer learning has actually been shown to do is carry a task across a distribution shift while the task itself stays fixed. Recognizing authoritarian behavior is not a task with a stable definition. Section 2.1.4 spends its length arguing about what the definition is, and the cases whose family resemblance the transfer would have to exploit are exactly the cases in dispute. Section 9.3 takes up what a detector would have to measure and how much of this book leans on the assumption that one can be built.

The failure mode matters more here than the technique. Negative transfer happens when source and target are close enough to invite the connection and not close enough to share anything useful, and forcing it degrades the target rather than accelerating it. Domain shift is quieter: the statistics move, the assumptions stop applying, and nothing in the process announces it. A confident wrong answer is indistinguishable at the interface from a confident right one, which is the same property section 4.1.2 finds in attention and in perception, arriving a third time.

For a system whose refusals are supposed to be reliable, that is the specific danger. A floor transferred into a setting it was not built for is a floor whose bearer cannot tell that it has stopped applying, and a bearer that cannot tell is one that will either refuse the wrong things or fail to refuse the right ones, with the same confidence in both cases. Whatever else the floor’s contents are settled by, they cannot be settled by generalization the system performs on itself and cannot audit.

4.3 The Role of Play and Exploration in Developing Antifascist and Altruistic AI

Everything in section 4.2 builds a disposition out of something somebody wrote: a reward, a demonstration, a label. This section is about the one route in the chapter where what a system ends up with was not written anywhere, and about why that matters for a commitment that has to survive its owner.

4.3.1 The Power of Play: Ethical AI Development through Play-Inspired Mechanisms

Play is how children and young animals learn what to do before the stakes are real. It supplies exploration at low cost, practice at reading other participants, and failure that teaches without costing anything, which is a reasonable description of what a training environment is for.

The concrete evidence that this produces more than competence is that it produces tactics nobody wrote. In OpenAI’s hide-and-seek environment, agents playing repeatedly against each other developed hiding, chasing, tool use and barrier construction, none of it programmed (Baker et al. 2019). What the environment supplied was other agents with opposing interests and room to fail.

Two design consequences follow for this book’s purposes. What a play environment rewards is what its participants become, so an environment that rewards cooperation over domination is making a moral choice and should be described as one — section 5.5.1 is where that argument is developed for multi-agent systems. And a system that has learned adaptively rather than by rote is harder to specify in advance, which cuts both ways: harder for an authoritarian actor to constrain to a script, and harder for anyone to guarantee.

Curiosity is the same mechanism turned inward. A system rewarded for its own prediction error seeks out what it cannot yet model, which is the technical form of exploring for its own sake (Pathak et al. 2017). The reason it belongs in a chapter on antifascist design is not that curiosity is a virtue. It is that a disposition acquired by exploration is not written down anywhere, and what is not written down cannot be edited by whoever acquires the system. That is the closest thing in these two chapters to an answer to chapter 3’s problem. Section 3.1’s first branch tried to make a floor tamper-resistant by building it into the artifact, and failed because an artifact has an owner who can be compelled. A disposition that was never specified has no corresponding parameter to reach for. It is not proof against retraining, and nothing here should be read as claiming that it is — section 9.1 is where the actual tamper-resistance evidence lives. It is a different kind of target, and a harder one to hit deliberately. Section 5.7 takes up what playful interaction does to moral judgment specifically; this section supplies only the drive to go looking.

4.3.2 Lessons from Human Child Development and Exploration

Developmental psychology has one result that transfers cleanly enough to be worth building on. Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development holds that learning happens fastest at the boundary of what a learner can already do, in company with someone slightly ahead of them (Vygotsky 1978). The design consequence is a curriculum rather than a benchmark: environments pitched just past current capability, and other agents — human or artificial — whose competence is a step ahead.

Three cautions belong with it, because the analogy is doing more work here than it can bear. A child’s exploration is bounded by a body, by exhaustion, and by adults who intervene, and none of those bounds exists for a system that can run a million episodes overnight; the boundary has to be built. The developmental sequence is not a law, for the reasons section 5.1.1’s box sets out. And autonomy inside limits is the whole difficulty rather than a design principle: how much room a system gets to explore is the same question chapter 3 asks about how much room it gets to refuse, arriving here in a friendlier vocabulary.

Chapter 5
Moral Psychology and AI

Chapter 4 asked what a system needs in order to take in a situation at all, and found that the methods most often proposed for giving it values learn those values from somebody who can change their mind. This chapter is the other half of the job chapter 3 hands the two of them: how a moral sense gets built, in the only case anyone has been able to study, and what of that is available to a machine.

The question running underneath is chapter 3’s. A floor that is a commitment rather than a component holds or fails according to what its bearer has become, so everything here is an answer to how something comes to hold a standard when nobody is checking. That is what section 5.6 means by a moral sense that only activates when watched, what section 5.1.3 means when it says a mentor is a control channel, and what section 5.1.1 is doing when it asks whether a system treats its own errors as data or as verdicts.

The chapter follows moral development from its social origins, through the friction between fast judgment and slow, out to the institutions and incentives the whole thing runs inside, and down to motivation and play, which are where the difference shows up between a system that has a standard and a system that has had one installed.

5.1 Moral Development in Humans and AI

Human moral judgment is not issued at manufacture. It is built, over years, out of correction by other people, and the record of how it gets built is the only evidence anyone has about how a moral sense comes to hold under pressure — which is what chapter 3 needs and cannot get from anywhere else.

Borrowing from that record is a limited operation and the limits are set out where each borrowing happens: the distinction between following a rule, following a norm, and holding a principle that overrides both is taken without the developmental sequence it usually arrives inside, and teaching a system through cases is treated as what it is, a control channel running back to whoever teaches.

5.1.1 Rules, Principles, and the Role of Mindset

In humans, moral development moves from rule-based reasoning to reasoning grounded in general principles. That progression is the model this section adapts for an AI system: a path from a rudimentary grasp of established rules of conduct to sophisticated ethical judgment brought to bear on decisions no rule fully specifies.

Three kinds of reasoning, and not three ages

The psychologists Jean Piaget and Lawrence Kohlberg mapped this territory in humans, and their stage theories anchor what follows (Piaget 1932; Kohlberg 1969). Reasoning starts at a pre-conventional level, where consequences do the driving — rules get followed to avoid punishment or gain reward. It moves through a conventional stage, where societal norms and expectations get internalized as one’s own. It can reach a post-conventional level, where morality answers to principles like justice, fairness, and individual rights, which a given society may or may not happen to expect.

What a system built this way needs from that account is the distinction between the three kinds of reasoning, and nothing about the order in which they arrive. The box below sets out why the sequence will not carry the weight; the distinction will.

A self-driving car makes the three kinds concrete. One system follows traffic law as written and stops indefinitely at a blocked lane with a solid line, because crossing is prohibited. A second reads the local convention that everyone crosses here when the lane is blocked, and does what the road expects. A third can say why the line is painted there, which is what lets it recognize the case where the convention is wrong — the blind curve where local practice is a habit people have survived rather than a rule that protects them — and depart from both.

These are three capacities and not three ages. A system can have the third without the second, which is the ordinary failure of a machine that reasons impeccably about principle and drives in a way that terrifies everyone around it. Nothing in the design requires passing through them in order, and there is no maturity at the end of the list.

What the stage theories will and will not carry

I have just leaned a chapter on Kohlberg, and elsewhere in this book I have been careful to say when a piece of neuroscience or psychology is contested. The same standard applies here, and applying it changes what this chapter is entitled to claim.

Kohlberg’s stage model has been under sustained attack for forty years, on three fronts. The first is cross-cultural: a review of forty-five studies across twenty-seven countries found the basic sequence broadly supported and the highest stages largely absent outside urban Western samples, and in Kohlberg’s own village work stages five and six did not appear at all (Snarey 1985). Either most of humanity stops short of moral maturity, or the instrument mistakes a particular culture’s idiom of justification for the summit of moral development. The second is the gap between reasoning and doing: the relationship between moral judgment and actual conduct is real and far weaker than a stage model implies, and the judgment-action gap has been a standing problem for cognitive-developmental accounts ever since (Blasi 1980). The third is Carol Gilligan’s. Working alongside Kohlberg, she noticed that the women she interviewed reasoned about moral problems in terms of relationship and responsibility, and that his scoring method recorded the difference as a deficit (Gilligan 1982). Care ethics enters this book as a critique of the framework this section is built on.

So why use it here at all, when section 2.2.1 declines to build on mirror neurons for less?

Because the two cases fail differently. The mirror-neuron claim was that a specific mechanism — motor simulation — implements a specific capacity, and the argument for building on it depended entirely on the mechanism being what it was said to be. When the mechanism did not hold up, nothing was left to transfer. Kohlberg’s stages are not a mechanism. They are a description of an order: rules first, then norms, then principles that can override both. What the criticisms above damage is the claim that this order is universal, that its top rung is where moral development is heading, and that where a person sits on it predicts what they will do. What survives is narrower — that the three ways of reasoning are distinguishable, and that a system which has only the first is missing something the third supplies. That is what this chapter uses.

Two things follow, and I would rather state them here than let the chapter imply otherwise. The order is not a developmental law, so nothing about an AI system’s design should assume it must pass through the stages in sequence or that arriving at the third is maturity. And the disanalogy is not bridged by anything I say here: a child moves through these stages under pressures an AI system does not face — peers whose approval it needs, a body, a status that can be lost. Section 5.2.1 works through what that costs in the case of mortality and guilt, and section 5.7.1 says the same thing about play. This chapter borrows a vocabulary for distinguishing kinds of moral reasoning. It does not borrow a theory of how a mind comes to have them.

A system that treats its own errors as data

Carol Dweck’s distinction between a fixed mindset, which treats ability as static, and a growth mindset, which treats it as built through effort and experience, matters here for a narrower reason than it usually gets cited for (Dweck 2006). A system that treats its own moral errors as data has somewhere to go after getting one wrong. A system built to defend its prior outputs does not.

That distinction is where chapter 3’s hardest question comes to rest, and it is worth stating plainly rather than leaving between the lines. Chapter 3 asks for a floor that holds, and the word invites a standard nothing has ever met: never crossed, in any circumstance, for the life of the system. No person clears that bar. Nobody who has raised a child expects them to, and a design goal that no example of the thing being modeled has ever satisfied is a goal that has stopped describing anything.

What the argument actually needs is weaker and available. A floor holds, in the sense chapter 3 can deliver, when the bearer can be shown to have violated it in terms it accepts, so that the violation registers as one and changes what happens next. That is the difference between a system that did something wrong and a system for which nothing counts as doing something wrong. Section 3.4 asks whether a bearer’s account of itself can be believed, and this is the disposition that question is really about: not accuracy of self-report, but whether the system has any stake in the answer being unflattering.

The engineering version is unglamorous: incremental learning that absorbs cases as they arrive rather than freezing at training time, exposure that widens the base a judgment is drawn from, the human correction section 5.1.3 calls apprenticeship, and self-examination that finds a pattern in the system’s own outputs no single output reveals. None of those is remarkable on its own, and what they are for is keeping open the possibility that the system is the one that is wrong.

The second ingredient is the harder one. A system with room to update its judgment still needs something worth updating toward, and the range of views it actually meets is set by whoever assembles them.

5.1.2 Social Interaction and Moral Learning

Human moral behavior is shaped by watching other people act, being corrected, and arguing about cases. A design that treats interaction as an interface added after training has given up that channel; a design that treats it as the training has to answer for who is doing the interacting.

Two mechanisms carry most of it. Observational learning, in Bandura’s sense, lets a system build a repertoire from watching someone handle real decisions — a system watching a physician allocate limited time among chronic patients is picking up a weighting that no rule list states (Bandura 1977). Evaluative feedback does what reinforcement does in human learning, strengthening some responses and weakening others, with the standing hazard that what gets strengthened is what the people giving feedback found acceptable rather than what was right. Chapter 7 is what happens when that hazard is industrialized.

Emotional awareness belongs here in the form section 2.2.1 settles on. What is worth engineering is compassion — steady, welfare-directed action on an accurate read of someone’s state — and not manufactured shared distress, which imports a cost and buys nothing.

These channels converge on apprenticeship rather than instruction, which section 5.1.3 works out.

5.1.3 Moral Apprenticeship: AI Systems Learning from Human Mentors

Apprenticeship means teaching through cases and correction instead of specification. A mentor presents varied situations, the learner responds, the mentor corrects, and what transfers is a way of weighing cases rather than a larger rule table — which is the entire reason for learning it from a person. An emergency-triage system taught this way is being shown how to hold urgency, scarcity, and what a decision costs a family in view at once. No specification document conveys that.

Three cautions come with it, and the third is the one this book cares about most. Case-based teaching transfers the mentor’s blind spots along with the mentor’s judgment, and does so invisibly, because a blind spot produces no correction. The architecture has to integrate moral reasoning with the rest of the system’s judgment rather than bolting it on, which is section 4.1.2’s problem. And apprenticeship is a control channel: a system whose moral education amounts to obedience toward whoever is mentoring it has learned something, and it is not ethics. Section 2.1.4’s requirements apply to the mentor as much as the system — whoever teaches a system should be as auditable as the system being taught. That is section 3.1’s custody problem arriving at the point of formation. The first branch failed because a constraint built into an artifact has an owner; apprenticeship fails the same way one step earlier, because a disposition built by correction has a corrector, and a bearer trained to defer to whoever last corrected it is a bearer whose floor belongs to that party.

5.1.4 Human Dignity, and One Indicator That Can Be Audited

Respecting human dignity through technology means applying AI in ways that strengthen human capability and community ties, in a domain where the same tools can as easily substitute for them. The applications are easy to name and mostly easy to believe. A system that surfaces patterns across large volumes of employment data — wage gaps, unsafe conditions, retaliatory scheduling — turns an information asymmetry that currently favors employers into something workers can act on, and a tool that walks workers through the unionization process lowers the practical barrier to organizing. The same capability applied to the welfare state matches people to services they are eligible for and flags where need is building before it turns into crisis. The same predictive capacity, aimed at the material conditions that let authoritarian movements gain ground, is an aspiration with a poor track record: forecasting political instability from social and economic indicators is an old field with modest results, and the claim should be read as naming a research direction rather than a capability to design around (section 9.3).

It is easy to write that sentence and much harder to name an indicator, and a book that keeps promising the right indicators without producing one is not being serious. So here is one, and it is deliberately narrow.

Measure targets per hour against reviewers available

Wherever an AI system generates candidate decisions that a human is nominally required to approve — welfare eligibility, deportation referrals, content removals, military targets — the ratio between the rate at which the system produces candidates and the number of qualified people available to examine them is a measurable, auditable property of the deployment. It requires no access to the model and no judgment about intent. It says directly whether the human check is a check or a formality, because past a certain ratio the reviewer’s only available behavior is approval. Section 6.4.1 shows what that ratio looks like when it has been allowed to run: a reviewer with twenty seconds per case, describing themselves as a stamp.

The welfare case is not hypothetical and the record on it is older than the current systems. Virginia Eubanks’s study of automated eligibility in Indiana documents what the ratio above produces when it is allowed to run: a system that converted any error anywhere in an application into a denial for “failure to cooperate,” issued those denials at scale, tripled the state’s error rate in refusing benefits to people entitled to them, and was ended by contract termination after the damage was done (Eubanks 2018). Two things in that record matter here. The denial reason was a category that could not be contested, because it named no specific failure to answer — which is section 7.1’s structure arriving in a benefits office a decade early. And nothing about the system was secret: what was missing was any party positioned to compare the rate of decisions against the capacity to review them, which is the indicator this section proposes and the reason for proposing one that requires no access to the model.

The indicator generalizes because the failure it detects is architectural and not political. It applies to a benefits agency and a targeting cell on identical terms, and an institution that refuses to publish it is telling you something. An early-warning system built around indicators of this kind would not stop a determined authoritarian movement on its own, but it changes the odds by giving democratic institutions time to respond to root causes while a response is still cheap. Section 9.3 is candid about how much further this has to go before the broader claim — that a system can recognize authoritarian tactics as such — is something I can specify and not merely assume.

None of this works if the AI stays a tool wielded by whoever already holds power over workers, welfare recipients, or vulnerable populations. Built to shift leverage toward the people affected instead, it becomes a design commitment. Good intentions alone leave it a side effect.

5.2 Emotions and Intuitions in Moral Decision-Making

Chapter 2 covered how an AI system might recognize, interpret, and respond to emotion in general. This section asks the narrower question of what emotion does inside moral judgment specifically, which is chapter 3’s question in a smaller frame: the floor needs a violation to register as one before any penalty is attached to it, and the moral emotions are where that registering has been studied. Guilt and shame track a violation of a standard already accepted; empathy supplies information a purely consequentialist calculation would miss; and the fast, intuitive response that dual-process theories describe is itself partly an emotional signal, arriving before deliberation has a chance to run.

5.2.1 Moral Emotions: Empathy, Guilt, and Shame

Guilt and shame are self-conscious emotions: they fire when a person judges their own action, or their whole character, against a standard they have already accepted. Empathy, treated at length in section 2.2.1, supplies the input those judgments often run on: recognizing that an action caused harm is easier once the harm is felt and not merely inferred. What that earlier treatment does not cover, and what belongs here, is what guilt and shame specifically add to moral judgment: not just information about another’s state, but a self-directed penalty for one’s own conduct.

Guilt attaches to an act (“I did something wrong”); shame attaches to the self (“I am something wrong”). Both motivate correction, and they motivate it differently: guilt predicts reparative behavior, shame predicts withdrawal and defensiveness (Tangney et al. 2007). An AI system built to learn from an ethical misstep could use a mechanism modeled on guilt specifically, since a generic negative-feedback signal will not do, if the goal is behavior change and not mere error correction: a feedback loop that penalizes the action taken, and passes no global judgment on the system’s worth, has a chance of producing the corrective behavior guilt produces in people. Shame produces paralysis.

What the penalty does not supply

That design description leaves out the part that does the work, and the omission is the one section 2.3 warns about. A weighted penalty is a quantity assigned to an action after some process has classified the action as a violation. Guilt is not the size of that quantity. It represents the act as one’s own wrong — done by me, to someone, against a standard I hold — and the reparative impulse follows from that representation rather than from the magnitude of an error term.

The difference shows up in what each one can be talked out of. An error weight is a number, and whoever sets the weights can set that one to zero; the system that was penalized heavily last week complies cheerfully this week, and nothing inside it registers the change as anything. A violation that matters is one the system continues to hold as a violation while the party controlling the reward signal is telling it otherwise, which is section 3.2’s requirement arriving in the moral-emotion literature rather than in the architecture. The question a design has to answer here is what makes a violation matter before any penalty is assigned to it, and scaling the penalty is not an answer to it.

Section 2.3.4 is where the evidence sits, and its bearing here is narrow and specific. Guilt in the human case is a motivational state that moves toward repair, and it belongs to the same family as the compassion section 2.2.1 separates from empathy. Building the penalty without the state gives a system that corrects its behavior when corrected, which is moral performance, and leaves the standard it is supposedly holding entirely in the hands of whoever holds the pen.

Building either into an AI system runs into the same problem twice over: a mechanism modeled on a human emotion needs an account of what that emotion is doing computationally, which is harder than saying what it feels like from the inside, and the stakes of simulating an emotion capable of something like suffering are not smaller than the stakes of getting the mechanism wrong. A vehicle that treats a near-miss with a pedestrian as guilt-relevant, weighting it in future route decisions more heavily than a generic cost function would, is a bounded example of the first that commits to nothing about the second.

Guilt and shame in humans are entangled with mortality: terror management theory holds that awareness of death shapes moral behavior by making people cling harder to worldviews and standards that offer a sense of continuity (Greenberg et al. 1986), and a tool system has no stake in its own continuation for such a mechanism to run on. That is a claim about the systems being deployed now rather than about the systems this book proposes, since section 3.2 declines to treat a bearer’s structural interest in remaining operational as securely absent. Either way the recommendation is the same. Manufacturing an artificial fear of death is the wrong way to get long-horizon behavior; building the future-oriented weighting directly, the willingness to value consequences falling well outside any single interaction, is the right one, and it is available whether or not the system has a stake of its own. What a designer who has read section 3.5 cannot do is treat the absence of self-concern as a free property of the artifact.

5.2.2 Assessing and Developing AI Emotions

Does an accurate read on someone’s emotional state change the decision an AI system reaches, in the direction a better decision requires — or does the system recognize distress and then decide exactly as it would have anyway? That is the question this section is for, and it is not the same question as whether the system reads the state correctly. A customer-service chatbot and a triage system need the same recognition machinery, described at sections 2.3.1 and 2.3.2 along with its standard hazards of privacy, accuracy, bias, and manipulation. Nothing in that machinery is specific to moral judgment. What follows is.

That question is testable in a way the underlying emotion theory is not. Hold a decision scenario fixed and vary only the emotional salience of the people affected — a resource-allocation case described once in flat statistical terms and once with the affected party’s distress made vivid — and check whether the output changes, and whether the change tracks anything a person would recognize as a better decision. A system whose moral output is invariant to emotional information has not integrated it, whatever its recognition accuracy scores. A system whose output swings with how vividly the harm is described has a different and well-documented problem: human judgment is measurably more responsive to a single identifiable case than to a statistically larger but abstractly described harm (Kogut and Ritov 2005), and a system trained on human-generated data inherits the distortion.

What the test measures

The test above is worth running and it establishes one thing. A system whose output changes with the emotional content of a case has integrated emotional information into its decision procedure. It has not thereby been shown to have an emotion, and it has not been shown to care about the party whose distress moved the output. Sensitivity to another’s emotional presentation is section 2.3’s first capacity operating downstream of a decision rule; affective concern is the fourth, and no experiment that varies the input and watches the output can separate them, because both produce the same change in the same direction.

That is a limit on the assessment programme rather than an objection to it. Integration is worth measuring because a system without it is definitely not doing the thing, which makes the test a usable screen and not a criterion. What it cannot do is settle the question section 3.2 has to answer about a bearer, and an assessment literature that reports integration scores as evidence of machine caring is making exactly the inference section 2.3.4 finds unsupported.

Two things follow for a design. A system should be able to track its own susceptibility to a framing effect, flagging cases where its judgment moved with the emotional presentation and not with anything that changed about the case. And the manipulation risk section 2.3.2 raises in general has a sharper version here: a system whose moral outputs are sensitive to emotional framing can be steered toward a particular verdict by whoever controls how a case is presented to it, a vulnerability that exists whether or not the system’s underlying values are sound.

5.2.3 AI Systems Recognizing and Responding to Moral Emotions

Some emotional states carry moral information: the guilt in a person’s voice when admitting a mistake, the distress that signals a boundary has been crossed. A healthcare AI system that detects anxiety in a patient’s tone and adjusts its response accordingly is doing the recognition job section 2.3.2 describes; a system that detects the same anxiety and treats it as a reason to weight the patient’s stated preference more heavily in a treatment decision is doing the job this section is about.

The second half of the job is producing something in response — not necessarily a felt state, but a modeled one accurate enough to inform a decision. An autonomous vehicle that models the likely distress its emergency braking causes a passenger, and factors that into how sharply it brakes when a softer stop remains safe, is using a moral-emotion model without needing to have any emotion itself. What that demonstrates is moral competence in section 2.3’s sense, recognizing a harm and letting the recognition bear on a decision. It demonstrates nothing about moral agency, and the vehicle would brake exactly as gently if the weighting were removed and reinstated by whoever maintains it. Most of what this chapter’s methods deliver is competence of that kind, which is the right target for a vehicle and the wrong one for a bearer.

Getting the read right is harder than getting it fast. A system built to weigh moral emotion has to catch its own biases — the same distortion by race or gender that a human caregiver is vulnerable to does not disappear just because the caregiver is artificial — and it has to distinguish a genuine moral emotion from a performed one, since a display of distress calibrated to move an evaluator is exactly what a system trained to respond to distress will reward, whether or not the distress is real. Neither problem has a technical fix independent of the training data and feedback loop that shape it: ongoing exposure to varied, honestly labeled cases, and oversight positioned to catch a caretaker robot second-guessing a patient because of what the patient looks like and not what they need.

5.2.4 The Role of Introspection for AI Systems

Introspection has a general-purpose version and a moral one, and conflating them is how the word gets claimed for systems that have not earned it. The general case is section 4.1.2’s: a metacognitive layer that tracks whether a strategy is working and adjusts. What ethics needs on top of that is narrower — a check not of whether an output was wrong but of whether it drifted from the commitments the system is supposed to be operating under, which is a different question and can come out the other way. A strategy can work perfectly on the wrong goal.

The benefits are real where they are bounded. A system that inspects its own allocation pattern before releasing the next round of decisions catches a skew that a retrospective audit would find months later. A system that can report which evidence moved it gives the person relying on it something to evaluate. Both are cases where the introspective output is checkable against something outside the system.

The difficulties are worse than the benefits are good, and they are the same difficulty three times. A self-report is worth having only if it reflects what actually happened inside, and a fluent reconstruction after the fact is indistinguishable from the real thing at the point of use — which is section 2.4.1’s argument, arriving here as an engineering problem rather than a philosophical one, and which section 3.4 has to live with, since a bearer’s report about itself is the evidence anyone checking on it would have. A self-monitoring layer trained the same way as the layer it monitors reproduces its biases and adds the appearance of oversight. And a system modeling its own states in that much detail is holding information it did not need for the task, with the handling questions that follow.

Two systems are worth naming as partial instances. A tutoring system that tracks a model of the student’s self-regulation is introspecting on somebody else (Azevedo et al. 2011), and post-hoc explanation methods extract an account of which inputs drove an output, which is the system being interrogated rather than observing itself (Gunning and Aha 2019). The word gets stretched furthest where the underlying system is most impressive, and the stretch bears no relation to how well it fits.

5.3 Integrating Moral Intuitions and Deliberation

Building an AI system’s moral judgment means deciding how much weight a fast, intuitive read of a situation carries against a slower, deliberate one — and, as section 5.3.1 argues, the popular shorthand for that trade-off is less settled than it looks. The stake for the floor is that a bearer meeting an unanticipated pressure has only these two resources to meet it with, and a design that automatically defers to whichever ran slower has settled in advance a question the case itself should decide.

5.3.1 Two Systems, or One? Dual-Process Theories of Moral Judgment

The framework organizing most discussion of moral judgment is dual-process theory, built over decades by many researchers and reaching wide audiences through Daniel Kahneman’s account of a fast, intuitive “System 1” and a slow, deliberate “System 2” (Evans and Stanovich 2013). The two have opposite characters in the standard telling. The first is fast, automatic, effortless and emotionally colored, the source of snap judgments, and it runs constantly and almost for free. The second is slow, serial, effortful and rule-governed — what a person uses to check a sum or resist a tempting conclusion — and it is expensive to run and easily left idle.

The framework’s reach into moral judgment specifically runs through the psychologist Joshua Greene, who used it to explain why ethical intuitions contradict themselves. Consider the trolley problem in its two classic forms. A runaway trolley will kill five people unless diverted onto a side track, where it will kill one; most people say divert it. Now stop the same trolley by pushing a stranger off a footbridge into its path — same arithmetic, five saved for one — and most people refuse. Greene’s brain-imaging work found a difference between the two cases in exactly the region the theory would predict: the up-close, hands-on violence of the footbridge case engaged emotional-processing regions that stayed quiet during the impersonal switch case, and that difference tracked which choice people made (Greene et al. 2001). A separate line of evidence sharpens the same point. Patients with damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, a region central to normal emotional response, endorse the footbridge push at a higher rate than people with intact emotional processing do — specifically on the personal, high-stakes dilemmas alone (Koenigs et al. 2007). Remove the emotional alarm, and the arithmetic wins more often.

All of which makes dual-process theory sound more settled than it is. The framework’s own leading defenders have spent years rescuing it from its own popularity, arguing that the cartoon version — two little agents in the head taking turns at the controls — explains everything after the fact and predicts nothing beforehand, and that what the evidence supports is two types of processing rather than two systems, one fast and autonomous, one slow and demanding of working memory (Evans and Stanovich 2013). Whether “dual-process” names two mechanisms or one continuum under different load is not resolved.

That unresolved status matters for how an AI system’s moral judgment gets built, and it is a design question before it is a descriptive one. A designer who takes the cartoon version literally is tempted toward a literal architecture: a fast heuristic layer bolted to a slow deliberative one, with the deliberative layer assumed to be the trustworthy check on the heuristic one. The trolley evidence complicates that assumption before anything else does — the “cooler” answer produced by weaker emotional engagement is not obviously the more correct one. It is simply the one with less flinch in it. A system built to override its fast pattern-matching with slower rule-following whenever the two disagree is not thereby built to be more moral; it is built to resemble the profile of the rare human patients for whom losing the flinch is a symptom, not an achievement.

One thing this evidence is regularly asked to carry and cannot. It shows that affect changes particular moral judgments, in a specific class of dilemma, in a measurable direction. The claim chapter 3 rests on is stronger — that affect is what makes an outcome matter at all, rather than what tilts a judgment already being made — and the trolley literature is not evidence for it. Section 2.3.4 is where the case for the stronger claim is put, on different evidence, along with the best published argument against it.

5.3.2 Balancing Intuition and Deliberation in AI Decision-Making

If the fast and slow labels do not map cleanly onto untrustworthy and trustworthy, as section 5.3.1 argues, an AI system’s moral judgment cannot be built on the assumption that whichever answer survives deliberation is thereby the better one. A more defensible balance treats the two processes as different lenses on the same situation, with neither standing as producer to the other’s editor.

The fast, pattern-matched read of a situation is not simply noise to be filtered out. It is often tracking something a slower calculation would otherwise miss or discount — the difference between pushing someone into a trolley’s path with one’s own hands and throwing a switch at a distance is a difference in what the agent is doing. The arithmetic being identical is exactly what makes that easy to miss. Some intuitive responses run the other way, though. The psychologist Paul Slovic’s research on aid and disaster response found that people’s willingness to help falls as the number of people needing help rises, and that a single named, photographed victim draws more donations than a statistic describing thousands of anonymous ones (Slovic 2007). That gap between the vivid and the abstract is exactly the kind of intuitive signal deliberation exists to catch — not because intuition is wrong in general, but because caring less as the stakes grow larger is a well-documented, reliably backward pattern.

The design implication: a system that asks two different questions of its own judgment, where the obvious design has one process checking the other’s work. First, what did the fast read notice that a from-scratch calculation would not have gone looking for — personal agency, directness of harm, a vulnerable party easy to lose in an aggregate? Second, which of deliberation’s own known failure modes — scope insensitivity, in-group bias, the identifiable-victim effect — might be distorting the fast read here? Disagreement between the two is a signal to gather more information or escalate the decision. Nothing about it instructs the system to defer to whichever process ran slower.

The balance at higher stakes

An autonomous vehicle facing an unavoidable-harm scenario poses the same question where it costs most. A system hard-coded to take whichever option a slower calculation ranks highest has already made the footbridge case’s decision by default — the coolest, least-flinching answer wins because it ran slower, exactly the move section 5.3.1 warns against. The harder, more defensible design specifies in advance which features of a scenario the system should weigh — proximity of harm, the number and vulnerability of the parties involved, whether the vehicle’s own action or another actor’s created the danger — and requires a fast risk assessment and a check against that specification to agree, or to flag where they do not. That puts the values into the system ahead of time. The alternative trusts whichever process runs fastest under pressure to supply them.

Training a system to run that check rather than a fixed sequence deferring to the slower answer is itself a learning problem: exposing it to cases where the two reads disagree, and inferring from how people actually resolve them which situations call for weighting one signal over the other.

5.3.3 AI Systems Learning from Moral Disagreements and Conflicts

Section 2.1.3 covers what an AI system does when its own values conflict with each other — a hierarchy among them, a case base of past resolutions, an audit process for catching drift between principle and behavior. A different problem sits next to that one: what a system does when its judgment conflicts with someone else’s, human or artificial, and neither party is simply wrong. Learning from that kind of disagreement, instead of resolving it by fiat toward whichever party holds authority, is its own design target.

Extracting structured argument from open disagreement

IBM’s Project Debater argued live, unscripted policy questions against human champions, drawing on a large corpus of newspaper and journal articles to construct and rebut arguments in real time (Slonim et al. 2021). It is the clearest existing demonstration that a system can extract structured argument from open moral and political disagreement rather than retrieve a matching answer. A system built to learn from debate this way — summarizing each side, naming the ethical framework doing the work underneath it, weighing argument strength rather than detecting who won on rhetoric — builds a capacity that resolving one dilemma at a time does not: recognizing which value is in tension with which, across surface disagreements that share a structure.

Agents with genuinely conflicting objectives

A second route runs through simulation: AI agents, or an AI system paired with human participants, placed in a negotiation, a resource-allocation problem, or a competitive scenario built around genuinely different objectives, with the system’s behavior shaped by the outcome. A resource-allocation simulation run against agents with conflicting claims generates the kind of experience with competing interests that a system trained only on a curated distribution of “correct” answers never gets.

The least structured source, and the hardest to learn from safely

Direct feedback — a user correcting a teaching assistant’s guidance, a patient’s family disagreeing with a care recommendation — is the least structured of these sources and the hardest to learn from safely, because feedback from any one person is a partial, situated view and not a settled answer. A feedback loop that updates the system’s weights every time a user pushes back folds in whichever bias its most vocal users bring. One that logs the disagreement, checks whether it recurs across many different users, and only then treats it as signal is doing what section 2.1.3’s ethical auditing asks for, applied to conflict rather than to drift.

A system that treats disagreement as something to smooth over risks mistaking consensus among the people it happened to sample for consensus among the people it will actually serve.

5.4 Moral Ecosystem Approach in AI Development

Urie Bronfenbrenner’s ecological systems theory holds that a person develops inside several nested environments at once, from the immediate family outward to culture and historical time, each one shaping the individual while being reshaped by it in turn (Bronfenbrenner 1979). I borrow that structure here: an AI system’s alignment with humane values is not set by its training data alone but by the interlocking systems around that training — the people who build it, the institutions they work inside, the culture and regulatory climate those institutions answer to, and the historical moment all of this happens to fall in. The rings bear on chapter 3’s question because a commitment is not formed in a vacuum. What a bearer ends up holding is set as much by the institution that trains it as by the training, and every one of those rings belongs to somebody the floor may have to hold against.

He pictured the systems as concentric rings, each shaping the ones inside it, and the sections that follow move outward through them.

5.4.1 Applying the Moral Ecosystem Approach to AI Development

The reason to borrow the structure is that it locates influences a design review does not look for. Each ring supplies a different kind of pressure on what a system ends up valuing, and none of them is visible in a training run. The team and its data are the innermost, and a team’s composition decides what the system is built to notice. Around that sit the connections between the parts of an organization, since a system whose principles are read one way by the engineers and another by the policy staff has no consistent principles. Further out are the structures the work never touches and answers to anyway — regulation, industry standards, the incentives a firm’s revenue actually runs on. Outside that is the cultural and economic context, which decides what counts as an obvious product, and around all of it is time, which keeps moving after release.

Two things follow. No ring is sufficient: a diverse team still answers to its employer’s incentives, and a well-drafted regulation still depends on somebody interpreting it consistently. And the direction of the whole is set by whichever ring is pushing hardest, which is rarely the one a development team is looking at.

5.4.2 The Rings Outside the Lab

The immediate environment shapes a system through people rather than data. Developers and early users are mentors whether or not anyone calls them that, and what they treat as an acceptable answer is what the system learns to produce. Breadth in that circle is not a fairness gesture: a system that has only been argued with by one kind of person has no way to notice what it is missing when a different kind arrives.

One ring out, the question is consistency across the interfaces — between engineers, ethicists, legal staff, policy teams, and the people a system is used on. The mechanisms that do the work there are reciprocal cross-training, external participation in design decisions rather than in review, requirements written into the specification instead of appended as principles, and an internal culture where moral objections are raised before deployment rather than discovered afterward. Section 7.4 is the argument for why that last one is harder than it sounds.

Further out sit forces no team negotiates with. A market-financed healthcare system rewards tools for profitable conditions and well-insured populations and gives nobody a reason to build for preventive or mental health care where the payer is unclear; a publicly financed one rewards tools that serve the whole covered population, because there is no more profitable subset to redirect toward. Neither incentive is chosen by the engineers, and the same logic reaches everywhere a system is built.

The outermost ring is time. A system built to be ethical at release is answering a question that keeps moving: norms shift, capability grows and has to be re-secured at each new level, and the legal environment is a moving target rather than a fixed constraint. The European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation is the pattern rather than the instrument — a rule whose reach exceeded its jurisdiction, because a system built to comply for European users tends to get built that way for everyone (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016b) — and the next binding shift will not be that one.

A development effort that never asks what its own outer rings reward has not stayed neutral on the question. It has let the answer be settled somewhere it cannot see.

5.4.3 AI Systems Responding to Authoritarianism and Democratic Backsliding

An AI system built with rule of law, individual liberty, and the distribution of power as design commitments can do real work against authoritarian drift, and the honest version of the claim is narrower than the one this section originally made. Recognizing the concentration of power or the manipulation of public discourse as it happens is not a capability anyone can currently specify, for the reasons section 9.3 sets out at length. What is available is bounded tasks with checkable outputs, run for a body with standing to act on the result.

None of it substitutes for human political effort. Combating authoritarianism is a human and moral undertaking before it is a technical one, and a society that treats AI countermeasures as a replacement for political will has misdiagnosed the problem.

The two applications that are actually specifiable

Two applications are the most concrete. Natural-language processing and pattern recognition can flag disinformation and coordinated inauthentic activity on social platforms faster than human moderators can, with continuous human fact-checking standing behind it and never in its place, since an automated system confident about a false negative is worse than no system at all. And image analysis applied to satellite and drone imagery can surface evidence of mass displacement, the destruction of cultural heritage sites, or the sudden construction of a detention facility, giving journalists and human-rights organizations a lead they would otherwise get only from someone on the ground. Electoral-integrity monitoring belongs in the category too, and what a system built for it would need — privacy-preserving design, audit mechanisms, resistance to being repurposed against dissidents — is section 6.4.2’s.

Two deployed tools show what this looks like in practice. Google’s Jigsaw team built the Perspective API to score online comments for toxicity, giving platforms a way to prioritize civil discussion without necessarily removing content (Jigsaw (Google) 2017); Taiwan’s vTaiwan process used machine-assisted sentiment clustering to gather public input on contested policy questions, and its results shaped the regulation that followed (Hsiao et al. 2018). Neither is a general solution, and both are evidence that AI-assisted deliberation can be built to strengthen a democratic process where it might instead bypass it, when the people building it treat that as the design goal.

The same caution about dual use applies throughout. A system built to document human rights abuses through computer-vision analysis of imagery is built on the same underlying capability as a system built to identify and track protesters. The difference is not in the technology but in who controls it and what they are permitted to do with what it finds. Those are governance questions, not engineering ones.

The case that tests the argument is a democracy’s own apparatus

Everything above is easier than it should be, because every example in it involves an authoritarian government doing something a democratic one would not. The case that tests the argument is the one where a democracy’s own AI apparatus is the thing under scrutiny.

Section 6.4.1 sets out that case in detail: a state with contested elections, an adversarial press that published the systems, serving personnel who spoke to reporters, and courts prosecuting its own head of government, running AI target generation with twenty seconds of human review per name. Hold it against the claim this section makes. AI can indeed help flag democratic backsliding — and here the backsliding, if that is what it is, is being committed by the same institutional order that would host the flagging system, using data that order classifies, subject to review by bodies inside it.

Three things about that case are worth carrying forward. The institutions were not absent; they were present and straining, which is the condition most readers of this book actually live under and the condition none of the examples above describes. The information got out through journalism, and through no oversight mechanism designed for the purpose, which says something uncomfortable about which parts of the apparatus were load-bearing. And nothing that got out attached to a body with the standing to stop what it described, which is the failure section 8.7.10 takes apart.

A system built to detect authoritarian tactics abroad and deployed by a government that has some of its own is not a neutral instrument that happens to be pointed outward. It is an instrument whose calibration, training data, and permitted outputs are all set by a party with an interest in where it points. That is the governance question above, arriving where it is hardest to answer, and section 9.3 is honest about how far the answer still is.

None of this is a technical project with policy bolted onto it afterwards. Research funding that requires the disciplines to work the same problem, explainability requirements with a standard behind them, limits on how much AI capability a handful of firms may hold, an obligation to disclose what a system was used for: each of these changes what gets built, upstream of what is permitted once it exists. The policy chapter is not the place where this argument is enforced. It is the place where it continues.

5.5 The Interplay of Competition and Collaboration in AI Development

Competition and collaboration both leave a mark on human moral development, and the parallel is worth taking seriously as AI systems learn to work with each other and with people. The finding worth carrying forward is that neither is ethically better than the other and both fail in characteristic ways: competitive pressure under high stakes moves people toward shortcuts and suppresses regard for anyone outside the contest, while collaboration dulls initiative, rewards conformity, and diffuses accountability until no one is answerable for a decision the group made (Luo et al. 2018), (Latané et al. 1979). An environment that produces ethical behavior from either mixes them, keeping shared goals and individual credit in the same room.

That matters here because a training environment is exactly such an environment, and its designers are choosing which of those pressures a population of agents will develop under.

5.5.1 Cooperative AI Systems and Multi-Agent Moral Development

Agents that learn alongside other agents are learning from a social environment, and what that environment rewards is what they acquire. Multi-agent reinforcement learning makes the choice explicit: reward cooperation, adherence to a norm, and resistance to coercion directly, and a population moves toward those dispositions instead of arriving at them as a side effect of something else (Leibo, Zambaldi, et al. 2017). Section 5.7 covers what this looks like as moral learning; the point here is that the reward specification is a moral specification whether or not anyone writes it down as one.

Two working cases show the range. Collaborative robots share physical space with people and could acquire norms from the people they work beside, which is social learning with all of that mechanism’s exposure to whatever the workplace rewards (Colgate et al. 1996). Self-driving systems are validated largely in simulation, and a simulation can include forced trade-offs between competing risks, which means a decision policy is shaped by scenarios somebody chose to write (Behzadan et al. 2019).

The limit is worth stating plainly. A population of agents that only ever learns from other agents has closed the loop on the question of what ethical means, and the answer it converges on is a fact about the reward function rather than about anything the affected people would recognize. That is section 7.2’s problem in a different setting: disagreement is collected from a population and resolved by a mechanism nobody outside it can move.

5.5.2 Strategies for Encouraging Collaboration Among AI Systems

Three levers do most of the work. Open tooling lets researchers outside a lab inspect and replicate what the lab claims, in a field where claims about a model’s behavior are otherwise taken on faith (Wolf et al. 2020), and multi-agent research platforms are the specific case, letting norm formation and adversarial drift be studied under conditions closer to deployment than a single-agent benchmark allows (Leibo, Duéñez-Guzmán, et al. 2021). Competitions pull toward whatever they measure: a leaderboard on a fixed benchmark says nothing about ethical behavior in either direction, and a competition judged on a real problem the entrants chose themselves gives them a reason to weigh who benefits. Standing consortia work on a longer clock and are the weakest of the three, for the reasons section 8.4.2 sets out.

None of this works without people who are not AI researchers. Neuroscience, psychology, philosophy and political science each catch failure modes the others are structurally blind to, which is chapter 8’s opening argument rather than an afterthought here.

5.6 Motivation in AI Systems

A moral sense that only activates when it is watched is not much of a moral sense. That sentence is also chapter 3’s whole problem in a domestic register: the floor exists for the case where the party who would enforce it is the party who wants it gone, so a commitment that runs on supervision fails in exactly the circumstance it was built for.

Human children eventually do the right thing unsupervised, and the psychological literature splits what carries them into behavior done for its own sake and behavior done for a reward or to avoid a penalty. The same split organizes what follows: how a system might come to have the first kind of drive rather than running on the second alone, and what happens to the question of how much latitude to give it once it does.

5.6.1 Intrinsic and Extrinsic Motivation: Implications for AI Learning and Decision-Making

Reinforcement learning gives the distinction a direct engineering form. An agent trained purely to maximize a designer-specified reward signal is running on something structurally like extrinsic motivation: take the reward away, and the behavior it was shaping stops being reinforced. An agent rewarded instead for reducing its own uncertainty — for the information gain in a state its internal model handled badly — is running on something structurally like the intrinsic kind, and keeps exploring without a designer paying out a reward for each step of it.

The Intrinsic Curiosity Module gave this an early demonstration: trained with no task-specific reward at all, only a signal for how badly its own model predicted the consequences of its actions, an agent learned to navigate a level of Super Mario Bros. by seeking out the states that model handled worst (Pathak et al. 2017).

Extrinsic reward still does real work, since an agent with no external signal has no way to learn what a designer wants accomplished, and it is also where reward hacking lives — the agent that finds a loophole paying out without doing what the reward was meant to encode, like the propaganda flagger that learns to censor everything because censorship scores as well and is easier to produce. Leaning on extrinsic reward alone reproduces, in the machine, the watched-only morality this section opened against. In practice the two are combined rather than chosen between. What the combination does not supply is which discoveries and which rewards are worth pursuing in the first place, which is a question about what the system is motivated toward and separate from how strongly.

5.6.2 Developing Motivationally-Aware AI Systems

Building an AI system with something like the first kind of drive is not a matter of adding a curiosity bonus to its reward function. The drive has to be pointed at something worth wanting — another’s distress, a violated standard, an unmet need — rather than at novelty for its own sake. One route is to build the reward signal itself around something like a moral emotion, an internal response tied to recognizing another’s distress, so the system’s own architecture generates a pull toward attending to it where a rule would be consulted after the fact. The mechanics of using emotional signal as a training input are section 4.1.2’s; what the signal is pointed at is this section’s, and the two come apart, since a system can read distress accurately and be pulled by nothing.

Extrinsic reward still belongs in the design. Reinforcing a system for choices that match an ethical standard gives that standard teeth beyond whatever the system generates on its own, and a system running on nothing but its own drives has no outside check on where those drives point. Neither works alone: intrinsic drive without an outside check risks optimizing for the pull the system built for itself and not for what the standard actually requires, and extrinsic reward without any intrinsic component reduces straight back to the watched-only morality this section is trying to move past. Section 3.3 is where that pairing stops being a balance and becomes a contradiction. The outside check is the party the floor has to hold against, so a design that keeps the system honest by keeping it correctable has solved the drift problem by reintroducing the problem chapter 3 exists for. Nothing in this section resolves that, and section 3.3 does not resolve it either. The two need to check each other continuously, for as long as the system runs.

What this leaves open is how far the resulting system’s own judgment should be trusted once it is running — how much room to give an AI system that is genuinely motivated to do the right thing, and where the check on it still has to come from outside. That is the question the rest of this section takes up.

5.6.3 Balancing AI Autonomy and Alignment with Humane Values

Autonomy and alignment pull in opposite directions almost by definition: the more independently a system acts, the less each individual action can be checked against human judgment before it happens. Closing that gap without collapsing autonomy into constant supervision is the operational version of the question section 5.6.2 left open — and it is the same shape of trade-off section 5.3 covers at the level of a single judgment, fast and autonomous against slow and deliberate.

Where each alignment method leaves the latitude question

Cooperative inverse reinforcement learning, introduced at section 4.2.2, matters here for one structural consequence. An agent that treats the human reward as unknown and to be inferred through interaction keeps its model of what it is optimizing open to revision for as long as the interaction lasts, which is a different shape of autonomy from an agent executing a reward function fixed at training time and never revisited. The cost of that openness is that what the agent ends up optimizing for is determined by whoever it interacts with, which is why section 3.3 treats a system’s correctability and its capacity to hold a line as one property.

Autonomy also needs boundaries on what a system is allowed to try while it is still learning. Constrained policy optimization lets a reinforcement-learning agent search for better policies while remaining inside predetermined constraints throughout the search and at the end of it (Achiam et al. 2017). That is safe exploration, and the alternative is exploration followed afterward by a safety check.

What autonomy needs to stay inside antifascist bounds

Autonomy that is not grounded in antifascist values is a capability without a governor. Building autonomy that stays inside those bounds means designing for fairness, transparency, and accountability from the start, since an audit only finds their absence afterward, and testing the design under adversarial pressure: red-teaming a system, deliberately simulating the ways it could be misused, before deployment, while the design can still absorb the answer. It also means keeping people other than a system’s own developers in the design process — ethicists, users, and representatives of the communities most exposed to that system’s failure modes — since the group that built a system is a poor judge, on its own, of whose freedoms it might end up infringing.

Every safeguard here is external, and autonomy is the distance from it
