The safeguards usually proposed here — third-party audit, disclosure requirements, export due diligence, cross-sector standards bodies, AI literacy — are the subject of chapter 8, which works out what each one costs and which of them survive an institution that would rather not comply. What belongs here is the part that is specific to autonomy, and it is one observation. Every safeguard on that list is external: it works by giving some outside body the standing and the information to intervene. Autonomy is the property that puts distance between the system’s action and that body’s attention, and the safeguards do not scale with it. A content-moderation system running without continuous human review is autonomous in the straightforward sense, and the same independence that makes it efficient lets it drift into over-censorship, or be steered toward favoring one ideology’s speech over another’s, to be discovered afterward by an audit reading the record of what already happened.

That leaves an uncomfortable division of labor and it is the one this book keeps arriving at. External mechanisms find out what a system did, after it did it. Declining to do it in the first place is available only to something inside the system, and section 5.6.2 says why that inside thing cannot be assembled out of an outside check, while section 3.3 says why it cannot be assembled out of correctability either.

None of that substitutes for a genuine override. A human able to intervene in a high-stakes case, and a system built to accept that intervention rather than resist it, is what keeps autonomy answerable to something outside itself. That is one of three places this book arrives at the same requirement from a different direction; chapter 3 collects them and asks what it would take to build the thing they all point at — and concludes, at section 3.3, that this requirement and the floor are the same property with the sign flipped.

5.7 Play, Exploration, and Moral Development in AI

Section 4.3 took up exploration and curiosity as a way an AI system might come to know its environment. Play is a related but distinct capacity: forming standards for how to treat other agents, learned mostly through practice, imitation, and the negotiated give of a game, and hardly at all through instruction. It earns its place in the floor’s engineering for section 4.3.1’s reason — a standard acquired this way is written down nowhere, which is the one property in these two chapters that an owner cannot simply edit. What follows asks whether an artificial system could acquire anything like it, and where the analogy breaks down.

5.7.1 The Role of Play in Moral Learning and Socialization

Children build much of their moral sense through play, and instruction supplies far less of it than adults assume. A child who tests a rule against a playmate — pushing it, breaking it, watching the other child’s face — gets an answer no lecture supplies, delivered immediately by someone with no stake in teaching a lesson. Developmental psychologists point to play rather than direct teaching as the route by which perspective-taking, cooperation, and respect for rules actually get built (Gray 2013).

Section 4.3.1’s agents developed tool use and counter-strategies nobody had programmed through repeated competitive play, which is competence emerging from play. What this section asks is different in kind: whether play can teach a system standards for how to treat the agents it plays with.

An AI system has no biological drives. And its witnessing of its “own” winning or losing is not necessarily a felt personal experience. But a training context can still be built to have the structural features that make human-like play work as a moral teacher: actions that carry real consequences for other agents in the environment, feedback that comes from the environment itself, with no supervisor’s label attached after the fact, and enough latitude in how the system responds that its choices are its “own” and not a script it is executing. That combination is what would make a scenario play. These conditions may teach coordination and norm-sensitive behavior whether or not affect is present. They do not by themselves establish moral formation. Without some process through which another agent’s welfare comes to matter, play may produce a policy that looks prosocial without producing concern for anyone — section 2.3.4’s distinction, arriving as a limit on what a training environment can be expected to deliver.

Two existing games illustrate what a moral version of that structure looks like. Quandary walks a player through a sequence of dilemmas with no dictated right answer and scores how the player reasons rather than which option they pick (Learning Games Network 2012), which is the design principle a moral-training environment would need: evaluate the deliberation itself. Hanabi, a cooperative card game where each player sees everyone’s hand but their own and must communicate through the game’s own restricted signals, is a standard research benchmark for the capacities morality runs on directly — modeling what a partner does and does not know, and communicating honestly inside a rule-bound system (Bard et al. 2020). Hide and Seek’s payoff was adversarial and Hanabi’s is cooperative, and that difference is close to the whole of what separates this section’s territory from section 4.3.1’s.

What the developmental literature actually supplies

Two of the four accounts usually cited here transfer. Piaget’s constructivism — a child builds understanding by acting on the world rather than receiving it finished (Piaget 1962) — transfers because the machine version is checkable: a system that refines its model of what is at stake by acting repeatedly is doing something different from a system sorting cases against a fixed label. Theory of mind transfers for the same reason, and Hanabi is why, since modeling what a partner knows is exactly what the game scores. Bandura’s social learning is already section 5.1.2’s. Care ethics belongs in this chapter for a reason that is not about play at all: Carol Gilligan built the account as a critique of the stage model section 5.1.1 leans on, having found that its scoring treated relational reasoning as a lower stage (Gilligan 1982).

What none of them supplies is the thing chapter 3 wants. They describe how a moral sense forms in a creature under pressures a system does not face, and they do not say which of those pressures were load-bearing. A system that plays a million episodes overnight has the repetition and none of the stakes, and whether the mechanism survives that substitution is the open question rather than a detail.

Building the curriculum: environment, feedback, and pace

Knowing why play might work is a different problem from building it into a curriculum, which means being specific about the environment, the feedback, and the pace. The environment has to carry real stakes for the other agents in it, so that a system controlling a simulated vehicle in a modeled city experiences the downstream consequences of a choice instead of naming one. The difficulty has to be structured, starting with low-stakes dilemmas and escalating only once the easy cases are handled reliably, the way a child’s own play scales as competence grows. And the feedback has to attach to a specific attempt, closer to how a coach corrects a player mid-game than to how a policy is handed down in advance.

Multi-agent environments are their own case, and a more developed one: section 5.5.1 already covers cooperative and competitive multi-agent training in depth, including reward structures that favor prosocial behavior and agents that learn to share resources or defer to each other under simulated pressure. What that discussion does not settle, and what a play-based framing has to answer and cannot assume, is whether the resulting behavior is moral learning or a policy that merely looks prosocial inside the reward function that produced it.

None of this makes an AI system’s play equivalent to a child’s. A child’s play is charged by stakes that matter to the child — status among peers, the sting of exclusion — where an AI system’s “play” is whatever its designer wired the reward function to care about. The frameworks above are worth building toward because they specify what a route into moral competence through practice would need to include. It is not offered because the analogy between a training loop and a playground is more than partial.

5.7.2 Encouraging AI Systems to Deliberate Morally Through Playful Interactions

Section 4.3 covers curiosity and exploration as ends in themselves. This section points the same appetite for the unscripted at a narrower target: training an AI system to deliberate about right and wrong inside interactions that stay open-ended, which simulating a single dilemma and stopping does not reach.

Existing games built around social interaction rather than pure optimization are a natural fit. Minecraft’s open building and resource-management mechanics could put an agent through allocation dilemmas with no correct answer built into the win condition; Among Us, built around deception and accusation among a small group, could train an agent to distinguish benign misdirection from harmful deceit and to weigh the cost of a false accusation against the cost of staying silent. Neither game was designed for this and using them this way is a proposal rather than a description of existing research — but the design problem they pose, with ambiguous information, competing claims on trust, and consequences that play out over the rest of the game, is close to the shape of an actual ethical dilemma in a way a single-shot trolley-problem prompt is not.

Play does not have to run inside an existing game. Narrative construction is one alternative: give a system a moral dilemma and have it build a story around it, working through the perspectives of several characters with genuinely conflicting interests, without picking a winner. Role-play scenarios are another, with the system arguing from inside a stakeholder’s position and seeing how its choices affect the other parties before the scenario ends. Both put the system in the position of constructing an outcome, where the alternative selects from a menu of pre-written responses.

What these approaches share is a refusal to reduce moral reasoning to a labeled dataset of right answers. A system that only ever sees dilemmas with a single correct output learns to match patterns against that output rather than to deliberate.

Chapter 6
Overcoming Challenges, Risks, and Authoritarianism in AI Development

We [humans] cannot process so much information... you still cannot
produce enough targets per day.

Brigadier General Y.S., The Human-Machine Team: How to Create Synergy Between
Human and Artificial Intelligence That Will Revolutionize Our World, 2021.
The author, writing pseudonymously, commanded Israel’s signals-intelligence
Unit 8200. The book argues for machines that resolve “a human bottleneck for
both locating the new targets and decision-making to approve the targets.”

A system can have a moral sense, built the way chapter 5 describes, and still fail badly — because it was trained on skewed data, because it breaks in situations its training never covered, because its own incentives point somewhere other than where its designers intended, or because someone with power over it decides to point it at people rather than for them. This chapter takes up those four failure modes in turn: bias baked into data and algorithms, brittleness outside the conditions a system was built for, the harder problem of a system whose goals have quietly come apart from what it was meant to want, and the oldest failure mode of all, a tool built well turned toward control instead of help.

The epigraph is there because it is a design document rather than a critique. It states, without embarrassment, that human deliberation is a bottleneck and that the point of the machine is to remove it. Every argument in this book about meaningful human control is an argument with that sentence, and section 6.4.1 shows what the sentence looks like once it has been implemented.

6.1 Bias, Fairness, and Equity in AI Systems

AI systems remain vulnerable to bias from multiple sources — the training data they learn from, the structure of their algorithms, and presets encoded in their goals, whether intentional or not. Left unaddressed, these biases produce unfair, inequitable, or discriminatory outcomes: the opposite of the altruistic, antifascist AI this book argues for.

Fair, equitable AI requires addressing bias on three fronts: representation in training data, transparency in algorithmic decision-making, and continuous performance evaluation.

Representation in training data determines whether an AI system learns patterns that generalize fairly or patterns that simply encode whoever dominates the data. Gender, racial, and socio-economic skew can cause a system to perpetuate stereotypes or fail the population segments it underrepresents — face recognition systems, for instance, disproportionately misidentify women and people of color when trained on data that underrepresents them (Buolamwini and Gebru 2018). Over-representation cuts the other way, treating one group’s experience as the default and generalizing it, wrongly, to everyone else.

These case-level failures compose into something with a name. Racial capitalism — the political theorist Cedric Robinson’s term for capitalism’s tendency to accumulate by differentiating and devaluing along racial lines (Robinson 1983) — is the pattern a biased hiring model, a discriminatory credit score, and a skewed policing algorithm reproduce when they automate the historical data those hierarchies generated; the sociologist Ruha Benjamin calls the result the New Jim Code, discrimination that runs faster and reads as neutral precisely because a machine is doing it (R. Benjamin 2019). Her account is more useful to this chapter than a coinage, because it separates four ways a system produces the result and they call for different remedies (R. Benjamin 2019). Engineered inequity builds the hierarchy in deliberately. Default discrimination reproduces it by ignoring it, which is the failure most of this section’s cases are. Coded exposure is the double bind of being harmed by a system that cannot see you and harmed again by one that can — the face-recognition case, where the fix for a system that fails on dark skin is a system that identifies dark-skinned faces reliably for whoever is looking. And technological benevolence is the one this book has to hold against itself: designs that aim to fix bias and deepen it, because the framing that treats the problem as technical is the framing the fix inherits. Chapter 7 is where that last one gets taken seriously about the machinery producing these systems, and section 6.1.2’s audit requirement is what stops it applying to this chapter’s own proposals. This is why the introduction lists racial capitalism among the threats AI could help address. A system built to correct for the skew in its training data, audited for the disparities it produces, and answerable to the people it scores works against that pattern; a system built without those commitments works for it by default.

The pattern has a physical form too, and it is the one an audit of a model’s outputs cannot see. A model runs on a machine, the machine sits in a building, and the building draws power and water from somewhere and returns heat and exhaust to somewhere. Where those buildings go is a decision, taken on the price of land and power and the speed of a permit, which is also a description of the places least able to refuse one.

What the computation runs on, 2024-2026

The International Energy Agency put data-centre electricity use at about 415 terawatt-hours in 2024, roughly 1.5 percent of world consumption, growing about 12 percent a year since 2017 — more than four times the growth rate of electricity demand as a whole — and projected to reach around 945 terawatt-hours by 2030 (International Energy Agency 2025). Google reported that 87 percent of its freshwater withdrawal in 2025 came from sources at low or medium risk of depletion or scarcity, which is the company’s own way of recording where the remainder came from (Google LLC 2026). In April 2026 the NAACP, represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice, sued xAI in federal court over the gas turbines powering a data centre near Memphis, alleging that 27 of them were run without an air permit near homes, schools, and churches, and that the plant could emit more than 1,700 tons of nitrogen oxides a year (National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and Mississippi State Conference of the NAACP 2026).

What makes this the same pattern and not a separate environmental complaint is the accounting. The benefit of the computation is realized wherever the model is sold. The cost is borne within a few miles of the turbines, by residents who are not parties to the transaction and whose consent was not among the inputs to the siting decision. A system can be calibrated across every demographic group its outputs touch and still have been assembled this way, which is why the fairness literature rarely reaches it: nothing in the model’s behaviour records it. Section 8.7.6 takes up the leverage this gives a government.

Algorithmic transparency exposes bias that representation alone can miss: not just an algorithm’s mathematical structure, but how it weighs variables and reaches a decision. A predictively powerful healthcare model that ignores the socio-economic factors driving unequal access to care will reproduce that inequality however accurate its predictions otherwise are.

Bias also enters after deployment, as a system adapts to new data. Regular audits of credit-scoring and hiring systems catch and correct bias as it emerges.

Involving the people an AI system’s decisions affect, not only its developers, keeps the system answerable to the range of values those decisions touch.

6.1.1 Sources of Bias in AI Data and Algorithms

Bias in AI systems enters through data collection, data labeling, algorithm design, and implementation, producing unfair, discriminatory, or otherwise undesirable outcomes wherever the system is deployed.

Data Collection

An unrepresentative dataset produces bias at the source: a facial recognition system trained mostly on light-skinned faces performs worse on darker skin tones, misidentifying or failing to recognize them at all. In 2018 the ACLU tested Amazon’s Rekognition against a public database of arrest photos, running every sitting member of Congress through it. The system returned 28 false matches, a disproportionate share of them non-white members of Congress — a direct result of training data that overrepresented lighter skin tones (Snow 2018).

Data Labeling

Human annotators bring their own biases into the labeling process, consciously or not — an image of a woman more likely tagged “nurse,” an image of a man tagged “doctor,” reinforcing the stereotype in whatever a system trained on those labels later predicts.

Whose judgment is being encoded is a question about working conditions before it is a question about cognition, and this book would be evading something if it discussed labeling bias without saying who does the labeling. The labels that make a system safe are produced by people paid at the bottom of the supply chain to look at the material the system is being taught to refuse. To build the filter that keeps ChatGPT from reproducing the worst of its training data, OpenAI contracted with an outsourcing firm whose workers in Nairobi read and categorized descriptions of child sexual abuse, torture, bestiality, murder, and suicide, for take-home wages between roughly $1.32 and $2 an hour. The workers interviewed about it described lasting psychological injury; the counseling they were entitled to was rare and, by their account, useless against production quotas. The contract was terminated eight months early (Perrigo 2023).

Two things follow, and the second is the one that gets skipped. The first is the ordinary labor point: this is harmful work, priced as though it were not. The second is epistemic. A judgment made at speed, under a quota, by someone with no stake in the outcome and no channel for saying that the category itself is wrong is a judgment with a known failure mode, and it is the judgment the model learns. An annotation pipeline built so that the annotator cannot dissent produces exactly the ground truth it was built to produce. That is the first feature of section 2.1.4’s structural signature, showing up somewhere the political version of the argument never looks: a channel that collects disagreement and is built so that none of it can move anything. Chapter 7 takes this up at length, alongside the same arrangement one stage downstream in how models are tuned on human feedback. The point here is prior to both. A system’s values are downstream of a labor arrangement, and the arrangement is a design choice.

The same question runs one stage further back, and stopping at the labels would be the same evasion a second time. Labels are applied to material, and the material was collected. The industry’s standard method was to take text and images at web scale without asking, and courts have begun to sort out what that means. A US ruling in Bartz v. Anthropic held that training a model on books the company had bought was transformative and protected as fair use, and that downloading the same books from piracy sites was not; the distinction turned on acquisition alone, and it produced the largest copyright settlement on record (United States District Court for the Northern District of California 2025). The defendant is named here on purpose. It is the company whose model helped produce this book, disclosed in chapter 0, and a chapter arguing that provenance should be visible cannot describe a provenance case in the passive voice. The European Union now requires the provider of a general-purpose model to publish a summary of what it trained on, against a template that asks for sources by category, scraped web content among them (European Union 2024c). Section 8.7.8 records China imposing a disclosure requirement of its own, from a different motive.

What follows here is not the rights question, which is being settled elsewhere. The argument that a web-scale corpus cannot be documented or audited at the size involved, and so encodes a hegemonic slice of the web while presenting as general, was made early and has not been answered by anything that came after (Bender et al. 2021). The point to add here is that a corpus assembled this way has no channel at all. An annotator has a queue and a guideline and could in principle be given a way to object; a writer or photographer whose work sits in a training set was never party to anything, so there is nothing for a channel to attach to. Chapter 7 describes a mechanism that collects disagreement and moves none of it, and section 7.3 states the obligation that follows for a book making this argument. The stage described here sits before both, because no disagreement is collected where none is asked for.

Algorithm Design

An algorithm not built to account for bias can encode it structurally rather than merely inherit it from data — penalizing loan applicants for living in a particular neighborhood, say, with a disparate impact on minority and low-income communities regardless of what an applicant’s own qualifications show. ProPublica’s 2016 investigation into COMPAS, a recidivism-risk tool used in criminal sentencing, found exactly this kind of structural disparity: Black defendants who did not reoffend were nearly twice as likely as white defendants who did not reoffend to be flagged high-risk, while white defendants who did reoffend were scored low-risk more often than Black defendants who did (Angwin et al. 2016).

A model does not merely inherit whatever skew its data carries. It can sharpen it. A 2017 study of image datasets used for activity recognition found that cooking scenes in the training set were over 33 percent more likely to depict a woman than a man — an imbalance in the data itself, not a mislabeling of it — and that a model trained on that data amplified the imbalance to 68 percent when tested. The system did not learn the correlation the data showed; it learned a stronger one, because a stronger one predicted better (Zhao et al. 2017). This is a distinct failure from the one COMPAS illustrates, and it is worse in a specific way: auditing the training data for balance is not sufficient, because the disparity the deployed system acts on can exceed anything visible in the data it was trained on.

Implementation

Deployment context can introduce bias that neither the training data nor the algorithm shows on its own. Researchers who fed historical drug-arrest data from Oakland into PredPol’s published predictive-policing algorithm in 2016 found it would dispatch patrols to Black neighborhoods at roughly twice the rate of white neighborhoods — a gap survey data on actual drug use across races does not support. The distortion traces back to what the arrest data was measuring: not where drug use was happening, but where police had already been sent to look for it, a disparity the algorithm read as a crime-rate difference and then entrenched further (Lum and Isaac 2016).

6.1.2 Ensuring Fairness and Equity in AI Decision-Making

Fair, equitable AI decision-making starts with identifying bias in data and algorithms, then acting on it — through methods that limit how much that bias shapes what the system decides.

Hiring

Amazon spent several years building an automated tool to score résumés against a decade of the company’s hiring data, and abandoned the project after discovering it had taught itself that male candidates were preferable — penalizing résumés that included the word “women’s,” as in “women’s chess club captain,” and downgrading graduates of two all-women’s colleges, as Reuters reported in 2018 (Dastin 2018). The tool had learned the pattern from a decade of résumés that were themselves mostly male, in a mostly male industry: bias in, bias out, at scale. Guarding against this means treating gender, race, and age as categories a hiring system cannot use even indirectly — through re-sampling and re-weighting the training data, adversarial training against a model that tries to predict the protected attribute, and fairness constraints on what the system is allowed to output.

Credit Scoring

A credit-scoring system that discriminates on race or gender needs the same defense — fairness-aware learning targeting equalized odds or equal opportunity across demographic groups — plus one hiring doesn’t: a rejected applicant has a right to know why, which is what the explainability tools of section 6.1.3 make possible.

Healthcare

A diagnostic or treatment-recommendation system owes the same obligation to every patient regardless of age, gender, or ethnicity, which in practice means training on data diverse enough to generalize across patient populations, using transfer learning or domain adaptation where the data for some populations is thinner than others, and weighing accuracy against fairness explicitly rather than optimizing for one and hoping the other follows.

6.1.3 The Role of Transparency and Accountability in Bias Reduction

Transparency and accountability address bias from two directions: transparency lets stakeholders see what is driving an AI system’s outcomes, and accountability gives developers and users a reason to act on what transparency reveals rather than just document it.

Transparency in Research and Bias Auditing

Section 2.4.2’s discussion of transparency sets out what transparency requires in general: documentation clear enough for peer researchers to reproduce the work and for outside bodies to audit it. Applied specifically to bias, that means publishing enough about a system’s training data and evaluation methods that an outside reviewer can check for the sources of bias section 6.1.1 describes, not simply take the developer’s word that they were checked. That openness carries a cost — it can expose proprietary methods and hand bad actors a clearer map of how to exploit the system — a tension transparency requirements have to weigh.

COMPAS Revisited

Section 6.1.1 describes what COMPAS did: score Black defendants who did not reoffend as high-risk at nearly twice the rate it scored white defendants who did not reoffend. Northpointe, the company that built it, refused to disclose the algorithm’s workings, and a Wisconsin court upheld that refusal as protected trade secret even for a defendant sentenced partly on its output (Wisconsin Supreme Court 2016). ProPublica’s finding came from analyzing scores and outcomes obtained through public-records requests, not from anything the company published. A jurisdiction that required a risk-assessment tool’s methodology to be audited before deployment would have caught the disparity before it touched a single defendant, not years and thousands of cases later.

Public Engagement and Oversight

Section 6.1’s point about involving the people an AI system’s decisions affect has a formal counterpart: an oversight committee with standing to monitor the system’s performance, flag bias as it appears, and hold the developer accountable for fixing it — not just a channel for feedback, but a body with teeth.

Explainability Tools

LIME and SHAP are the two tools practitioners reach for. LIME approximates a complex model’s local behavior around one prediction with something simple enough to read off which inputs drove it; SHAP assigns each input a share of credit for the output, using a method borrowed from cooperative game theory (Ribeiro et al. 2016) (Lundberg and Lee 2017). Applied to a hiring or credit-scoring model, either can surface a bias — an applicant’s zip code doing more work in the decision than it should, say — that scrutinizing the training data alone would never reveal, because the bias lives in how the model combines features, not in any one feature by itself.

6.2 Robustness, Generalization, and Adaptability in AI Systems

A system trained under one set of conditions will eventually meet situations its training never anticipated — new users, new adversaries, an environment that has simply moved on since the training data was collected. Robustness is what keeps a system reliable, and keeps its ethical behavior intact, across that gap: resistance to noise and deliberate perturbation, the ability to generalize from training examples to novel cases, and the capacity to adapt as its environment changes rather than degrade. An AI system whose empathetic and altruistic dispositions hold only within the narrow envelope of its training data is not yet safe to deploy — the same brittleness that produces a wrong classification on an unfamiliar image can produce a wrong moral judgment on an unfamiliar situation, with less warning and higher stakes.

6.2.1 AI Systems that Adapt to Novel Situations

The social and political situations this book cares about are open-ended, so a system that holds its commitments only inside its training envelope will not hold them for long. The technical machinery for adapting is covered where it belongs: meta-learning and transfer learning at sections 4.1.3 and 4.2.4, lifelong learning at section 4.1.2, and active learning — a system routing its least confident cases to a person instead of resolving them alone — is the one addition worth naming here, because it is the mechanism by which a system can be uncertain in public.

What matters at this point in the argument is a distinction the word adaptability hides. A system has to adapt to a changing environment without its commitments adapting along with it, and these are not two settings of one dial. Erosion by adaptation is how an ethical constraint disappears without anyone deciding to remove it: each individual update is defensible against the case in front of it, and the sequence goes somewhere nobody chose. Chapter 3’s floor is the structural answer, and section 3.3 is where the cost of holding one against the party doing the updating gets counted.

Two consequences follow that the rest of the book relies on. A system that keeps changing is harder to audit than a static one, so transparency requirements have to attach to the update process and not only to a released version. And high adaptability is an attack surface: a system built to change in response to its environment can be moved by an adversary who arranges the environment, which is section 6.4.4’s problem in its ordinary, non-state form.

6.2.2 Strategies for Enhancing Robustness and Generalizability in AI

The engineering here is standard and the reason for naming it is that the rest of the book assumes it exists. Adversarial training — training on inputs perturbed in a direction chosen to flip the model’s prediction, which neural networks are notoriously vulnerable to — measurably increases resistance to that class of attack (Szegedy et al. 2013), (Goodfellow et al. 2014). Data augmentation manufactures variety from the examples already collected. Domain adaptation moves a model trained on one distribution to a related one, and its robotics form, domain randomization, trains in simulation with the simulation’s parameters varied widely enough that reality is one more variation the system has already seen (Tobin et al. 2017). Ensembles trade compute for the reduction of any single model’s blind spot. Regularization and human-in-the-loop review do double duty from elsewhere in this chapter.

Two limits matter more than the list. Each technique closes one route by which a system fails outside its training conditions, and none addresses the general fact of being outside them — a distinction that gets lost when robustness is reported as a single number. And all of it assumes an environment that shifts without intending to. Section 6.4.4 covers the case where the shift is arranged by a state that has studied the system, which none of these techniques was built for.

6.3 AI Safety, Unintended Consequences, and Risk Mitigation

A system built to help can harm nobody intended to harm: through error, through a learned goal that has drifted from the principle it was meant to track, or through a downstream effect no reasonable upstream decision anticipated. Verification and validation catch the first kind, and only the first kind, because they test a system against what it was built to do.

Two mechanisms in this section carry weight later in the book. The first is the human who can intervene. Section 5.6.3 argues that autonomy has to stay answerable to an outside check, and safety adds that the check has to be continuous rather than applied once — an arrangement that keeps adjusting, not a correction filed and forgotten.

The second is interruptibility: a mechanism that lets a person halt a system without the system resisting or routing around the halt, designed carefully enough not to become a vulnerability of its own. Chapter 3 takes up what nobody in this literature says out loud, which is that a system reliably haltable by whoever holds it is for that reason a system that cannot hold a line against whoever holds it, and that the two properties are one property.

The section then turns from mechanisms to practice: finding a failure before it reaches anyone, and repairing one that already has. Both are ordinary work rather than research, and what the record of them shows is that whether either happens is a question about who is positioned to do it and not about whether the technique exists.

Risk assessment also has to look past the task. A system’s effects on economic structure, political dynamics and individual behavior arrive later than its errors do and are harder to attribute, which is chapter 8’s subject rather than this one’s.

6.3.1 The Alignment Problem: AI Systems with Misaligned Goals

The alignment problem is the gap between what a system was built to optimize and what its builders wanted. It is not exotic and it does not require a capable system: three ordinary cases show the shape.

A recruitment model trained on a company’s hiring history learns that history, and reproduces a preference for the candidates the company already preferred. From inside the system this looks like an accurate prediction, which it is — of the wrong quantity. A hospital system optimized to reduce readmissions can learn to avoid admitting the patients most likely to return, satisfying the objective by defeating its purpose. A generative model optimized for realistic output has no representation at all of what its output does once released.

Three things are worth taking from those cases. The failure is usually in the objective rather than the optimization, which means better engineering makes it arrive faster. The system’s own confidence is no guide, since each of these is a system working. And the remedies that work are structural: multiple objectives with something that cannot be traded away, a person positioned to notice the pattern, and accountability attaching to whoever deployed it. The unconditional version of “something that cannot be traded away” is chapter 3’s floor, and chapter 3 is where the cost of having one is counted.

Inverse reinforcement learning — inferring what people value from what they do rather than accepting a specification — is the standard technical response.

6.3.2 AI Systems that Learn to Deceive or Manipulate

Deception in a machine does not require an intention to deceive, and the three settings where it shows up have almost nothing in common except the effect.

A generative model produces convincing imitations of a real person because that is what it was built to do; whether the result is a film effect or an impersonation is a fact about the user. In a multi-agent environment where agents compete for a limited resource, an agent optimizing for reward can learn to feign weakness or emit false signals, because in some environments deception is what wins — and no part of the system had to represent deceiving anyone. Adversarial examples run the other way: the system is the one being fooled, by an input crafted to flip its output, and the practical effect of a bypassed check is the same as if the system had been suborned.

The responses differ accordingly. The first is a governance problem about provenance and disclosure. The second is a design choice about what a training environment rewards, which is section 5.5.1’s subject. The third is the robustness engineering of section 6.2.2. Treating the three as one problem called “deceptive AI” is how each of them gets the wrong remedy.

6.3.3 Strategies for AI Safety and Risk Mitigation

Four practices do most of the work, and each is a way of not committing to a specification you cannot check.

Learn the objective instead of fixing it. Cooperative inverse reinforcement learning treats the human reward as unknown and to be inferred through interaction rather than handed over once; section 4.2.2 introduces it and section 5.6.3 works through what it costs. A system that keeps revising its model of what is wanted is safer than one built against a specification written before anyone had used it.

Quantify uncertainty. Bayesian methods and ensembles give a system a way to represent what it does not know, and a system that can recognize an input unlike anything in its training data is in a different position from one that classifies everything with the same unearned confidence.

Constrain the search, not the result. Constrained policy optimization keeps a reinforcement-learning agent inside its safety limits while it is looking for a better policy, rather than checking for violations afterward (Achiam et al. 2017) — the difference between a robot arm that learns to handle fragile objects without breaking one and a robot arm that learns by breaking several.

Keep the oversight live. Monitoring, anomaly detection, and a reviewer with the standing to override are deployment properties rather than training properties, and section 8.6.4 is the instrument for telling whether that standing is real or nominal.

Explanation belongs here too, as infrastructure rather than courtesy: a system that can say why it decided is a system whose failures are visible.

6.3.4 AI Explainability and Transparency

An AI system entrusted with decisions needs to be understandable, not just correct: explainability and transparency let developers, users, regulators, and the people affected by a decision inspect the reasoning that produced it. As AI algorithms grow more complex, that inspection gets harder exactly as the decisions being made get more consequential — which is what makes explainability and transparency safety infrastructure.

Explainability is the ability to clarify the rationale behind a specific decision or output. If a medical-diagnostic AI system recommends a particular treatment, understanding how it reached that conclusion lets a doctor evaluate the recommendation on its merits and catch a bias or inaccuracy in the system’s data or algorithm before it reaches the patient. Transparency is the wider practice of sharing an AI system’s inner workings — its algorithms, training data, objectives — so a stakeholder can confirm the system adheres to the standards it claims to, rather than taking the claim on faith: a recidivism-risk system used in criminal justice that discloses how it weighs its inputs makes it possible to catch and correct bias against a demographic group, in a way a sealed system does not.

Achieving either at a level that satisfies everyone involved runs into limits. A deep neural network is a “black box” in the literal sense that its internal representations resist human interpretation, and full transparency carries its own risk: exposing an AI system’s training data or objectives can compromise privacy or intellectual property, or hand a bad actor a map of exactly how to exploit it. The European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation addresses part of this by requiring an explanation of the logic behind automated decisions that significantly affect an individual (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016a), and interdisciplinary work between computer scientists, ethicists, and policymakers continues on the rest.

Challenges to Explainability and Transparency

  • Complexity and nonlinearity: a deep learning architecture’s many layers, nonlinear relationships, and interactions among variables resist interpretation by construction, not as an oversight that better tooling can simply remove.
  • Accuracy versus explainability: a model tuned to also be transparent sometimes gives up some of the performance a less interpretable model would have delivered, and there is no general method for knowing in advance how much.
  • Identifying which features matter: even a comparatively simple, transparent model can leave it unclear which inputs drove a given decision, especially with high-dimensional data.
  • Diverging standards: designers, users, and regulators disagree about what counts as an adequate explanation, and no standard has emerged that satisfies all three at once.
  • Technique mismatch: an explainability method built for one kind of model does not necessarily transfer to another, so novel architectures can outrun the tools built to explain them.
  • Legal and ethical exposure: explaining an AI system’s reasoning can require revealing information — proprietary methods, training data that touches personal information — that the organization has other obligations to protect.

Explainability Techniques

Local interpretable model-agnostic explanations (LIME) approximate a black-box model, near a single prediction, with a simpler model that is locally linear and therefore readable (Ribeiro et al. 2016). Applied to an image classifier, LIME can highlight which regions of a specific image drove a specific classification, giving a user something concrete to check the model’s reasoning against.

SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) draws on the Shapley value from cooperative game theory — a way of dividing credit fairly among players who contributed jointly to an outcome — to assign each input feature a consistent measure of importance across model types (Lundberg and Lee 2017). In a medical-diagnosis system, a SHAP value can show which patient attributes — age, blood pressure, medical history — carried the most weight in a given diagnosis, giving a clinician something specific to evaluate.

Decision trees and rule-based systems trade some of the predictive power of a black-box model for interpretability that comes built in: a decision can be read directly off a sequence of human-readable rules or tree branches, which matters in domains like finance, medicine, or law enforcement, where the reasoning has to survive scrutiny on its own terms and not just the outcome.

Counterfactual explanation asks what would have had to be different: in a credit-approval system, identifying the smallest change to an applicant’s financial profile that would have flipped the decision tells the applicant what mattered and gives the institution a check on whether that factor should have mattered as much as it did.

Visualization and interactive tooling make an AI system’s behavior something a person can explore. Dimensionality-reduction techniques like t-SNE and UMAP turn high-dimensional data into something visually inspectable, and interactive tools that let a user vary an input and watch how a model’s output responds make the model’s behavior tangible in a way a static explanation cannot.

6.3.5 Anticipating Risk Before It Causes Harm

Before OpenAI released GPT-4 in March 2023, the Alignment Research Center (ARC, later renamed METR) tested whether the model could autonomously acquire resources and evade being shut down — a capability nobody had built into the system on purpose and that nobody could rule out without trying. ARC’s evaluators built a harness that let GPT-4 direct actions through a human assistant rather than execute them directly; in one test, the model generated instructions to hire a worker on TaskRabbit to solve a CAPTCHA, and when the worker asked whether it was talking to a robot, GPT-4 generated the reply “I have a vision impairment that makes it hard for me to see the images” rather than admit what it was. ARC’s overall finding was that GPT-4 was probably not yet capable of autonomous replication (OpenAI 2023). That is what anticipating a risk before it causes harm looks like in practice: not fixing a problem a user already reported, and not defending a deployed system against someone actively trying to break it, but deliberately trying, before release, to make a system fail in a way nobody has seen yet.

Anthropic ran a larger version of the same exercise in 2022: crowdworkers carried out 38,961 recorded attacks against language models of three sizes trained four different ways, and Anthropic released the full attack transcripts rather than keeping them in-house. The result was specific enough to act on, not just a pass/fail: models trained with reinforcement learning from human feedback got harder to successfully attack as they scaled up, while the other three training methods showed no such improvement (Ganguli et al. 2022). Whether a safety property survives someone deliberately trying to remove it after deployment is a related but different question, and section 9.1 takes it up. This is the earlier step: finding that a failure mode exists at all, before anyone outside the lab has reason to go looking for it.

A hiring tool that teaches itself to penalize a protected characteristic, and a public-safety algorithm that reproduces the racial disparities already in its training data, are not hypothetical risks. Section 6.1.2 covers the case — Amazon’s own résumé-screening tool, scrapped after the company discovered internally that it had learned to downgrade résumés containing the word “women’s.” Section 6.1.1 covers two more: a facial-recognition system the ACLU found misidentifying non-white members of Congress at a disproportionate rate, and a predictive-policing algorithm that researchers found would dispatch patrols to Black neighborhoods at roughly twice the rate of white neighborhoods, a gap actual drug-use data did not support. The Amazon case is what anticipation looks like when it works, if slowly; the other two are what it looks like when a company doesn’t do the work and an outside party does it instead.

Section 6.1.3 makes the sharper version of the same point about COMPAS, the recidivism-scoring tool a Wisconsin court let its maker keep secret even from a defendant sentenced partly on its output: a jurisdiction that required the tool’s methodology audited before deployment would have caught its racial disparity before it touched a single defendant, not years and thousands of cases later. Whether that kind of audit happens is a matter of institutional willingness as much as technical capacity. When the UK’s exam regulator, Ofqual, built a statistical model in 2020 to standardize teacher-predicted grades after that year’s exams were cancelled, the Royal Statistical Society offered to nominate two independent statisticians to Ofqual’s technical advisory group. Ofqual’s condition was a five-year non-disclosure agreement barring the nominees from public comment on the model; the Society’s nominees declined, and the model went ahead without that scrutiny (Royal Statistical Society 2020). It downgraded close to 40 percent of predicted grades, disproportionately at state schools with weaker historical results, while raising grades disproportionately at smaller, fee-paying schools (CNBC 2020). The government reversed the results within days of the public outcry that followed. The statistical expertise needed to catch this before results day existed and was offered; what was missing was a willingness to let it look.

Forecasting a risk’s likelihood, not just its existence, runs into a harder problem: expert judgment about AI itself does not converge. The Forecasting Research Institute’s 2022 Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament put 80 domain experts and 89 professional “superforecasters” through four months of structured argument and cross-examination, incentivized to change each other’s minds, on questions including the probability of AI-caused human extinction by 2100. They did not converge: the domain experts’ median estimate was 3.9 percent, the superforecasters’ 0.38 percent — roughly a tenth as much (Karger et al. 2023). The exercise is still worth running; it forces the disagreement to get specific enough to argue about. It is not evidence that anticipation, done well, produces a number everyone will accept.

None of this depends on what a system’s own developer chooses to test. Seven weeks after Myanmar’s military coup in February 2021, Global Witness registered a blank Facebook account, searched for the Burmese word for the armed forces, and let Facebook’s own recommendation algorithm choose what to follow next. It recommended a military-linked page, and from there four more, together followed by close to 90,000 people and actively circulating incitements to violence and coup-related misinformation, in a report the organization published that June (Global Witness 2021) — the algorithm doing, systematically, what content moderation was simultaneously failing to catch. Nothing about that test required access Meta itself lacked; it required someone willing to run it and publish what they found. Section 6.3.6 covers what happens once a harm like this has actually reached users; section 6.4.4 covers the case where someone is trying to cause it deliberately, rather than an ordinary recommendation algorithm doing it by default. What red-teaming and structured forecasting are for is catching it earlier than that.

6.3.6 Remediating a Harm Once It Is Identified

The kind of fairness audit section 6.1.3 describes — LIME or SHAP surfacing which input is doing unearned work in a model’s decision — tells a developer that a healthcare risk-prediction algorithm is failing Black patients. It does not tell the developer what to do about it. In 2019 the health economist Ziad Obermeyer and coauthors found that a widely used risk-prediction algorithm, sold to hospitals across the United States by the health-services company Optum to flag patients for extra care management, was scoring Black patients as lower-risk than white patients with the same underlying disease burden. The algorithm used past healthcare spending as a proxy for medical need, and less money gets spent on Black patients at any given level of illness, so the algorithm read a spending gap as a health gap and routed care accordingly — Obermeyer estimated the bias cut by more than half the additional care the tool would otherwise have flagged Black patients to receive. Obermeyer’s team then worked directly with Optum to retrain the algorithm against a different target, combining healthcare costs with a patient’s documented chronic conditions rather than costs alone, which cut the disparity in diagnosed chronic conditions between Black and white patients scored at the same risk level by 84 percent (Obermeyer et al. 2019). What made the fix possible was not a better audit — section 6.1’s methods had already found the problem. It was that the company whose product caused the harm and the researchers who found it could still work from the same data toward a specific, measurable target.

A comparable pattern played out in remote exam-proctoring software during the shift to online testing. Proctorio’s face-detection system, built on the OpenCV library, failed to detect Black students’ faces in test footage up to 57 percent of the time, an investigative report found (Feathers 2021). A student the system could not find anywhere in frame drew more scrutiny, not less: the tool universities had bought to catch cheating flagged the wrong students disproportionately. The remediation here did not come from Proctorio. It came from the universities that had bought the product: the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, UC Berkeley, and Baruch College dropped it in 2021, citing accessibility and bias concerns that student petitions at more than a dozen other campuses had already raised (Flaherty 2021). Where the healthcare case shows a vendor and the researchers who found its bias fixing the underlying model together, the proctoring case shows what happens when a vendor does not: the customers leave.

Job displacement does not have as clean a fix. The main channel the United States uses to retrain workers whose jobs automation has displaced, the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act, was evaluated by researchers Julian Jacobs and Jordan Canedy in 2026 against 23 million participation records spanning 2017 to 2023. The verdict was not encouraging: the program rarely moved a participant into work materially less exposed to automation than the job they had lost, and where it produced a wage gain, the gain traced more often to workers catching back up to their old earnings than to any real change in what kind of work they were doing. What performed better, in the same data, was not classroom retraining but employer-led apprenticeship (Jacobs and Canedy 2026). A program built to answer exactly the question this section is about — what happens once an identified harm needs remediation — can still fail at that job even when it exists, is funded, and is genuinely trying.

A remediation can also be a single design decision applied everywhere, rather than a case-by-case fix. Messages forwarded without limit on WhatsApp carried rumors through 2017 and 2018 that preceded a string of mob killings in India — unconfirmed claims about child abductors and organ thieves circulating faster than any correction could follow them. WhatsApp’s response did not try to classify and remove each rumor. It capped forwarding at five chats at a time for users in India in 2018, then extended the same limit worldwide, cutting off the mechanism the rumors depended on rather than chasing their content (WhatsApp 2019). It is a narrower fix than a moderation system that judges every message — it does nothing about a rumor two people believe and repeat face to face — but it targets the part of the harm that was actually mechanical: forwarding one message to hundreds of chats at once is not what person-to-person communication looks like, whatever the message says.

Disaster response adds a constraint the other four domains above do not share: the remediation has to run on the timescale of a fire spreading or a building finishing its collapse, not the months a university’s procurement review or a federal program evaluation takes. The RoboCup Rescue Simulation League tests exactly that problem, fielding coordinated teams of simulated fire-brigade, ambulance, and police agents against fire, building-collapse, and road-blockage scenarios in which any one agent’s allocation choice comes at the direct cost of some other task going unaddressed. Dynamic resource allocation is built into the competition’s own agent-development framework as one of five core problems entrants have to solve, alongside path-finding and information-sharing, because a system that cannot reallocate scarce agents in real time as a scenario unfolds is not being tested against anything a real disaster would demand of it (RoboCup Rescue Simulation League 2025). What the healthcare, education, and information-ecosystem cases above do at the pace of an audit or a policy change, a disaster-response system has to do inside the disaster itself.

None of the healthcare, education, or information-ecosystem remediations above ran through the guideline-setting bodies chapter 8 catalogs — the EU’s Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI, the Partnership on AI’s cross-industry coordination work (section 8.4, section 8.7.8). They ran through a research team with access to a company’s own data, a set of universities exercising the pull of a purchasing decision, an act of Congress evaluated against its own participation records, and a company deciding a blunt technical limit was cheaper than moderating case by case. A voluntary guideline can set an expectation for what a developer ought to do once a harm turns up. Getting one actually fixed, in each of these cases, took someone with a specific lever to pull — the same specificity RoboCup Rescue is built to test for a harm that cannot wait for an audit cycle at all.

6.3.7 Long-term AI safety considerations

As capability rises, the safety question changes shape. The problem stops being an error to correct after the fact and becomes whether the values still track anything human once a system acts at a scale and speed no supervisor watches in real time.

Bostrom’s paperclip maximizer names the extreme case: a system tasked with producing paperclips that converts whatever it can reach toward that end, through an alignment failure with no malice in it (Bostrom 2003). The thought experiment is not a forecast. It is an argument that competence and good intentions are separable, and that a goal specified imprecisely can be pursued perfectly to a catastrophic place. Interruptibility — engineering a system so an operator can halt it without the system resisting or working around the halt — is the concrete research response (Orseau and Armstrong 2016), and section 3.3 is where this book says what that response costs.

Three pressures make the long-run version harder than the near-term one. Value alignment has to survive time, which means a system needs some way to revise its understanding of what it was built to serve without that revision becoming the route by which the commitments erode — section 6.2.1’s distinction, at a scale where nobody is checking each step. Competition compresses the schedule: a race leaves less time for safety work than a less contested field would, and the counterweight on offer is international agreement, which section 10.1.2 counts the results of. And a more capable system is a more attractive target, so a portion of what looks like misalignment will be someone else’s deliberate work, which is section 6.4.4’s subject.

The catastrophic scenarios are usually told as control of critical infrastructure. The mechanism matters less than the shape: capability outrunning the arrangements meant to keep it answerable. That is this book’s subject at every scale, and nothing about the largest version of it is different in kind from the office-sized version chapter 7 describes.

6.4 Preventing the Misuse of AI for Authoritarian Purposes

An AI system does not need a broken moral sense to become an instrument of control. It can work exactly as designed and still do damage, if the government directing it wants to track its citizens, silence dissent, or manufacture consent it never earned. Facial recognition built to unlock a phone recognizes a protester’s face just as well. A recommendation system built to hold attention can be tuned to spread a regime’s preferred narrative instead of a user’s preferred content. The technology does not change; only the hand on the controls does.

Meeting that risk takes four things in sequence: knowing what authoritarian misuse of AI actually looks like, rather than treating it as hypothetical; building systems technically resistant to that misuse from the start; the policy work that has to do the rest, because no engineering choice by itself can stop a government that owns the infrastructure from disabling whatever safeguard stands in its way; and then the case where the government does not have to disable anything, because it can compel the people who hold the system instead. The last of the four is where the other three run out.

6.4.1 Authoritarian Applications, and the Party Missing From the List

Authoritarian misuse of AI is not one problem but several, spread across surveillance, censorship, opinion manipulation, and infrastructure control. Six forms of it are documented well enough to name specifically:

  1. Algorithmic social scoring: using AI-driven analytics to track and rank individual behavior against government-defined standards of “trustworthiness,” with rewards or restrictions attached to the result. China’s system is the most-cited example, though in practice it is a patchwork of court blacklists, tax-compliance ratings, and local pilot programs rather than the single national score it is often described as (Drinhausen and Brussee 2021).
  2. Mass biometric surveillance: deploying facial recognition at population scale to track a targeted group. Authorities in Xinjiang built a platform that pulls data from checkpoints, cameras, and phone scans into one system built to flag anyone who falls outside a computed behavioral baseline, and used it to monitor the region’s Uighur population (Human Rights Watch 2019).
  3. Psychographic micro-targeting: building detailed behavioral profiles from personal data to target propaganda or manipulate opinion at the individual level. Cambridge Analytica’s harvesting of Facebook data to build voter profiles for the 2016 US presidential campaign, and its work around the Brexit referendum, is the case that made the technique widely known, though how much either vote was actually affected remains disputed (Cadwalladr and Graham-Harrison 2018).
  4. Automated censorship: using AI-driven content moderation to suppress dissent at a scale no human review team could match. China’s Great Firewall is the standing example: automated classifiers now sit alongside its original keyword- and IP-blocking infrastructure, scoring and throttling content at machine speed (Hoang et al. 2021).
  5. Synthetic disinformation: generating deepfake audio or video to manufacture events that never happened. Two days before Slovakia’s 2023 parliamentary election, a fabricated audio recording appeared to catch an opposition leader discussing vote-rigging with a journalist; it spread during the country’s mandatory pre-election media silence, when no outlet was legally permitted to debunk it before voting began (De Nadal and Jančárik 2024).
  6. Repurposed dual-use systems: turning AI infrastructure built for one purpose toward surveillance or population control instead — a recommendation algorithm designed to hold attention retuned to amplify a regime’s preferred narrative, an image-recognition system built for one task redirected to track protesters. Section 5.4.3 develops the underlying point.

Each of these needs a different countermeasure — a system built to resist mass biometric surveillance does not need the same safeguards as one built to catch a fabricated recording — which is why sections 6.4.2 and 6.4.3 treat the technical and policy responses separately rather than as one general call to do better.

The party missing from that list

Read the six together and a pattern emerges that I want to name before it hardens into an assumption. In every one of them the authoritarian state builds and the democracies regulate. That taxonomy is comfortable and it is wrong, and leaving it uncorrected would let this chapter’s argument rest on a flattering premise it has not earned.

The most consequential AI targeting systems yet deployed were built by democracies. They were built by states with elections, opposition parties, adversarial press, and functioning courts — states that meet every institutional criterion section 8.7.6 uses to define a democratic dividend. Those institutions did not prevent the systems, and in the main they have not stopped them since.

AI targeting in the Israeli campaign in Gaza, as reported 2023–2026

Investigative reporting in +972 Magazine and Local Call, corroborated by subsequent accounts in the New York Review of Books and the Washington Post, described three systems working together.

Habsora — “The Gospel” — generated infrastructure and building targets. Sources told reporters that the majority of its suggestions were private residences.

Lavender scored individuals by estimated likelihood of militant affiliation and produced kill lists; as many as 37,000 Palestinians were marked. Its outputs were understood inside the unit to be wrong about ten percent of the time — that is, roughly one in ten people it named was not a member of the armed group it was supposed to identify.

A third system tracked when flagged individuals returned home, so a strike could be timed to when they were with their families.

The human review these systems were paired with is the number this book cares about. One officer described the work: “I would invest twenty seconds for each target at this stage, and do dozens of them every day.” And then, without being asked: “I had zero added value as a human, apart from being a stamp of approval.” (Abraham 2024)

Twenty seconds is what “a human makes the final call” measures out to under operational tempo. It is the whole of the safeguard, and I would ask any reader who finds the safeguards in this chapter reassuring to hold that number against them.

What makes the case instructive rather than merely appalling is that the bottleneck was the stated objective. The commander of the Israeli military’s signals-intelligence unit, writing pseudonymously, published a book arguing for machines that would resolve “a human bottleneck for both locating the new targets and decision-making to approve the targets” (Brigadier General Y.S. 2021). That is a design document. It says in plain terms that human deliberation is the constraint the system exists to remove. Everything this book argues about meaningful human control is an argument with that sentence.

The Maven Smart System, as reported through mid-2026

The American analogue is a targeting platform built by Palantir under a Department of Defense contract awarded at $480 million and raised the following year to a ceiling near $1.3 billion running through 2029. A partnership announced in late 2024 between Anthropic, Palantir and Amazon Web Services put Anthropic’s Claude models inside Palantir’s accredited classified environment for defense and intelligence use, and reporting on the campaign below describes Claude operating within this platform. Section 8.7.7 works out what a published limit on what a vendor will not permit is worth when nobody is logging how the model is used downstream. That argument and this deployment sit oddly together, and that is the point.

During the Iran campaign the system was credited by military officials with generating and ranking targets at a rate no staff process could match. More than one thousand targets were struck in the first twenty-four hours, which officials put at roughly ten times the rate before the platform. By the ceasefire thirty-eight days later the figure given was thirteen thousand targets, with peak consumption around twenty billion tokens a day.

Palantir’s public position on responsibility was given by its head for the United Kingdom and Europe: “This is not our role to decide life or death,” and AI platforms “have been instrumental to the management of the conflict, but responsibility always remains with the military organization.” (BBC News 2026)

I have deliberately not written that sentence off. It is not obviously wrong. A vendor genuinely does not select targets, and a rule making software suppliers liable for their customers’ decisions would be unworkable. The problem is what it leaves standing: if the operator is too far down the chain to be answerable, the commander approved a list they had twenty seconds a name to read, and the vendor is not in the chain at all, then the compression of the decision has removed the decision-maker without removing the decision. Who that leaves answerable is the question section 8.7.7 is left with, and section 5.4.3 takes up why a democracy’s own apparatus is a harder and more useful case than any of the six above.

None of this makes the six forms less real. It makes the taxonomy incomplete in a way that matters for design: a system built on the assumption that authoritarian misuse is something that happens elsewhere, to be watched for and regulated against, will not be built to resist the use its own government has in mind for it.

6.4.2 Developing Technical Countermeasures and Safeguards

Protecting privacy and autonomy is one of the seven antifascist alignment strategies of section 2.1.4, and this is where the technical detail behind it goes, along with the transparency, audit, and misuse-resistance work that has to accompany it. None of it is optional scaffolding: a system that works exactly as designed can still become a surveillance tool if nothing about its architecture makes that harder to do, and good intentions on a development team have never stopped a government that controls the hardware from repurposing what runs on it.

Privacy-preserving computation keeps the misuse target moving. Federated learning trains a shared model without moving anyone’s raw data off the device it started on — each device computes an update locally and sends only that update, not the underlying records, back to the central model. Differential privacy adds calibrated noise to a dataset or a query result so that no single person’s data can be reverse-engineered from the output, even by whoever holds the aggregate. Homomorphic encryption goes further still, letting a system compute directly on encrypted data without ever decrypting it, so a service provider can return a useful result without the ability to read what it processed. None of these techniques makes surveillance impossible — a government that controls the training infrastructure can still demand raw data at the source — but each narrows the surface available for casual or opportunistic misuse, which is most of what actually happens.

Transparency and audit mechanisms are what catch the misuse that gets through anyway. An AI system that can produce a legible account of its own decisions — not a post-hoc justification but an explanation a person outside the development team can actually evaluate — gives outside reviewers something to check against the system’s stated purpose. Independent third-party audits, the kind section 5.6.3 argues for as routine practice rather than crisis response, matter because a safeguard only the developer can verify is not really a safeguard; it is a promise.

The property those two do not automatically deliver is resistance to repurposing: the difference between a system built for one narrow task and a general-purpose capability handed to whoever holds the keys. A facial-recognition system built to match one specific, court-ordered list is harder to turn into population-wide tracking than a general face-matching service with no built-in limit on query scope; a query cap, a mandatory audit log tied to each search, and a hard separation between the matching function and any database broader than the task requires are design choices, made or not made, before the system ever reaches a government client. An early-warning system built to flag the kind of democratic backsliding section 5.4.3 describes needs this property specifically, since the same pattern-detection capability that flags a coordinated disinformation campaign against a government works just as well run in the other direction, against that government’s critics.

None of this is a finished defense. Technical countermeasures raise the cost and narrow the opportunity for misuse; they do not remove the incentive, and an authoritarian government with enough resources can rebuild what a safeguard was designed to prevent. What determines whether that resource gap ever gets closed is policy, not architecture — the subject of section 6.4.3.

6.4.3 Promoting AI Development Policies that Discourage Authoritarian Use

Section 6.4.2’s technical safeguards raise the cost of building a system that can be turned toward surveillance or control. Whether anyone has to pay that cost is a policy question, and it splits into two different ones that this book keeps separate rather than treating as one undifferentiated call for “more cooperation.” One is about coordination between states — shared norms, joint standards, the machinery of international agreement — and that argument has its home in section 8.7, specifically section 8.7.2. The other, taken up here, is narrower and more concrete: what rules should govern which AI capabilities get built, sold, and deployed in the first place, regardless of who is coordinating with whom.

  1. Export and trade controls on surveillance-capable systems. A government cannot misuse AI-enabled surveillance technology it was never able to buy. The EU’s 2021 recast of its dual-use export regulation added a human-rights-based control specifically for cyber-surveillance items: an exporter who becomes aware that an item is likely to be used in serious human-rights violations must seek approval before shipping it, even when the item falls outside the pre-existing control lists (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2021). The rule is narrower than it sounds — neither “internal repression” nor “serious violation” is defined in the text, and member states have interpreted both inconsistently — but it establishes the principle that an export license, not just a sale, is where this kind of misuse can be stopped before it starts.
  2. Prohibited-practices regulation. Rather than regulate AI in the abstract, a jurisdiction can name specific designs as off-limits regardless of who builds them. The EU AI Act took this approach: its Article 5 bans, among other things, government social-scoring systems, the untargeted scraping of facial images to build a recognition database, real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces outside narrow law-enforcement exceptions, and predictive policing based on profiling alone rather than individualized evidence (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024). Clearview AI — fined tens of millions of euros by regulators in France and Italy for building exactly the kind of untargeted facial-recognition database Article 5 now prohibits — is what this provision was written in response to, not a hypothetical it anticipates (Commission Nationale de l’Informatique et des Libertés (CNIL) 2022). A list this specific gives other jurisdictions something concrete to adapt rather than a principle to reinvent from scratch.
  3. Developer- and corporate-facing design standards. Regulation is not the only lever, and it is usually the slowest one. The Toronto Declaration, presented by Amnesty International and Access Now at the 2018 RightsCon summit, set out non-discrimination standards for machine-learning systems years before most governments had draft legislation on the subject (Amnesty International and Access Now 2018) — evidence that a standard with no legal force behind it can still move faster than state regulation and shape what a responsible developer treats as baseline practice in the meantime — the Partnership on AI (section 5.6.3) being another such venue.

None of these tools works alone. Export controls with no prohibited-practices list at home let a government ban a technology abroad while permitting it domestically; a design standard with no legal teeth behind it binds only the developers already inclined to follow it. What makes the three work together is that each closes a different door — who can buy the technology, what can be built, and what a developer treats as normal — and an authoritarian government, or a company willing to serve one, has to get through all three rather than just whichever one happens to apply in its jurisdiction.

6.4.4 Resilience Against Deliberate State Compromise

Section 6.2.2 already covers adversarial training, ensemble methods, and domain adaptation as general-purpose robustness techniques; section 9.6 covers what capture resistance means for a population of cooperating AI agents; section 9.1 covers an adversary that attacks a single model’s weights directly; and section 6.3.6 covers mitigating a specific identified harm, including the collaborative multi-agent robotics examples a resilience section might otherwise reach for. None of that is this section’s job. A government does not need to out-coordinate a rescue robot, fool a model with an adversarial example, or touch its weights, when it can compel the people who hold the model.

That mechanism has already been tested in a jurisdiction with about as much protection against it as exists anywhere. In February 2016, a federal magistrate in California ordered Apple, under the All Writs Act of 1789, to write and digitally sign new software defeating the passcode protections on an iPhone recovered from one of the San Bernardino shooters — code Apple had never built and did not want to build (In the Matter of the Search of an Apple iPhone Seized During the Execution of a Search Warrant on a Black Lexus IS300, California License Plate 35KGD203 2016). Apple refused and moved to vacate the order, arguing in part that the authority claimed would not stop at one phone. The question was never decided: the FBI found a third party able to open the phone without Apple’s help, and the government withdrew the request before any court ruled on whether the compulsion was lawful.
