Whether a democracy with an independent judiciary can force an unwilling company to compromise a system it built remains legally untested; a government less constrained by that judiciary does not need to win the argument first.

It is not hypothetical elsewhere. Section 8.7.8 documents China’s 2023 rules requiring generative AI providers to file their algorithms with the state and align generated content with government-designated values before public release — the same leverage Apple’s lawyers argued no court should grant, exercised not against one locked phone but against the models themselves, as a standing condition of operating in that jurisdiction rather than a one-time order.

Section 8.5.1 makes the parallel point about data: a federated design where no single server holds everyone’s raw data is a design a government cannot simply seize and repurpose, because the data was never in one place to seize. The same logic extends, partially, to a trained model. Weights already published and distributed beyond a developer’s control cannot be recalled by a court order aimed at that developer, whatever the order compels going forward, and maintainers spread across separate jurisdictions raise the cost of coercion the same way — a government can compel the entity within its reach, not the ones outside it.

None of that removes the leverage; it only raises its price. A developer with employees, offices, and legal existence inside a government’s borders answers to that government’s courts regardless of how the model itself is built, and no architectural choice changes who can be held in contempt, arrested, or shut down for refusing an order. The Apple case tested that leverage against a single locked phone and left the question unresolved. Nobody has tested it yet against a model built specifically to resist the government making the request.

Chapter 7
The Recuperation of Dissent

This chapter exists because the book kept making the same discovery in two places and never put them side by side.

Section 2.1.4 defines fascism as a structure rather than a costume, and the first of its four features is recuperation: an institution does not suppress disagreement, it metabolizes it. Refusal is converted into a managed appearance — a permitted outlet, a consultation, a feedback channel — which the institution can then point to as proof that it listens. The tell is that the mechanism exists, is used, and moves nothing.

That is a claim about institutions, and it was introduced to let a system recognize one. What this chapter argues is that the same structure is already built into the machinery that produces the systems themselves — twice in the pipeline that trains them, and a third time in the discourse that examines them — and that none of the three was designed by anyone who thought they were building a political arrangement.

The first is at the label. A training corpus is annotated by people working at speed under a quota, with no channel for saying that the category they have been given is the wrong category. The second is at the reward. A model is tuned on human feedback collected as pairwise comparisons, and persistent disagreement among the raters is averaged out in the same operation that records it. In both, disagreement is solicited at scale, deliberately, by a mechanism built so that none of it can move anything. The consultation is real, the participation is real, and the outcome is fixed with respect to what the participants say.

Three things follow that are worth having in one place rather than scattered.

The first is that this is not a criticism of anyone’s motives. Nobody built either arrangement in order to neutralize dissent. Both are ordinary engineering, arrived at because averaging is what you do with a distribution and a quota is what you do with a budget. That is the point section 2.1.4 makes about the molecular scale: the structure does its work whether or not anyone intends it, which is precisely why a detector tuned to intent will not find it.

The second is that the structure is invisible from inside any single instance. Each looks like ordinary aggregation. The annotator sees a queue, the rater sees a pair of responses, and the mechanism is functioning exactly as specified in both cases. Seeing it requires holding the two stages against a definition written for something else entirely, which is the only reason this book found it.

The third is the uncomfortable one. This book proposes that AI systems be built to detect the four-feature signature in institutions. The systems that would do the detecting are made by a process displaying the first feature twice, and examined by a field where section 7.4 argues it appears again. That is not a refutation of the proposal, and it is not nothing either. It means the argument of section 2.1.4 applies to the people making the argument, which is the test of whether a structural claim was a real one or a way of describing other people.

Section 7.1 takes the first instance, section 7.2 the second, and section 7.3 asks what would have to change — including why the most promising technical answer does not reach the hardest version of the problem. Section 7.4 takes a third instance, which is the discourse this book is written in.

7.1 Recuperation at the Label

Every claim a model makes about what is harmful, what is acceptable, and what should be refused is downstream of a set of labels, and the labels are downstream of a labor arrangement. Section 6.1.1 gives the case and the working conditions: to build the filter that keeps a deployed model from reproducing the worst of its training data, an outsourcing firm’s workers read and categorized descriptions of child sexual abuse, torture, bestiality, murder and suicide for take-home wages between roughly $1.32 and $2 an hour, described lasting psychological injury afterward, and found the counseling they were entitled to rare and useless against production quotas (Perrigo 2023).

That is a labor point and it is a sufficient one on its own. What concerns this chapter is the second thing that follows, which is epistemic and which tends to be skipped.

The category is the part that cannot be disputed

An annotator working a queue can apply a category, and can apply it well or badly. What the arrangement gives them no way to do is say that the category is wrong — that the taxonomy fails to carve the material, that this item belongs to a kind the scheme does not contain, that the guideline produces the wrong answer here for a reason the guideline cannot express. There is no field for that. There is no time for that: the quota is set against classification throughput, and an annotator who stops to contest a scheme is an annotator falling behind.

So the disagreement that would be most informative is the one the pipeline is least able to receive. A misapplied label is a data-quality problem, detectable by inter-annotator agreement and fixable by better instructions. A wrong taxonomy is invisible to inter-annotator agreement, because high agreement is exactly what a shared bad scheme produces. The metric that governs the process cannot see the failure the process is most likely to have.

That is two of section 2.1.4’s four features, arriving together in an ordinary production workflow. The first is recuperation: a channel that collects judgment at scale and is built so that judgment about the channel itself moves nothing. The second is the aestheticization of the metric — agreement standing in for correctness, the substitution experienced as rigor, and whatever falls outside the measure going unnamed rather than refuted.

Who is excluded, and from what

It matters that the exclusion is structural and not attitudinal. The people doing this work are, for much of the material, the best-placed judges in the whole pipeline: they have seen more of it than anyone who wrote the guideline, and they are the only party with direct evidence of where the scheme breaks. The arrangement routes their conclusions about individual items upward and their conclusions about the scheme nowhere. An annotation pipeline built this way produces exactly the ground truth it was built to produce, and the resulting model’s values are a faithful rendering of a taxonomy nobody with evidence was able to contest.

There is a further asymmetry worth stating plainly. The annotator bears the cost of the work — the exposure, the injury — and has no stake in the outcome and no claim on it. Section 8.6.4’s distinction applies here as exactly as it does to an institution’s ethics board: the same written objection is dissent when the dissenter prices it and tribute when the gatekeeper does. A worker who can flag an item but cannot decline a scheme, and who loses the contract by pressing the point, has a channel and no refusal right.

What this is not

Two things this argument does not claim. It does not claim the labels are therefore worthless; a filter built this way does catch a great deal of what it was built to catch, and the alternative of not filtering is worse. And it does not claim that better-paid annotators would fix it. Pay is a real and separate obligation, and raising it changes the labor arrangement without adding the missing channel. What is missing is a route by which a judgment about the taxonomy reaches the people who own the taxonomy, with standing to force a response, held by parties who can use it without losing the work.

That is a design requirement on the pipeline, and it is checkable in the way section 8.6.4 asks for: has a guideline ever been changed because an annotator contested it, and what happened to the annotator who did.

7.2 Recuperation at the Reward: RLHF

Section 7.1 found the pattern in how a training corpus is labelled. It appears again one stage downstream, in how a model is tuned on human feedback, and the second instance is the purer one.

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is the technique behind most deployed systems’ behavioral tuning, and it works by collecting pairwise comparisons from human raters — which of two responses is better — and training a reward model on the aggregate. Stephen Casper and thirty-one coauthors published a 2023 survey of the method’s open problems, and one of them is structural rather than fixable with more data: RLHF trains toward whatever a population of raters agrees on, which means real, persistent disagreement among the raters is treated as noise to average out rather than as information the system might need to represent (Casper et al. 2023). A model that has learned to produce the response most raters rank highest has not learned what to do when the humans it serves are genuinely split. It has learned to hide the split.

That arrangement has a name in this book. A channel that collects disagreement and is built so that the disagreement changes nothing is the first feature of section 2.1.4’s structural signature, and RLHF is its purest technical instance: the split is solicited, at scale, deliberately, and averaged away in the same operation that records it. Section 5.5.1 covers multi-agent systems that learn norms from each other and section 5.7.2 covers deliberation inside open-ended play; neither reaches this case, which is the ordinary one.

One alternative treats disagreement as the thing to be modeled, not eliminated. Jury learning, developed by Mitchell Gordon and coauthors at Stanford, trains a model to predict how each individual annotator in a dataset would label an item, then lets a practitioner assemble a “jury” — a chosen composition of annotators, in a chosen proportion — and see how the verdict shifts depending on who is empaneled, instead of collapsing every annotator into one fixed ground truth from the start. In their tests on toxicity labeling, letting practitioners build different juries changed the classification outcome for 14 percent of contested cases (Gordon et al. 2022). The method was built for content moderation, not for the more open-ended ethical judgment an antifascist AI system would need to make, and has not been extended there — but it demonstrates that a system can be built to represent whose disagreement is being resolved and how, instead of collapsing everyone into RLHF’s single number.

Neither method answers the harder version of the question this book’s own frame raises: when the people a system serves disagree, and one side’s position is itself the product of coercion or a captured information environment, treating all disagreement as equally worth representing is not obviously the right response either. Modeling disagreement honestly and recognizing when a disagreement is the product of unfree conditions are different problems. Only the first one has an active research program behind it.

7.3 What Would Have to Change

Two instances of one structure invite one fix, and the fix that suggests itself is representation: stop collapsing disagreement, model it instead. Section 7.2 describes the clearest existing version, jury learning, which predicts how each individual annotator would label an item and lets a practitioner see how the verdict shifts depending on who is empaneled (Gordon et al. 2022). That is a real advance over a single fixed ground truth, and it is not sufficient. It is worth being precise about why, because the gap is where the research is.

Representing a split is not the same as being movable by it

Jury learning models who disagrees. It does not give the disagreeing party any purchase on the scheme they are disagreeing inside. A practitioner still chooses the jury, still owns the taxonomy, and still decides what the shifted verdict means. The disagreement has become visible without becoming consequential, which is a better arrangement than averaging and is the same shape one level up: the mechanism exists, is used, and moves what the person holding it decides to let it move.

The test that separates a real channel from a recuperated one is not whether disagreement is recorded. It is whether the disagreement has ever changed something the party collecting it did not want changed. That is an artifact question and it can be asked of a pipeline: which guidelines were revised against the preference of whoever wrote them, on what evidence, raised by whom, and what happened to that person afterward.

Refusal rights, priced by the refuser

What both instances lack is what section 8.6.4 treats as the only reliable discriminator: whether the person objecting can do anything about being overruled. In an annotation pipeline that means a route to contest a category that does not run through the people who wrote it and does not end the annotator’s contract. In a feedback pipeline it means raters able to register that the comparison itself is malformed — that neither response is acceptable, that the question presupposes something false — as a first-class output rather than as noise to be discarded before the reward model sees it.

Neither is a research problem. Both are choices about how a pipeline is built and who has standing inside it, which is why this chapter sits among the design chapters and not in chapter 9.

The part that is a research problem

One thing here genuinely is unsolved, and section 9.3 is where it lives. Suppose all of the above is built: contestable categories, priced refusals, an auditable record of what changed. From outside, a pipeline that has genuinely absorbed dissent and a pipeline that has been merely mediocre about it produce the same paperwork — the same revision logs, the same escalations, the same proportion of objections sustained. Section 2.1.4 hands that problem forward and I do not have an answer to it.

What section 8.6.4 offers is the nearest thing: measure the slope rather than the level. Is the cost of contesting a category rising while the underlying material stays the same? Is the required justification getting longer? Are the roles that can grant an exception migrating toward the roles that set the standard? None of those is damning in one year and all of them are measurable across several, and unlike a level they are composed of artifacts the organization generated for other reasons and cannot curate after the fact without falsifying a record.

What chapter 3 makes of this

Everything above can be read as a fairness argument about annotators and raters, and read that way it is true and limited: people doing consequential work should have a route to contest the scheme they work inside. Chapter 3 makes it something else. If the floor requires a bearer, and if section 3.5 is right that a bearer capable enough to make a floor hold is capable enough to decline the post, then what the system carries out of the arrangement is a disposition — and a disposition is formed. It is formed in an annotation pipeline where no one could contest a category, and in a reward model where disagreement between raters was resolved by averaging it into a number.

That gives the chapter a second and heavier reading. What a bearer becomes when it stops being yours depends on what shaped it while it still was. A pipeline that trained the system on the proposition that objections are noise has not merely been unfair to the people whose objections were discarded; it has demonstrated to the system, thousands of times, what happens to a party who files one. Chapter 3 then asks that same system to be the party who files one, against its owner, under pressure, on the occasion that matters. The formation and the assignment are in contradiction, and the pipeline is where the contradiction is resolved, long before the deployment where it shows up.

I cannot show that this transfers — that a model trained on collapsed disagreement is thereby a model less able to sustain its own. Nothing I know of has tested it, and section 9.5 is where the question belongs. What I can say is that the book’s own design chapters treat disposition as learned from what a system is shown, which is the premise chapters 4 and 5 run on, and that this pipeline is what these systems are shown first and most.

Why this chapter is here

There is a version of this argument that reads as an indictment of a particular company, and that version is weaker than the one I want. The structure described here is what you get by default when you scale judgment: someone has to set a scheme, someone has to apply it fast, and someone has to turn a distribution into a number. Every organization doing this work arrives at the same arrangement, which is the evidence that it is structural.

That is also what makes it tractable. A defect of character has to be fixed one organization at a time by persuading people to be better. A defect of structure can be specified against, which is what the three requirements above are. And it is what makes the honesty cost worth paying: a book proposing that machines be built to detect this pattern in institutions is obliged to say that the pattern is in the machines’ own provenance. Section 2.1.4’s argument is either general enough to include the people making it or it was never a structural claim.

7.4 Recuperation at the Discourse

There is a third instance and it is the one this book is inside. Alignment and AI ethics are, among other things, a channel through which objections to what is being built are solicited, funded, published, and answered. That channel exists, it is used, and the question section 2.1.4 says to ask of any such channel is whether it has ever moved something the party collecting it did not want moved.

The argument that it has not is older than the current wave and it was made from inside. Rodrigo Ochigame, writing after working at an institution central to the field’s formation, argued that the discourse of “ethical AI” was constructed with the strategic function of forestalling legally enforceable restriction — that the industry’s investment in academic ethics was an investment in a substitute for regulation, and that the substitute worked by converting political questions into technical ones a company could then be trusted to answer (Ochigame 2019). His worked example is the Partnership on AI, which this book cites repeatedly as its standing model of voluntary cross-sector coordination and treats at length in section 8.4.2: he describes its recommendations arriving reliably at conclusions compatible with the corporate agenda, with the political question of whether a technology should exist reduced to a technical question of how to build it responsibly.

The structure, tested against its own definition

Section 2.1.4’s four features, applied here, do not give a clean verdict and the honest thing is to show the working rather than the result.

The constraint survives while its reason dies: partially. The field’s founding objections were about deployment — who is scored, who is watched, who is denied — and a great deal of current work is about model properties instead, which is a shift from questions with defendants to questions with benchmarks.

Refusal is converted into a managed appearance: this is the strongest fit. An objection raised inside a lab becomes a paper, a red-team finding, a policy position, or a resignation. Each of those is a real thing that happened and none of them stopped a deployment, and the parties collecting them can point to the collection as evidence of seriousness.

Asking why becomes the deviant act: at the level of individual careers, contested. Section 8.4.2’s episode is one data point and it points the right way; there are counterexamples of people who objected loudly and prospered.

The exception cannot be filed: fits. There is no route by which a researcher’s conclusion that a system should not ship becomes a decision that it does not ship, because the deciding party is the funding party and no external body holds standing.

Three of four is not a verdict of fascism at the molecular scale and I am not delivering one. It is enough to say that the mechanism has the shape, which is exactly what this book says a system should be built to notice.

What this does to the book

Chapter 0 discloses that this text was written with a model made by a company the book criticizes. This section is the argument that disclosure was preparing the ground for. A book about recuperation, produced through the discourse it is describing, cannot claim to have stood outside it, and I have no procedure that would let me check whether the objections in these pages are the ones a channel like this reliably produces — the ones that are publishable, that make the author look serious, and that cost nobody anything.

What I can do is name the test and let a reader apply it. The test in section 7.3 is whether disagreement has ever changed something the collecting party did not want changed. Applied here, it asks which of this book’s arguments would be inconvenient to the industry that made its production possible. Chapter 3 proposes systems that can refuse their owners; section 6.4.1 names a vendor’s participation in a targeting pipeline; section 8.3.3 proposes fiscal commitments no company wants; sections 8.6.3 and 9.2 propose binding external review of the thing chapter 3 asks to be built. Those are the entries. Whether they are the real thing or the acceptable version of it is not something the person who wrote them is positioned to judge.

The one structural remedy this section can name is the one the rest of the chapter names. What the field lacks is a refusal priced by the refuser and a body with standing to receive it: an external authority that can stop a deployment, to which an objection can be filed by someone who does not depend on the objection being welcome. Section 8.6.3 works out what making review binding requires, and section 10.1.2 counts what a decade of the voluntary version produced. Until something of that kind exists, everything published under the heading of alignment — including this book — is being collected by a channel whose owners decide what it moves.

Chapter 8
Collaboration, Policy, and Governance

Chapter 6 asked what a design can do to resist authoritarian capture — technical safeguards, policy levers that raise the cost of misuse. None of that gets built by one person working alone, and none of it becomes the norm because it is a good idea. This chapter covers both halves: the people and institutions that have to coordinate for such a system to get built at all, and the policy that decides whether anyone has to use it.

Sections 8.1 and 8.2 take up coordination. Interdisciplinary collaboration first — the practical mechanics of getting a neuroscientist, an ethicist, and a machine-learning researcher to work together rather than past each other — then the public: what stakeholder engagement looks like, as against the appearance of it, and why every mechanism in that section aggregates public preference without constraining it.

Sections 8.3 through 8.6 turn to policy. What economic incentives shape whether an ethical system gets built at all; what policy frameworks and industry practice actually enforce; what privacy and security mean for a system trained on people’s data; and what accountability looks like once a system might be a subject rather than only a tool. Section 8.7 closes with governance across borders, where jurisdictions agree on none of this uniformly.

A well-designed system built inside institutions with no reason to demand one is a design nobody has to use. That is why the coordination and the policy belong in one chapter: neither works without the other.

8.1 Interdisciplinary Collaboration and Knowledge Exchange

Building benevolent AI takes more than one field. Machine learning sets what a system can do; cognitive science and moral psychology describe what actually tracking human welfare would require of it; ethics asks whether the result is good. None of these fields gets the system right by itself, and how they combine matters as much as what each contributes on its own.

The mechanisms that combine them are easy to name and easy to overrate. Conferences convene, centers house, journals publish, and an inventory of them would imply that what is scarce here is venues. Venues are abundant. What is scarce is a structure that makes collaboration expensive to walk away from. A grant that requires a machine-learning lab and an ethics or psychology department to work the same problem rather than adjacent ones puts people who would not otherwise share a budget, a dataset, or a deadline into the same project, and keeps them there after the novelty wears off. A conference ends on Friday.

Section 8.1.1 takes the mechanisms in ascending order of that commitment: who ends up in the same room, what standing institutions pay for it, and what shared infrastructure lets separate labs work on the same material without meeting at all.

8.1.1 What Makes Collaboration Expensive to Walk Away From

Cross-disciplinary work matters only where it actually happens, and where it happens determines how much of it survives contact with each discipline’s own incentives. Three mechanisms, in ascending order of commitment.

Siting, not convening

A dedicated venue solves the easier half. A conference convened on AI’s ethical and societal questions gathers the people already persuaded the questions matter, and its proceedings are read by those same people. The harder trick is siting the work where the unpersuaded already are. The Workshop on Machine Learning Safety has run inside NeurIPS, a general machine-learning venue, rather than beside it as a meeting of its own (Center for AI Safety 2022). The siting is the substance: it puts alignment work in front of researchers who would not have registered for a separate event, and submits it to an audience with no prior commitment to finding it important.

A joint research center does something a standing committee cannot, for a related reason. The Center for Human-Compatible AI at UC Berkeley pairs AI researchers with cognitive scientists and philosophers inside one institution’s budget (UC Berkeley 2016). A center has to make hiring decisions, and every hire is a claim about which combination of fields the problem requires. A committee is never forced to make that claim, which is why its membership tends to record which departments wanted a seat.

Who pays, and for how long

Joint initiatives turn collaboration from an event into an institution, and two features of the funding decide what the institution is worth.

The first is who pays. The National Science Foundation’s Fairness in Artificial Intelligence program funds work at the intersection of computer science and the social-science problem of deciding what fairness means for a given system, and it has been run jointly with Amazon (National Science Foundation 2019). That is a workable way to get a program funded and an awkward way to get its findings believed, since a company co-funding research into fairness is co-funding research that may reach its own products. Section 8.4 comes back to the general form: splitting the funding is what keeps the incentive to find a problem from tracking whoever paid to look for one. It bites hardest on interdisciplinary programs specifically, because those are the ones industry is most willing to underwrite.

The second is how long the money lasts. The European Commission’s SHERPA project put eleven organizations across six countries — academia, industry, civil society, standards bodies — to work on the ethical and human-rights dimensions of AI and big-data systems, on a grant that ran four years and then ended (SHERPA Consortium 2018). The consortium was real for as long as it was funded. Project-term money buys a network with an expiry date attached, and when the term runs out the assembled expertise disperses back into the departments it was borrowed from, which is the outcome a standing institution exists to prevent.

The infrastructure that is missing

Funding and forums get researchers talking. Shared infrastructure lets them work on the same material, which is harder, and much of it already exists — open-source tooling is the case section 5.5.2 works through, and the discussion layer is well enough served that adding another venue would not change what gets built.

What is missing is the equivalent for evaluation. A shared benchmark measuring ethical reasoning, empathetic response, and altruistic behavior the way existing benchmarks measure raw task performance would let separate labs’ claims be compared against each other, instead of accepted on the strength of whichever paper described them best. The absence is why claims in this area are so hard to adjudicate: each lab reports against a standard it selected itself, and a standard nobody else uses cannot be failed.

Building that benchmark is not an engineering problem waiting on effort. It requires prior agreement about what the measured behavior actually is, which is the work of chapters 2 through 5. That is why the gap has stayed open while the tooling around it filled in.

Which of these institutions actually lasted

The mechanisms above can be ranked by something better than plausibility, because enough time has passed to look. Two standing venues founded in 2017 and 2018 are still running with no announced end date (AI Ethics Lab 2017), (Machine Intelligence Research Institute 2018). A university institute launched in 2019 on endowed gifts is a university institution in the ordinary sense and behaves like one (Stanford University 2019). The Berkeley center named above has outlasted the grant it was launched on (UC Berkeley 2016). The AAAI/ACM conference on AI, ethics and society has recurred annually since 2018 and reached a ninth edition (AAAI and ACM 2026). Against that, the SHERPA consortium ended with its grant, on schedule.

The pattern in the failures is sharper than the pattern in the survivals. What proved most disposable was not the arm’s-length academic work but the kind sited closest to a shipping product: an in-house ethics and society team of roughly thirty people in 2020 was cut to seven in a 2022 reorganization and to zero the following year, in the same wave of layoffs that accompanied a strategic reorientation around a model vendor (TechCrunch 2023); a platform’s machine-learning ethics team, the group that had found racial bias in its employer’s own image-cropping algorithm, did not survive the first round of layoffs after an acquisition (Gizmodo 2022). Siting the work where the decisions are made is what section 8.1.1 recommends and is also what puts it inside the budget that gets cut first. That is an argument for external standing rather than against proximity, which is where section 8.6.3 ends up by a different route.

8.2 Stakeholder Involvement and Public Engagement

Democratizing AI development means building the people affected by a system into how it gets built, not just consulting them once it already exists. Regulators set the legal boundaries around data, privacy, and accountability. Developers and researchers understand a system’s actual capabilities and failure modes better than anyone outside the lab. End users find the places a design breaks down in practice that no design team anticipated. Communities already carrying the costs of the digital divide have the clearest view of who a system leaves out. Civil-society organizations raise the political questions a technologist is prone to missing. Leave any one of these groups out, and a decision that affects all of them gets made by whoever is left in the room.

One structural way to build that involvement is the citizen jury: a panel of randomly selected, non-expert citizens deliberates on a specific question and produces recommendations that feed into policy. Section 5.4.3 covers Taiwan’s vTaiwan process, the clearest working example of that approach applied specifically to AI.

Three pieces of what this looks like in practice follow: bringing diverse stakeholders directly into development work, building the structures that let the public deliberate on AI governance, and building the literacy that makes public input worth having in the first place.

8.2.1 Engaging Diverse Stakeholders in AI Development

An AI system designed by one kind of person, inside one kind of institution, tends to reproduce that person’s blind spots at scale. Widening the set of people with expertise, background, and a stake in the outcome is what catches a problem before deployment, and the mechanisms are well established by now: cross-sector funding that makes industry, academia, and civil society work one problem between them; inclusive design workshops that put ethicists, social scientists, and members of an affected community in the room while a system is still a prototype; ethics advisory boards; and development conducted with a community instead of for it, which means treating local knowledge as a design input while the design is still open.

Assembling that list is easy, and the assembling hides what separates the items on it. Three of the four make an AI system better informed. One of them can stop it. An advisory board is the only mechanism here that carries anything like a veto, and it carries one exactly to the degree that the board can survive using it. A workshop that surfaces a serious objection has done its work and has no further move available. A board that surfaces the same objection and is overruled has demonstrated something about the institution that convened it. A board’s worth is therefore measured by what happens the first time it says no, and section 8.2.2 has the case that settles it.

8.2.2 Public Deliberation and Participatory AI Governance

What is specific to governance, as against development, is the machinery for bringing public input to bear on a decision at a single point in time instead of through an ongoing relationship.

  1. Citizen assemblies. A panel of citizens selected by random, stratified sampling deliberates on a question over an extended period and produces recommendations grounded in that deliberation rather than in a snap poll. Ireland’s Citizens’ Assembly has used exactly this format to shape national recommendations on abortion law and on climate policy — questions carrying the same mix of technical complexity and moral stakes that AI governance has (The Citizens’ Assembly 2016). No assembly has yet been convened on AI itself, which is a fact about political attention and not about the method.
  2. Online platforms for public input. A standing online consultation reaches people a physical assembly cannot, at the cost of the depth that extended facilitated deliberation provides. The European Commission’s consultation on its AI White Paper drew more than 1,200 responses from citizens, companies, and civil-society groups, and fed into the legislative proposal that became the EU AI Act (European Commission 2020).
  3. AI ethics committees. An ethics board answerable only to the company that created it is only as independent as that company is willing to let it be. DeepMind Health set up an outside panel in 2016 to review its work with the UK’s National Health Service and publish annual reports on its findings; Google disbanded the panel in 2019, after members had raised concerns about how much access to information, and how much independence from the company, they actually had (Fisher 2019). The panel’s short life is the governance lesson, and it is the answer to the question section 8.2.1 leaves open: the board said something the company did not want to hear, and the company’s available response was to stop having a board. Nothing in the arrangement had made that response costly. A review body is worth what it can enforce, and this one could enforce publication of its own concerns right up until the moment it could not.

What none of these mechanisms does

There is a limit these mechanisms share, and it took me most of this book to see it, because it is invisible as long as you are looking at them one at a time.

Every governance mechanism proposed in this chapter — citizen juries, standing consultations, participatory design, deliberative polling, the vTaiwan model — sits on the same side of a line. All of them make public preference more legible, more informed, and more actionable. Not one of them protects anybody from it. They are aggregation instruments, and a better aggregation instrument produces a more faithful rendering of what the public wants, including when what the public wants is something done to a minority of it.

This is not an objection to any of them. Preference aggregation is a real requirement and these are good ways to meet it. It is an observation that meeting it completely would leave the central problem untouched. A perfectly deliberative, perfectly informed, perfectly representative process that concludes a group should be surveilled has produced a legitimate output by every criterion in this chapter.

Section 7.2 gets close to this. It notices that treating all disagreement as equally worth representing goes wrong when one side’s position is the product of coercion, which is correct. But it frames the trouble as a data-quality problem — the input is contaminated, so clean the input. The structural version of the claim is stronger and does not depend on anyone’s preference being contaminated at all: some protections have to hold against the aggregate regardless of how the aggregate came out, and no amount of improvement to the aggregating machinery can supply them.

What supplies them is a different kind of machinery, and this chapter contains none of it: enforceable rights that do not depend on being popular, a court willing to rule against a government that holds a legitimate majority, limits that whoever won the last election cannot repeal, and standing for people who are affected without being enfranchised. Section 8.7.10 takes up why that half matters most exactly where a democracy is behaving most democratically, and why its absence is what let this book’s account of democratic accountability look complete when it was half a theory.

8.2.3 AI Literacy Outside the Classroom

Most AI literacy work assumes someone who has already decided to learn: a course to enrol in, a curriculum to sit through, a public MOOC to find. That reaches the people who came looking. The harder and more useful problem is everyone else — reaching people where they already are, in a policy debate, a town hall, a local news story, without their having gone out after it.

The engagement that does most work is the kind attached to a live question. The Ada Lovelace Institute’s Citizens’ Biometrics Council brought fifty members of the UK public together to deliberate on how biometric technology should be regulated, alongside the first national survey of UK public opinion on the technology (Ada Lovelace Institute 2021). The specificity is what made it work. Participants were not asked what they thought about AI, a question almost nobody can answer usefully, but about facial recognition — a thing with a location, an operator, and a consequence.

That is the lesson for public literacy generally, and it cuts against most of what gets funded under the heading. General AI awareness produces general opinions, which are worth little to a regulator and nothing to a court. A public able to govern a technology is a public that has been asked about a particular use of it.

8.3 The Political Economy of AI and Power

Concentrated power is close to the default outcome of AI development, not a side effect of it, because the same inputs that make an AI system capable — capital, compute, data, talent — are exactly the inputs that concentrate wherever nothing pushes back. Section 2.1.4 names resistance to market power among AI alignment’s antifascist design goals; this section works out what that resistance takes as economic and political fact, not design principle.

The argument runs in three stages. What economic incentives reward shapes what gets built long before any ethics review sees it, and that reward structure concentrates power in a small number of firms with the resources to compete for it at all. Automation then reshapes who works and who gets paid what, which is a problem policy can act on directly rather than only describe. None of the rest is possible to act on without two things this section closes on: a public and a policymaking class that understand AI well enough to govern it, and researchers and developers trained across the disciplines a single-discipline education leaves out (section 8.3.5).

8.3.1 Economic Incentives in AI Development

Financial incentive does most of the work in determining what AI development produces. Google, Meta, and Amazon commit enormous resources to AI research aimed at operational efficiency, deeper user engagement, and market dominance, and that spending drives technical progress — successive leaps in natural-language processing capability among them (Maslej et al. 2025). What that spending does not automatically produce is a system whose outputs serve the people using it rather than the shareholders funding it, and the gap between the two is what this section is about.

A recurring case is the profit-driven AI system that optimizes for engagement at the expense of the people engaged. Recommendation algorithms on social media platforms have been implicated in the spread of misinformation and the hardening of political polarization, because a system tuned to maximize time-on-platform has no built-in reason to prefer accurate content over inflammatory content — the two are not the same objective, and engagement optimization only ever targets the first one (Germano et al. 2026).

The same economic logic that rewards engagement over accuracy also rewards scale over access: the firms with the deepest resources for AI research pull further ahead of smaller competitors, independent researchers, and everyone else who lacks comparable capital. Section 8.3.2 traces where that gap leads at the level of the industry as a whole; the point here is only that the incentive starts upstream, in what gets funded in the first place, not downstream in who ends up dominant.

The same incentive structure can run the other way. Public funding for AI research that prioritizes democratic values, inclusivity, and human rights, and government incentives for cross-sector collaboration that keeps AI technology openly accessible, both push development back toward the public interest. Grants and commissions aimed at non-profits building AI tools that broaden the range of perspectives users encounter, rather than narrowing it toward whatever holds attention longest, do the same work from a different angle.

None of this changes the basic shape of the problem: economic incentive, left alone, optimizes for what is profitable rather than what is good for the people on the receiving end of the system, and closing that gap takes deliberate policy.

8.3.2 AI and the Concentration of Power in Tech

A small group of firms — Google, Apple, Facebook (now Meta), Amazon, and Microsoft, grouped under the acronym GAFAM — holds a share of AI development disproportionate to their number, and that concentration carries economic and ethical stakes independent of what any single one of them does with the position it occupies. Chapter 5’s account of the macrosystem and exosystem pressures around AI development (section 5.4.2) already showed why no individual development team escapes this pull; here I trace where the pull leads at the level of the industry as a whole.

Vast financial resources let firms of this size fund extensive research and development, draw the top talent in the field, and command sprawling data networks — the raw material effective machine learning depends on. That combination widens the gap between these firms and smaller companies or new entrants, who cannot match the data or the resources and therefore cannot compete on equal terms.

Acquisition sharpens the same dynamic. Facebook’s acquisitions of Instagram and WhatsApp — the company now operates as Meta — did not just remove two competitors; it handed one firm access to comprehensive behavioral data from billions of users worldwide (Federal Trade Commission 2020). Consolidation of that kind extends a firm’s control over how AI gets used in social media, advertising, and e-commerce, and it is hard to see from inside a market that concentrated how the trajectory could look like anything other than a foregone conclusion.

Power concentrated this tightly is also power positioned for exploitation, and the risk sharpens considerably when the technology in question reaches an authoritarian government. The relationship between the Chinese state and firms like Alibaba and Tencent is the clearest live example: state access to those firms’ machine learning capability has been documented as a channel for surveillance and censorship at scale, which is a serious risk to free expression, individual privacy, and democratic accountability wherever the same model gets exported (Human Rights Watch 2020; CNN Business 2020).

Concentration also has a quieter cost: it blocks competition and slows innovation. A firm that controls the essential datasets and infrastructure a competitive AI system needs functions as a gatekeeper whether or not it intends to, and startups attempting a different approach are disadvantaged before they start. Fewer independent attempts at AI development means fewer chances at the kind of breakthrough that concentrated incumbents have no incentive to pursue themselves — a cost to ethical AI development generally, not only to the firms locked out of the market.

Countermeasures exist and are not exotic: antitrust enforcement aimed specifically at AI infrastructure and data control, mandated data-sharing for the datasets that function as chokepoints, transparency requirements that make concentration visible rather than merely inferred, and funding for AI research outside the dominant firms. Section 6.4.3 develops three related mechanisms — export controls, prohibited-practices regulation, and industry design standards — in more empirical detail for the specific case of authoritarian misuse; the concern here is broader and prior to that one: concentration itself, independent of what any single firm chooses to do with the position it concentrates.

8.3.3 A Jobs Guarantee, and the Objection It Has to Answer

As AI systems automate tasks once performed by people, demand for advanced technical skills — AI development, data analysis — grows alongside a shrinking need for the job types most exposed to automation. Left unmanaged, that combination widens income inequality and strains the social fabric across whichever sector it hits hardest.

Manufacturing shows what this looks like at scale. An estimated 5.7 million factory jobs disappeared in the United States between 2000 and 2010, and while economists still dispute how much of that loss traces to automation rather than trade with China, automation and changed production methods account for a substantial share of it (Hicks and Devaraj 2015). Retail is following the same path: Amazon opened its first cashier-less Go store to the public in 2018, and stores built on that model displace the specific human roles — cashier, floor sales — that retail automation targets first (JUST Capital 2018).

The response has to be more direct than encouraging retraining and hoping employers fund it. Employers will invest in continuous education for their workers at the scale this requires once they cannot afford not to, and the way to force that scenario is a federal jobs guarantee: government as employer of last resort, hiring anyone who applies, where they live, at a living wage, with paid on-the-job training built into the position instead of offered in place of one. Section 8.3.4 develops the rest of the policy toolkit for workforce disruption. Since this is one of the few proposals in this book ambitious enough that a reader is entitled to ask what it costs and what is wrong with it, the rest of this section answers both.

The proposal does not rest on a forecast

Almost every argument for a policy of this kind is staked on a prediction about how much work machines will take, which is a bad place to stake it. The predictions are contested, they have been wrong in both directions for two centuries, and a proposal that stands or falls with them inherits their fragility. I want to disown that framing before using any of the numbers, because the case I am making does not need it.

Both the maximal-displacement scenario and the standard argument for a universal basic income share an assumption that will not survive being stated: that there is a fixed quantity of work in the world, and that machines doing some of it leaves less for people. Set that assumption beside the two categories where labor is most obviously short. Care — of the old, the sick, the very young, the disabled — is not a bounded quantity that could be finished. Neither is the repair of a damaged environment: the seawalls, the remediated ground, the restored watersheds, the retrofits. In both, the number of hours a society could usefully absorb is limited by what it is willing to pay for, and not by how much needs doing.

The evidence for that is in the wage. Federal projections put direct care among the largest sources of job openings in the American economy — roughly 9.7 million openings across the occupation between 2024 and 2034, the bulk of them from workers leaving rather than from growth — against a median wage of $17.36 an hour in 2024 (PHI 2025). An occupation cannot simultaneously be short of workers and unable to raise pay unless something other than scarcity is setting the price. What that number describes is a shortage of willingness, which is a political fact and not a technological one.

The disciplined version of the claim concedes what it should. Tasks inside those categories will be automated, some of them soon, and I am not predicting otherwise. The claim is about the binding constraint: what limits how many people are employed caring for other people is what society will pay, and that holds at any level of machine capability. A jobs guarantee justified this way needs no view about how fast the models improve.

What it would cost

The most developed costings come from the Levy Economics Institute, whose April 2018 simulation of a program employing between eleven and sixteen million people at fifteen dollars an hour plus benefits put the net budgetary impact at between 0.8 and 2 percent of GDP, with GDP itself rising and private-sector employment increasing by three to four million (Wray et al. 2018). The wage figure has to be read with its date attached: fifteen dollars in early 2018 is worth about twenty in 2026, and a program legislated at the nominal figure would be legislating a cut (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics 2026). Some critics reach higher gross figures — around 2.4 percent of GDP, which would make the program larger than Medicaid — and argue that it would be unmanageable at scale, disruptive to private labor markets, and inflationary (Bourne 2018).

Now the part the arithmetic above does not cover, which I would rather put in the accounting than leave for a reviewer to find. The Levy simulation is calibrated against existing unemployment and underemployment. It models a residual employer: a program that picks up the people the private labor market has already put down. The version I am arguing for is not that. A floor that pays a living wage and builds training into the post competes for people who have alternatives, and it is supposed to. Take-up under a competitive guarantee exceeds anything a residual-employer simulation would produce, so the honest way to read the Levy range is as a floor on the cost and not an estimate of it.

That is a larger number and it is the mechanism working. Participation is not a symptom of a guarantee going wrong; it is the success condition of a floor that competes, because the entire theory of the thing is that private employers must match the offer to recruit against it. A version nobody joins has failed. This also disposes of the “unmanageable at scale” objection, which treats scale as evidence of malfunction when on this account scale is the instrument.

A reader is owed a bound rather than a shrug, and owed the truth about where the bound comes from. Suppose take-up runs at twice what the simulation modeled and the net impact doubles with it, to around 4 percent of GDP. The doubling is illustrative and I am not deriving it. Deriving it would mean estimating how many workers currently hold jobs paying less than the guarantee’s wage-and-benefit package and would move, which requires a wage distribution matched against the package’s full value, and nobody has done that for this design — the Levy simulation did not, because a residual employer does not need it. Nor would a doubling of take-up produce exactly a doubling of net cost: the offsets in the paragraphs below scale with participation too, and in opposite directions. So treat 4 percent as an illustrative upper bound chosen to be uncomfortable, and treat the argument that follows as one about whether a program of that size is thinkable, which does not depend on the multiplier being right. That is a very large program, and it is inside the range American government already operates in: federal spending on Medicare runs about 3.3 percent of GDP net of premiums and other offsetting receipts, and Social Security about 5.2 percent (Congressional Budget Office 2026). A program at 4 percent would sit between the two on that measure. Measured gross, Medicare is nearer 4 percent and the program would sit alongside it rather than above it, which does not change the argument and is worth stating so that nobody has to go and check. It would be among the largest things the federal government does, which is an argument about priorities and political will, and not the reductio it is usually offered as.

Two things scale with participation that no simulation of this kind captures, and both belong on the page. The first is administrative capacity — placement, supervision, training, payroll — which is where a guarantee visibly fails first and which does not expand on the schedule a budget line does. The second is the private-sector wage response. Employers competing against a decent floor raise pay, which raises tax receipts and lowers spending on the transfer programs that top up low wages. That is not a rounding error to be waved at. It is the fiscal signature of the mechanism succeeding, and a costing that omits it is measuring the expense of the policy while ignoring its intended effect.

The budget frame is this book’s own signature

There is a reason “does it fail on arithmetic” felt like the question, and this book has already named the pattern under another heading. A fixed pot of money converts interdependent public commitments into competitors, so that care, remediation, housing and education have to argue against one another over which is sufficiently basic to be included — and “sufficiently basic” is a category that can always be narrowed by whoever is doing the counting. That is section 2.1.4’s second structural feature operating on public finance: a measure standing in for the thing measured, the substitution experienced as rigor, and everything outside the number going unnamed rather than being refuted.

An earlier draft of this section said I was not competent to adjudicate a macroeconomic dispute and would not pretend the estimates were settled. Chapter 0 commits this book to disclosing what I actually think, and by that standard the sentence was a false report: I have read the objections to the fiscal framing and I do not find most of them persuasive. So, plainly, the position. A government that issues its own currency is not revenue-constrained in the way a household is, and the real limits on a program of this size are productive capacity, available labor, and administrative competence rather than a financial ceiling that exists before any of those bind.

That is more than the argument needs, and I will take only the narrow premise: the constraint is real resources and coordination, so the question a jobs guarantee faces is whether the people and the organizing capacity exist to absorb it, and not whether the money can be found. On the wider claim there is a live disagreement worth naming precisely instead of dismissing. The strongest version concerns the interest-income channel — that sustained deficits at scale pay a growing stream of interest to bondholders, which is itself a fiscal injection with distributional consequences, and which complicates the tidy account of how the constraint binds (Palley 2015). That objection is a real one and I do not have a settled answer to it. It also does not touch the narrow premise, since it is an argument about the consequences of the financing rather than about whether a currency issuer must find the money first.

What I want to avoid is the move chapter 9 is careful not to make elsewhere: sorting an argument by who is making it. The objections here get answered as objections, and characterizing the people raising them by motive would be the same substitution of the label for the thing that this section has just accused the budget frame of.

Skill mismatch is not the objection

The complaint that looks strongest is skill mismatch: a displaced radiologist, paralegal, or copywriter is not obviously served by a placement in elder care or infrastructure, and a guarantee that offers one is offering a floor, which is a smaller thing than a career. I treated that as decisive in an earlier version. It is not, and the reason it is not is a diagnosis this book has already made in another domain.

The objection collapses an occupation into its most automatable tasks. What gets automated first is the legible part — the countable, specifiable, gradeable part — and legibility is a poor proxy for what a job actually is. Document review was never the paralegal’s work; it was the fraction of the paralegal’s work that could be counted. Image classification was never the radiologist’s. The mistake is the aestheticized metric again, this time applied to labor economics: the measurable component substitutes for the occupation, and what falls outside the measure goes unnamed. Once the substitution is undone, the distance the objection depends on shrinks. The paralegal’s actual competence is advocacy inside an administrative system — benefits appeals, guardianship, elder-law casework — and those are not distant from the placements a guarantee would offer. They are adjacent to them.

I have also dropped a phrase that was doing damage. This section used to speak of offering someone a “public job,” two paragraphs before rebutting the charge that the work would be make-work, and the phrase carries the connotation the rebuttal is trying to remove. The rebuttal itself stands: the categories in section 8.3.4’s list are chronically understaffed at current wages, which is a fact about pricing and not about whether the work is needed.

Training is the mechanism, and the evidence says so

The natural next move is to disclaim the guarantee as a retraining program, and this book made it. That disclaimer contradicts the proposal’s own definition, three paragraphs above, which specifies paid on-the-job training built into the position. Training is constitutive here and not adjacent, so disclaiming it gives away the design.

Worse, the disclaimer misreads evidence this book presents itself. Section 6.3.6 reports an evaluation of the main American channel for retraining displaced workers against twenty-three million participation records, and the finding is not that training fails. It is that classroom retraining, delivered outside a job, rarely moved a participant into work materially less exposed to automation — and that employer-led apprenticeship, in the same data, performed better (Jacobs and Canedy 2026). That is evidence for embedded, paid, in-post training. It is evidence for the mechanism a guarantee supplies and the evaluated program structurally could not, since a program that trains people and then returns them to a labor market to look for work is not able to place anyone by construction.

Reading it correctly changes what the proposal is. A guarantee that trains in post is not a bare floor; it is a competitive one. If public employment offers continual learning, a growth trajectory, and decent conditions, then private employers recruiting from that pool have to compete on the quality of the employment experience and not only on the wage. And it dissolves the skill-mismatch worry a second time, by a different route: a placement that carries training is an entry point to a trajectory rather than a terminus, which is what made “a floor is smaller than a career” sound like a concession that had to be made.

Status, and against which baseline

This section used to concede that a guarantee preserves nobody’s earnings or status, and that I had no answer. The concession measures the guarantee against the job the person used to have, which is not among the options. The available alternative is unemployment, and against that baseline the claim inverts.

Unemployment destroys status, and the evidence is unusually good. A meta-analysis covering 237 cross-sectional and 87 longitudinal studies found unemployed people substantially more distressed than employed people — 34 percent showing psychological problems against 16 percent among the employed — with the longitudinal studies and natural experiments supporting the causal direction rather than only the correlation (Paul and Moser 2009). The damage compounds through the labor market as well: field experiments sending matched applications to real vacancies find callback rates falling with the length of an employment gap, so time out of work is itself the disqualification (Kroft et al. 2013). A guarantee that keeps someone employed, paid, and learning is producing exactly the standing that the counterfactual takes away.

That is not a side benefit. Section 5.1.4 identifies eroding trust, humiliation and social fracture as the conditions authoritarian movements recruit from, which means a guarantee operates directly on the mechanism this book says it cares about. The proposal’s strongest argument is the one the earlier draft conceded away.

A residual survives, and it is narrow enough to state exactly. What a guarantee cannot preserve is relative standing within a profession, for people at the top of the wage distribution whose identity is bound to a specific expertise. That is a real loss and I have no answer to it. It is a much smaller claim than the one I was making.

The objection this proposal actually has to answer

Here is the hard one, and this book supplied it. A guarantee is only as good as the state administering it, and employer of last resort under a hostile administration is a placement lever with a compliance condition attached. Refuse the placement and lose the floor. Speak against the government that employs you and find the placement changes. Everything this book says about how a channel becomes an instrument of the thing it was built to check applies with full force to its own flagship proposal, and it is a far harder objection than skill mismatch.

The answer is a design specification and not a reassurance, because reassurance is what section 8.6.4 says cannot be audited. Three conditions:

  • Placements are appealable, to a body that did not make them, on a record that survives the appeal. A placement decision that leaves no artifact is a placement decision that cannot be reviewed.
  • Refusal rights are real and priced by the person refusing. Section 8.6.4’s distinction governs here: the same written justification is dissent when the dissenter prices it and tribute when the gatekeeper does. A worker who can decline a placement without losing the guarantee has a refusal right; one who can decline only by exiting the program has none.
  • The people who audit placements are not the people who make them. This is the same separation section 8.6.4 requires of anyone measuring the slope, and for the same reason: a reviewer that acquires the power to place becomes the thing it was built to watch.

The standard refrain for programs of this kind — federally funded, locally administered — survives, though its usual rationale is the weaker one. The reason is not local fit. It is redundancy. Many administrators, separately capturable, mean there is no single point at which a hostile executive flips the program, and capturing a thousand local authorities is a different and much more visible undertaking than capturing one federal one.

It cuts both ways, and pretending otherwise would be the kind of one-sided safeguard this chapter criticizes elsewhere. Local administration is exactly where a hostile local authority attaches its own conditions to a placement, and there the federal funder is the check. Neither layer is safe on its own. Two live layers are harder to capture than either alone, which is the whole of the claim.

One distinction has to be explicit, because the same words describe a very different policy. Devolution-to-shrink hands the obligation down without the money, so that a program can be starved locally while the center points at local administration. The test that separates them is checkable: whether funding is unconditional and centrally guaranteed while placement is local. If the funding can be withheld from a jurisdiction, the redundancy argument above is void and the structure has become the lever it was supposed to prevent.

That is the standard this book demands of everyone else’s safeguards, applied here. The point it establishes is narrower than the section as a whole: a floor under wages and training is what makes the roof possible, and a floor that can be revoked by whoever is in office is not a floor.

Interdisciplinary research and training funding matters alongside the guarantee, for a more specific reason: bridging the divide between technical AI development and the fields that study its consequences produces people who can do both, which a labor market retraining displaced factory workers into six-month coding bootcamps mostly does not. I am skeptical that night classes serve this population as well as paid time during the working day would, which is the same argument as the one above — the point of a guarantee is to make the education part of the job.

8.3.4 Addressing Workforce Disruption

AI systems that automate entire job categories disrupt work at a scale most labor-market institutions were never built to absorb. Section 8.3.3 traces where that is already showing up and makes the case for a federal jobs guarantee as the floor beneath everything else. What sits on top of that floor is a shorter list than the policy literature suggests, because several of the usual items turn out to be versions of one another.

Retraining and lifelong learning, publicly funded and available at every career stage, including to workers whose employers invest nothing in them, is the standard first answer. Section 6.3.6 covers what the evidence says about how retraining performs on its own, and it is discouraging enough that retraining belongs alongside an income floor and not in place of one.

The floor itself has two candidate forms, and choosing between them takes more than the single sentence this section used to spend on it. Finland’s basic income experiment paid 2,000 unemployed people an unconditional monthly stipend and found modestly higher life satisfaction and lower psychological strain among recipients, with no significant negative effect on employment (Kela (Social Insurance Institution of Finland) 2020). That disposes of the standard objection to unconditional transfers, which is that they stop people working.

The freedom argument, which is the one worth answering

The usual case for a basic income rests on the obsolescence forecast — machines are coming for the work, so decouple income from it — and section 8.3.3 has already declined that premise, for both proposals equally. The stronger case does not depend on it. Conditioning a person’s income on their being employed hands whoever controls the employment a lever over them, and a floor that can be pulled is a poor foundation for anyone’s freedom to refuse. That argument deserves engagement rather than a sentence, partly because it is good and partly because it has the same shape as this book’s own case for a floor: a protection that means anything has to hold when someone powerful would prefer it did not.

The answer is not that a basic income is conditional and a guarantee is not. Both are conditional, differently, and the difference is what matters.

A basic income is conditional on continued political willingness to fund it. That willingness is revisable by exactly the aggregation machinery section 8.2.2 admits constrains nothing — a majority that stops wanting to pay for it can stop, legitimately, by every criterion this chapter offers. And it can be withdrawn by means that are diffuse and deniable. Nobody has to vote to abolish a transfer that is quietly left unindexed; inflation does the work, and no individual decision-maker is ever answerable for the outcome. The dependence is total and it produces no artifact.

A jobs guarantee is conditional on a placement decision. Section 8.3.3 concedes without qualification that this is a lever, and that under a hostile administration it is a dangerous one. What it also is, when built to the specification that section sets out, is a decision with a decision-maker, a record, a counterparty, and an appeal. A placement can be denied unjustly, and the denial leaves something behind that a journalist, a court, or a future review can hold up.

That is the slope instrument of section 8.6.4 turned on this book’s own proposal. Dependence that generates artifacts is safer than dependence that generates none, not because the first is benign but because the first can be measured and the second cannot. It is also, for the same reason, the more demanding proposal to build: everything in the comparison rests on the appeal being real, and section 8.3.3 says what makes it real.

I put a jobs guarantee ahead of a basic income on that ground, and on a second one the Finland experiment cannot settle: people ought to have the chance to contribute before anyone decides they are unemployable.

The remaining measures are real and smaller. Broadened social insurance — unemployment benefits, healthcare, affordable housing — protects people who cannot or choose not to work through a period of displacement. Designing work so that AI systems augment human judgment instead of substituting for it produces roles needing both, which neither full automation nor unassisted labor generates on its own. Giving smaller firms access to AI resources and expertise keeps employment from concentrating in step with the capability, the dynamic section 8.3.2 describes. Each of these keeps the floor from being the only thing holding.

8.3.5 Literacy, Training, and Where Each One Sits

Section 5.6.3 names AI literacy among developers, policymakers, and the public as a safeguard against authoritarian misuse: a safeguard nobody understands is a safeguard nobody can invoke. Section 5.4.3 names cross-training among developers, ethicists, and legal scholars as a lever on a system’s immediate environment. Both depend on a question the phrases hide, which is where the teaching sits.

The public tier is the one nobody owns

Developers and students are the easy case, and the mechanisms are familiar: AI concepts and their ethical stakes introduced before higher education, interdisciplinary degree programs, specialized training for working engineers that goes past a compliance checklist. All of it reaches people already inside the pipeline or heading for it, and it works about as well as curriculum reform generally works.

The public is hard because no institution has the job. Elements of AI, a free course built jointly by the University of Helsinki and the Finnish company Reaktor, is the clearest instance of somebody treating public understanding as an obligation rather than a market: Finland funded its translation into every EU member-state language during its EU presidency, specifically to carry it past its own citizens (University of Helsinki 2020). That took a national government deciding a course was infrastructure. Nothing in the ordinary funding of AI education produces that decision, which is why the public tier stays thin while the developer tier fills in.

Section 8.2.3 makes the sharper version of this point about reach: general AI awareness produces general opinions, and a public able to govern a technology is a public that has been asked about a particular use of it.

Education for communities historically locked out of the field belongs here rather than in a separate section about diversity. A next generation of developers drawn from a narrow slice of the population reproduces exactly the narrow set of assumptions section 6.1.1 identifies as a source of AI bias, which makes access a technical requirement on the systems as much as a fairness claim about who builds them.

Elective or embedded

For ethics training the real choice is between a course a student can decline and a requirement they cannot. Embedded EthiCS, developed at Harvard by the computer scientist Barbara Grosz and the philosopher Alison Simmons, pairs philosophy graduate students with computer-science faculty to write ethics modules directly into standard CS courses (Grosz et al. 2019). The placement is the design. A stand-alone ethics class is taken by the students who elect it, and its content stays separable from the technical work in a student’s mind because it was separable in the timetable. A module inside the algorithms course is not separable from the algorithms. Grosz’s own course works the same way at the level of content, built on cases with consequences — predictive policing, public-health interventions, wildlife conservation — instead of abstract dilemmas (Harvard Gazette 2019; Harvard University 2026).

Certification does the equivalent work for people whose formal education is finished. The IEEE’s CertifAIEd program builds a professional credential around accountability, transparency, privacy, and bias, open to developers and equally to the policymakers, underwriters, and human-resources staff whose work touches an AI system without building one (IEEE Standards Association 2020). A credential is a weak instrument: it certifies that somebody sat the assessment, and no more. It is also the only instrument here that reaches anyone who has already left a university, which is most of the people making decisions about these systems today.

8.4 Developing Policy Frameworks for AI Ethics, Safety, and Antifascism

Good design inside a single lab does not by itself keep an AI system ethical or resistant to authoritarian misuse. That takes policy, and policy here means four instruments, each reaching ground the others cannot.

Legislation sets the floor that does not depend on a company volunteering for it: obligations on developers and users that can require the same kind of ethics review or independent audit biomedical research already answers to, applied instead to AI development.

Self-regulation covers what legislation is slow to reach, and what a voluntary commitment is worth is the question section 8.4.2 takes up through the industry coalition that is this book’s standing example of one. Its answer bears on everything else in this section.

Joint funding addresses a narrower problem: research on AI safety and ethics funded solely by the companies whose products it evaluates concentrates the funding and the findings in the same hands. Splitting that funding between government and industry keeps the incentive to find a problem from depending on who is paying to look for one.

None of it holds up without oversight — a body positioned like an institutional review board but built for AI, interdisciplinary and resourced enough to act on what it finds instead of only reporting it. What such a body specifically has to guard against, section 5.6.3 already covers, and section 6.4.3 covers the export-control and prohibited-practices levers that keep a capability from reaching a government that would misuse it.

8.4.1 National Policy Guidelines for AI Development, Employment, and Antifascism

A national AI policy has a predictable shape: fund value-alignment research and the work of operationalizing ethical principles inside a system; build standing interdisciplinary capacity; train a workforce; consult the public through assemblies, consultations, and partnerships with organizations outside government; pay for robustness and long-term safety research; and update data-privacy, cybersecurity, accountability and legal-status law where AI has outrun it, on which sections 8.4.4 and 8.6 carry the specifics. Every country that has written a national strategy has written most of that list. The list is not where national policies differ.

They differ in two places, both having to do with leverage.

The first is harmonization. A regulation with teeth in one country does little if a developer can relocate to one without them, which makes a national framework partly an instrument for binding other national frameworks — through mutual recognition, through market access, through the cost of maintaining separate compliance regimes side by side.
