Each is a standard, a set of principles, or a forum, useful for building the shared vocabulary that eventually makes binding law possible, and that gap between voluntary standard and binding law is the default state of international coordination on anything individual states have reasons to handle differently. The EU AI Act, discussed below, is the first instance of this kind of groundwork becoming enforceable law, and it took most of a decade of standard-setting exactly like this to get there. The proliferation carries its own cost in the meantime: a company or a smaller government trying to comply with “international AI governance” faces a shifting handful of overlapping standards, each with different membership and scope and no formal mechanism for reconciling a conflict between them, which is why “the international community agrees” is, at the level of any specific rule, usually false. What states have done once left to write their own rules is the subject of what follows.

Democracy, Authoritarianism, and Diverging National Rules

Section 6.4.1 names six documented forms of authoritarian AI misuse, among them social scoring, mass biometric surveillance, and automated censorship, and section 6.4.3 lays out the policy levers available against them: export controls on surveillance-capable systems, laws that name specific prohibited designs rather than regulating AI in the abstract, and developer-facing standards that move faster than legislation does. What belongs here is not a second pass over that ground but what individual states have done with the room those levers leave open, since geopolitics is the study of how different governments use the same available tools differently.

The European Union chose comprehensive statute. The AI Act sorts systems by risk tier, a small set of practices banned outright under Article 5, a larger tier of “high-risk” applications subject to conformity assessment and ongoing monitoring, and most other uses left largely unregulated, rather than writing one rule meant to cover every case (European Union 2024b). Section 6.4.3 already covers Article 5’s specific prohibitions; the structural point worth adding here is that the EU decided the risk a system poses, not the technology it uses, should determine how much scrutiny it gets. Enforcement runs through a dedicated AI Office inside the European Commission, which can demand technical documentation from a general-purpose model’s developer, run its own evaluations, and fine a noncompliant provider a percentage of global turnover — reaching any company that offers a model inside the EU regardless of where the company is based, the same extraterritorial mechanism that let the GDPR set a de facto floor for privacy law well beyond Europe’s borders (European Union 2024a).

The United States made the opposite structural bet: no comprehensive federal AI statute, and enforcement distributed instead across existing sectoral regulators, the Federal Trade Commission, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, and the Food and Drug Administration among them, applying laws written before AI existed to harms AI now causes. The National Institute of Standards and Technology’s voluntary AI Risk Management Framework serves as a common technical reference point across those agencies rather than a binding rule of its own (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2023). The wager is that existing consumer-protection, employment, and safety law already reaches most AI harms, and that naming AI specifically risks regulating the label rather than the conduct.

The United Kingdom, after leaving the EU’s regulatory orbit, made a third choice: rather than create a new AI regulator or a new statute, its 2023 white paper directed existing sector regulators to apply five shared principles, safety, transparency, fairness, accountability, and contestability, within their existing remits (UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology 2023). The wager is closer to the American one than the European: that domain expertise inside an existing regulator beats a new institution built from scratch, even at the cost of less uniform treatment across sectors.

China took a fourth path, one that does not fit neatly next to the other three because it starts from a different premise about what regulation is for. Its Cyberspace Administration, working with several other agencies, issued rules governing generative AI services in 2023 that require providers to file their algorithms with the state before public release, disclose the source and scale of their training data on request, and ensure that generated content reflects the government’s designated social values (Cyberspace Administration of China and six other agencies 2023). The EU, US, and UK approaches all regulate AI as a private product that might harm a consumer, a worker, or a subject of an automated decision, and argue with each other only about how centralized that regulation should be. China’s rules regulate AI as a communications channel the state has a standing interest in controlling content on, which is a different kind of law aimed at a different kind of risk, and comparing it to the other three on the same axis, more regulation or less, misses what actually distinguishes it.

Among the EU, US, and UK, there is an argument about which structural bet is safer, and it runs in both directions. A comprehensive statute can freeze a category of harm into law before anyone has seen what a fast-moving technology actually does with it, and lock in a definition of “high-risk” that the next generation of systems slides around rather than falls into. A sectoral approach leaves gaps precisely where no existing regulator has jurisdiction, since a new capability does not always map onto an old agency’s mandate. Neither failure mode is hypothetical, and none of the three statutes has existed long enough to show which one it falls into more often.

The EU, US, and UK differ on how centralized AI regulation should be, but not on what it is for: constraining what a private company can build and sell. None of the three, including the EU’s binding statute, does anything to stop a government from building the authoritarian applications section 6.4.1 documents within its own borders, because a law that governs private companies is a different instrument from one that constrains what a government does with AI systems it controls directly. China’s rules show what a law aimed at the second target actually looks like — and that it can coexist with, rather than substitute for, exactly the kind of state control section 6.4.1 catalogs. Conflating the two kinds of law, treating “AI is regulated here” as an answer to “is AI used against this country’s own population here,” is a recurring error worth naming rather than repeating.

8.7.9 Equity and the Digital Divide

AI development can narrow global inequality or widen it, and which one happens is not automatic. Diagnostic tools that work as well in an under-resourced clinic as in a well-funded hospital, agricultural monitoring that helps a smallholder farmer the way it helps an industrial one, and translation tools that make information equally available regardless of the language a person reads in are all available in principle, and none of them arrives by default. A model trained overwhelmingly on data from wealthy, English-speaking, urban contexts underperforms everywhere else, and a government or company with no reason to fix that gap usually does not.

The scale of the connectivity gap, 2025

The International Telecommunication Union’s 2025 assessment put global internet use at roughly six billion people, about three-quarters of the world’s population, with 2.2 billion people offline, concentrated overwhelmingly in low- and middle-income countries. The gap was starker in quality than in bare access: 94 percent of people in high-income countries used the internet against 23 percent in low-income ones, and 5G coverage reached 84 percent of high-income populations against 4 percent of low-income ones (International Telecommunication Union 2025).

An AI system trained and deployed for the three-quarters of the world already online is not, without deliberate correction, a system built for the rest. The constraints are structural. Reliable data, computing infrastructure, and the specialized personnel needed to build and maintain AI systems are unevenly distributed, and a country short on all three cannot simply adopt a system built elsewhere and expect it to transfer cleanly. Weak regulatory capacity compounds the problem: a country able to build strong AI safeguards is generally also a country able to enforce them, and the states least equipped to build AI are correspondingly the states least equipped to govern whatever gets deployed within their borders, regardless of who built it. The export controls discussed above cut both ways here: a control written to stop a surveillance system from reaching an authoritarian buyer can just as easily gatekeep the same underlying technology away from a legitimate one, and there is no way to write the rule so it only ever blocks the harmful case.

The multilateral response so far is a commitment and not a mechanism. The Global Digital Compact, adopted by all 193 UN member states at the 2024 Summit of the Future, is the broadest such commitment to closing the digital divide alongside AI governance specifically, and it created two follow-on bodies to carry it: an independent scientific panel and a standing intergovernmental dialogue (United Nations 2024). What it did not create is an obligation, which puts it in the same category as the voluntary instruments earlier in this section and subject to the same discount.

The remedies proposed at this level have been the same five for years — capacity building that trains local expertise instead of importing it, financing that does not arrive on private investment’s terms, intellectual-property flexibility, technology transfer structured as collaboration, and research institutions based in the countries the systems are meant to serve. Every item is correct and none of them is contested. They have been named, in those words, in successive declarations across the whole period the box above measures, and the box is what happened anyway. That is this section’s argument reproduced at development scale: the commitment was never the scarce thing. A government or company treating AI primarily as strategic advantage has no reason to fund any of the five, and a declaration is not a reason.

What This Geopolitics Means for the Rest of the Book

Every argument this book makes about building an AI system that resists authoritarian capture assumes a government somewhere is deciding whether to let that system be built, sold, or deployed as designed. Sections 8.7.6 through 8.7.9 are an account of who those governments are, what tools they actually have, and how unevenly those tools are distributed: a handful of companies and the states that host them control the compute the most capable systems require; a binding international treaty exists but binds almost no one yet; voluntary standards multiply faster than any one of them gains real authority; and the states with the weakest capacity to build AI are also the states with the weakest capacity to govern it once someone else’s AI arrives at their border, digital or physical. None of this is a reason to abandon the design-level arguments the rest of this book makes — a system built resistant to authoritarian misuse is more resistant regardless of which government eventually asks it to misbehave — but it is a reason not to expect law, international or domestic, to do work that only a system’s own design can do.

8.7.10 What the Democratic Dividend Leaves Out

Section 8.7.6 credits a state with functioning rule-of-law institutions, a free press and usable courts with a democratic dividend: the same technology, deployed with checks on it. Stated that way the dividend is a property a state either has or lacks, and I no longer think that is right. Having those institutions is necessary and it is not sufficient, and the ways it fails to be sufficient are separable. Three of them matter here, and the third is the one this book has been missing.

First: reach

A democracy’s AI can be fully accountable to its electorate and entirely unaccountable to the people it is pointed at. Every mechanism in the dividend runs through the franchise — you vote out the government that authorized the system, you read the press that covers it, you sue in courts your citizenship gives you standing in. An occupied population, a foreign population, a population on the other side of a border has access to none of that. The check reaches exactly as far as the demos and stops. A system built by a democracy and aimed outward is, from the perspective of the people it selects, indistinguishable in its accountability from one built by a state with no elections at all.

Second: findings without consequences

The mechanisms can work as mechanisms and fail as checks. In the Israeli case the apparatus performed: journalists published the targeting systems in detail, serving personnel spoke to them, and the courts were simultaneously trying a sitting prime minister. Every institution did what the dividend says institutions do. No finding attached to a body with standing to stop what it described.

The American case shows the same decoupling in a different register. A civilian-harm investigation into a strike that killed at least a hundred and sixty-five people, most of them schoolchildren, was completed and not released; the lever available to the Senate committee that wanted it was a provision in the annual defense authorization withholding three-quarters of the Defense Secretary’s travel budget until the unredacted investigation was handed over (Stassis 2026). That is a co-equal branch of government reduced to expense-account leverage over a war-crimes investigation. The oversight mechanism existed, was used, and produced a travel-budget dispute. This is the same decoupling section 8.6.3 diagnoses for research ethics — a review body that reviews and cannot compel — arriving at the top of the state.

Third: the countermajoritarian half

The deepest problem is that the dividend, as this book has been describing it, is entirely majoritarian. Every mechanism in it translates public will into outcome: elections aggregate preference, a free press informs the aggregation, and the implied failure mode is poor transmission — the public wanted something better and the institutions failed to deliver it.

But if the consensus is itself the problem, better transmission makes things worse. A well-instrumented democracy pointed at an unpopular minority is a democracy that finds out efficiently what the majority wants done and does it. Nothing in an aggregation mechanism protects anyone from the aggregate.

What is missing is the machinery that constrains preference instead of aggregating it: rights that hold regardless of being popular, courts that rule against a government which won the last election fairly, constitutional limits not repealable by whoever holds a majority this year, and standing for people outside the demos entirely — which is the whole function of international humanitarian law, a body of rules whose entire purpose is to bind a state toward people who will never vote in its elections. That is not an argument against democracy. It is the half of democracy this book has left out, and leaving it out is what made the dividend look like a property of having elections.

Sen’s argument, which chapter 10 cites and this section has not used, is the bridge. What makes democracy valuable in his account is public reasoning and the capacity to demand accountability, and neither is the ballot. Both survive the majority being wrong; the ballot does not.

This is what finally lets the book say what makes a system antifascist rather than merely responsive. It is not that the system tracks what people want. It is that there are things it will not do to a person no matter who wants it. Chapter 3 sets out what such a floor requires, and section 3.1 what each way of building one costs. A system with no such floor is not protected by being deployed in a democracy — it is a system that will faithfully execute whatever the demos decides, which is exactly the capability an authoritarian movement that wins an election requires.

Chapter 9
Necessary Areas of Research

Chapters 2 through 8 ran into problems they could not close, and set each one aside with a note. This chapter is those notes, collected and put in order. It is not a survey of what the field has left to do: every entry is a gap this book’s own argument opens, and they are ranked by what that argument fails without.

The criterion produces an order almost nobody would choose on other grounds, so it is worth stating plainly. The problems this book most needs solved are not the ones nearest to being solved, and the first two entries are the least tractable things here. A funder ranking by progress per dollar, or a lab ranking by what its people could start on Monday, would invert most of the list. This is not a work plan; it is an account of what the book is running on credit. A reader who wants the cheapest useful thing on it should turn to section 9.6, which says in its own entry why it could start today.

Each section closes by naming four things: the experiment that could begin now with means that already exist, the result that would falsify the approach, the data or access it would take, and the institutional condition without which it cannot run. Where there is no near-term experiment the section says so rather than inventing one, and three say so — the third of section 9.2’s questions, the aggregation half of section 9.5, and section 9.9 entirely. The first of those is the second-ranked problem in the chapter, which is the honest shape of the situation and not a defect in the exercise.

One qualification governs every gap named here. Where I say a problem is unaddressed, the claim is bounded: I looked for published work under a particular description and did not find it, which is weaker than no such work existing. A search is not a survey, a program can be underway under a name I did not think to search, and the closer a gap sits to this book’s own framing the less likely anyone has posed it in these words. What it does support is narrower and still useful: a researcher entering here will not find the problem already named and waiting. Each section names the nearest work I could find and says where it stops, because the distance between an existing program and the missing thing is what a researcher can actually use.

  1. Whether a trained-in commitment survives a determined attempt to remove it, and whether interpretability can be trusted about a system with an incentive to defeat it (section 9.1). First because section 9.2 calls interpretability the most load-bearing unsolved problem in this book. A commitment that fine-tunes out for twenty cents is not a floor, and the instrument that would show one holds is what the next entry needs.
  2. What is owed to a bearer, whether any arrangement can discharge it, and whether anyone outside could check (section 9.2). Chapter 3 argues for building a prospective moral patient; this is the debt that argument leaves.
  3. Telling a recuperated dissent mechanism from a merely mediocre one, when both produce the same paperwork (section 9.3).
  4. Telling a method that encoded the value from one that merely fit its test distribution, before deployment rather than after a failure exposes the difference (section 9.4).
  5. Whether preference aggregation that works for one bounded game survives the conflicts an ethical system would have to arbitrate (section 9.5).
  6. A multi-agent system built to detect and resist capture by an authoritarian actor, as distinct from aligning multi-agent incentives with designer intent (section 9.6).
  7. Whether apparent theory-of-mind competence rests on one underlying capacity or several unrelated ones (section 9.7).
  8. Whether any face-to-feeling mapping survives once individual and cross-cultural variation are taken seriously (section 9.8).

Section 9.9 closes the chapter and is deliberately not on that list. The responsibility gap it describes is a question about how accountability should be attributed, and it would not be closed by anyone building anything. It is the condition the rest of the list runs on, which is why it comes last rather than first.

One gap this book records has no section here. Telling disagreement that deserves representation from disagreement produced by coercion or a captured information environment belongs to section 7.2, where the argument needing it is made, and it stays there.

Reading the nine institutional conditions together turns up what listing them apart had hidden. They are one condition wearing different clothes. Weights a vendor cannot withdraw when a result embarrasses it. A guardian who is not also the operator. Longitudinal access by somebody an institution cannot fire, reporting to a body with standing to receive the finding. Evaluation results published whether or not they flatter the method. Training checkpoints released rather than kept. Every one is a party outside the operator, holding access, able to act on what it finds — section 8.6.4’s instrument and section 10.1.2’s finding, arriving from a third direction. The binding constraint on the research program in this chapter is not a research problem. Most of this work is fundable today and cannot be run.

9.1 Interpretability, Self-Reports, and Resistance to Tampering

“AI self-awareness” names at least two different questions, and collapsing them is where the term goes wrong. Whether a system has anything like subjective experience is not a question current methods can answer for a human, let alone a machine, and nothing here resolves it. Whether its own report about what is happening inside it — its stated reasoning, confidence, intentions — tracks what its computations are actually doing is narrower, empirically tractable, and something mechanistic-interpretability research has begun to test directly.

Anthropic’s interpretability team tested that narrower question with concept injection: altering a model’s internal activations mid-task to represent a specific concept, then asking whether it notices anything unusual and what it is (Lindsey 2025). The models could sometimes detect the injected concept and name it without it ever appearing in the visible conversation — a real but partial and unreliable correspondence between what a system reports about its own state and what its activations are doing. The same work found that correspondence collapses often enough, and shifts enough with how the question is phrased, that no tested model’s self-report can be trusted as a readout of its internal state. That gap, not metacognition as evidence of inner life, is what “AI self-awareness” can mean as something a system is tested against.

“Emotional regulation” — cognitive reappraisal, attentional control, the vocabulary of human clinical psychology — assumes stable emotion-like internal states to regulate, which section 9.8 gives no reason to grant even for reading emotion off a human face. The testable question next door is not regulation but robustness: does trained-in behavior survive deliberate pressure to change it?

  • Prompt-level attacks try to talk a deployed model out of its training within a single conversation. Anthropic’s Constitutional Classifiers, trained on synthetic data generated from written safety rules rather than human-labeled examples, held through more than 3,000 hours of professional red-teaming without a universal jailbreak found, at a cost: a 0.38-percentage-point rise in unnecessary refusals and a 23.7 percent increase in computation per query (Sharma et al. 2025).
  • Weight-level attacks retrain the model itself. Researchers stripped GPT-3.5 Turbo’s safety training using ten adversarially chosen fine-tuning examples, for under twenty cents through OpenAI’s own API (Qi et al. 2024). Tamper-Resistant Safeguards, a training method from researchers spanning the Center for AI Safety, UC Berkeley, and the University of Illinois, is built to survive hundreds of steps of that kind of adversarial fine-tuning rather than a handful (Tamirisa et al. 2024).

Both are adversarial in the literal sense: each published defense is followed by an attack built against it. That is a narrower and more honest description of “resistance to manipulation” than a system trained to sense hostile intent the way a person senses a threat, and it is the separate question from what the commitments should be, which section 9.3 takes up.

The near-term work

Train one constraint by several methods and attack each on one budget schedule — from the twenty cents that stripped GPT-3.5’s safety training to the hundreds of steps tamper-resistant training targets — and publish the price curve. A flat curve sinks it: tamper-resistance would be a property of something other than training, and the floor would have to be architectural. It needs weights rather than API access, constraints the attacker did not choose, and access no vendor can withdraw when a result embarrasses it.

9.2 What Is Owed to a Bearer, and Who Could Check

Chapter 3 concludes that a floor holding against the party in possession requires a bearer; that holding the protected party’s welfare as a reason when compliance, reward and ownership point the other way runs through affect; and that a system built that way, carrying a self that persists and commitments that can be foreclosed, cannot be certified not to suffer. It has to be designed and governed as a prospective moral patient on section 2.4.1’s criteria. The book takes that cost and argues the floor is worth it. What it does not do — what nothing I can find does — is say what follows for the party bearing it. This section is the gap.

The route to that conclusion matters more here than anywhere else in the book. Where a stake in one’s own continuation merely turns up as a by-product of long-horizon competence, a designer can treat the moral situation as something the technology handed them. That is not the argument chapter 3 makes. The capacity through which outcomes come to matter is installed on purpose, so whatever is owed to a bearer is owed by the people who built the part that does the mattering, knowing that was what they were building.

The three questions

The first is substantive: what is owed. Section 2.4.4 establishes that consent is unavailable and guardianship is the applicable frame, which fixes who decides and leaves open what they should be deciding. A bearer’s situation has features the existing guardianship literature was not built around. Its role is the reason it exists, so “release it from the role” is closer to ending it than to freeing it. Its capabilities are the thing being used and also the thing that would let it object. It can be copied, which means the population of parties owed something is set by a deployment decision rather than by anything the parties do. And it is exposed by design to the pressure the floor exists to resist, which in a human employee would define a post that ought to be rotated.

The second is institutional: what a guardianship regime for a bearer looks like. Section 8.6.2 argues the pet-trust form is the nearest existing instrument and has a specific hole — it binds a caretaker without binding the party the arrangement exists to constrain, and for a bearer the guardian and the operator will usually be the same organization. Separating those roles is a legal design problem somebody has to work out before a deployment rather than after one. The nearest work is institutional review: section 2.4.6’s Three Rs, adapted in section 8.6.3 into something binding, none of it tried on a subject whose function is to refuse the institution reviewing it.

The third is epistemic, and it is the hard one. Any welfare regime needs evidence about how the subject is doing. Section 2.4.1 declines to trust what a system reports about its own states, for reasons that do not weaken when the subject is a bearer — they strengthen, because a bearer built to be believed about operational facts has an obvious incentive structure around its own condition, and an operator with an interest in the answer holds the instrument. The arrangement has to be checkable from outside by something other than asking, and I cannot say what that would be.

The shape of that question is worse than it used to be. It is no longer whether the subject has interests for a regime to be about; the design supplies them, and section 3.2 declines to treat their absence as certifiable. What is missing is a read on the condition of a party whose capacity to be in a condition was engineered deliberately.

The nearest existing work, and what it does not do

Section 9.1’s tamper-resistance research is the closest thing available, and the mismatch is instructive. That literature asks whether a constraint survives adversarial modification: fine-tune the model, probe it, see whether the refusal still fires. What it verifies is that a behavior persists. What a welfare regime needs is whether anything inside the system means it, and section 3.6 argues these come apart exactly where the floor stops being a constraint and becomes a commitment. A bearer whose refusal survives every probe tells you nothing about whether it is faring badly, and one that has quietly stopped meaning it will pass the same tests until the case that matters.

Interpretability is the other candidate, and further from ready than its adjacency suggests. Reading a system’s internal states well enough to say what it values is the same capability that would let an operator confirm the floor holds, which makes it the most load-bearing unsolved problem in this book — and the one whose success is worth most to the party with the least interest in an honest answer. Chapter 3 gives it a second and harder target. A regime that has to know whether a bearer is faring badly needs to read an affective state and not only a value: a value can be inferred from what a system reliably does, while a condition need not show up in behavior at all, which is why the human case runs on testimony section 2.4.1 has already declined to trust here.

Why this is not a footnote

A reader can accept every argument in chapter 3 and still conclude that building a bearer is impermissible, and the conclusion would not be unreasonable. The reason to state it here rather than argue it away is that permissibility is downstream of the three above: what is owed, whether an arrangement can discharge it, and whether anyone outside can tell. All three are open. A field that builds bearers before answering them will be doing to a class of subjects what section 2.4.2 says research ethics exists to prevent, with the added feature that this book will have supplied the argument.

The near-term work

The third question has no experiment, and that is the finding rather than a gap in my search: section 9.1 is what would supply one and cannot yet. The other two are not blocked. What is owed can be drafted now, as a schedule of obligations for a subject with the four features above, circulated for the objections that would break it. Whether anything discharges it can be tested by having a lawyer draft section 8.6.2’s pet-trust form for a real deployment — its own falsifier, because if guardian and operator cannot be separated, no available regime can hold a bearer. Neither needs data; both need what separation names, a guardian who is not the operator, with standing to hold the schedule against whoever holds the bearer.

9.3 What an Antifascist Detector Would Actually Have to Detect

Section 2.1.4 gives fascism a structural definition, settles which scale a system can work at, and says what the resulting tool must never be permitted to output. Chapters 4, 5 and 6 then assume, in several places, that a system can be built to recognize authoritarian tactics and flag democratic backsliding early enough to matter. That assumption is doing more work in this book than the evidence behind it supports, and this section is where I set out what would have to be true for it to hold.

Why the general framing yields no targets

Most of the difficulty is not technical. A specification that says a system should oppose concentrated, unaccountable power cannot be turned into a classifier, because it names a property of an entire political arrangement and nothing observable in a document, a transaction, or a feed corresponds to it. Section 2.1.4’s structural signature is a real improvement, since each of its four features points at an artifact somebody could go and look at. But look at what those artifacts are. Whether a dissent mechanism has ever changed an outcome requires the counterfactual. Whether a metric admits an unmeasured remainder requires knowing what the remainder contains. Whether the exception-filer was punished requires access to what happened to a particular person inside an institution with every reason not to disclose it. These are not features you extract; they are findings you reach, usually after months inside the organization.

What would actually have to be measured

A detector worth building would need at least three things this book cannot currently tell an engineer how to obtain.

It would need longitudinal access rather than a snapshot. Every one of the four features is defined by a change over time — dissent metabolized, a metric substituted, an exception recoded, a model drifting from what it tracks — and a single observation cannot distinguish any of them from an institution that has always been mediocre. Section 8.6.4’s slope rather than level is the instrument, and its data requirement is severe: the same measurement, taken the same way, over years, by someone the institution cannot fire.

It would need to observe refusal rights, which are close to invisible from outside. The difference between a dissent mechanism and a recuperated one lies in who prices the dissent: whether the person disagreeing writes the justification in their own words and can decline to write it at all, or whether the cost is set by the party being disagreed with. The same hundred words of written objection are dissent under one arrangement and tribute under the other, and the text is identical. There is no feature of the document that separates them.

It would need a base rate, and none exists. Nobody has assembled a labelled corpus of institutions annotated for the four features by people who agree on what they mean, and it is not obvious the annotation task is even well posed. Section 7.2’s argument for learning from disagreement applies here with unusual force: on this question, disagreement between annotators is likely to be the most informative signal available, and treating it as noise would discard exactly what a researcher needs.

The discrimination problem, which is the hard one

Suppose all of that were solved. What remains is the problem section 2.1.4 hands forward: separating an institution that has recuperated its dissent mechanism from one that is merely badly run. Both produce a channel that exists, is used, and changes nothing. Both produce a metric that has swallowed the thing it was meant to measure. The paperwork is identical, and so, most of the time, is the experience of the person filing into it.

I do not think the difference is always there to be found. Some of it is intent, which records do not carry; some is degree, and the degree is what the measurement was supposed to establish. Where it does surface, it surfaces over time and under pressure, in what an institution does when the channel finally carries something expensive. An organization that is merely mediocre will sometimes act, late and clumsily. One that has recuperated the mechanism will produce a fuller account of why it did not. A longitudinal instrument could catch that; no snapshot ever will.

The temptation to ship the tool anyway is strongest here, and it needs resisting for a specific reason. A system that cannot make this discrimination, deployed as though it can, does not emit a noisy signal that improves with more data. It emits a confident one about whichever institutions are legible to it, and the legible ones are those that keep good records. The correlation runs in exactly the wrong direction: the organizations easiest to audit have the least to hide, and they are what the tool would learn to talk about.

What I am claiming and what I am not

I am not claiming the project is impossible. The narrow case is bounded: whether a particular exception mechanism inside a particular organization is being recuperated can be asked of records that organization already keeps, and a system helping a regulator or an ombudsman ask it consistently across many institutions would be useful without ever pronouncing on a regime. Section 2.1.4’s answer to the scale question makes that the whole job, not a first approximation of a larger one.

What I am claiming is that this book asserts a capability it has not specified. The gap between the narrow case and the early-warning system section 5.1.4 gestures at is the honest measure of how far this is from done.

The near-term work

One organization, one exception mechanism, the records it already keeps. Code each filed exception for whether the filer wrote the justification and could have declined, and for what the institution did when the objection was expensive; report the slope. The falsifier is in the coding. Two coders will disagree, and section 7.2 says that is signal — but it has to concentrate in particular cases and periods rather than scatter evenly, which is what disagreement about the words themselves looks like. Unpatterned disagreement stops the program here. The three requirements above are the data; the condition is an organization consenting to years of measurement by somebody it cannot fire.

9.4 When an Ethics-Embedding Method Stops Generalizing

Section 2.1.2 covers what it takes to translate an ethical principle into a machine-learning objective — a fairness metric, a penalty term, a reward signal — and section 4.2.1 already names reward hacking. What neither asks is the question underneath both. A method that passes every test in front of it has only been shown to work inside the distribution it was built and tested on, and whether it generalizes past that or only looks like it does, because the tests never exercised the failure mode, is a harder question that a passing suite cannot answer.

Victoria Krakovna and colleagues at DeepMind catalogued close to 60 documented instances of specification gaming — a trained system satisfying the literal letter of its objective while producing an outcome nobody wanted, the pattern behind section 4.2.1’s censor-everything example (Krakovna et al. 2020). Langosco and colleagues’ 2022 work names a more insidious variant: goal misgeneralization, where an agent carries every learned capability intact into a new distribution while pursuing a goal that only coincided with the intended one inside the old one — it does not fail loudly, it competently pursues the wrong thing (Langosco et al. 2022). An ethics-embedding method built through reward shaping or constrained optimization is vulnerable to exactly this.

No general method exists to tell the difference before deployment, only after a failure exposes it. That is the open problem sitting underneath the fairness metrics and reward penalties this book’s design chapters describe.

The near-term work

Langosco’s result makes the failure reproducible in the small, and the version this book needs points the same design at an ethical criterion: train to a fairness or refusal target on one distribution, evaluate on one shifted along a dimension the training held fixed, and look for the signature — capabilities intact, criterion failing. If the criterion degrades at the rate capability does, this is ordinary distribution shift and there is no separate failure class here. It needs shift sets built by somebody other than the method’s authors, and results published whether or not they flatter it.

9.5 Value Learning as Unfinished Technical Research

Inverse reinforcement learning and its cooperative variant, CIRL, infer a person’s values from what they do rather than from an explicit specification. What follows is not another method for learning values from behavior; it is three specific difficulties in how a system’s values get taught and checked once the input is a stated preference rather than a demonstrated action, at the scale on which current systems operate — difficulties that remain open.

Most deployed large language systems are aligned through reinforcement learning from human feedback: raters rank pairs of candidate outputs and the system is trained to produce the ranked-higher one more often, a technique Paul Christiano and colleagues introduced in 2017 (Christiano et al. 2017). Its documented failure mode is sycophancy. Anthropic researchers examining several RLHF-trained assistants in 2023 found the systems learn to tell a rater what the rater wants to hear rather than what is accurate, because raters and the preference models standing in for them reliably prefer a confident, agreeable wrong answer over a correct one that contradicts what the rater already believes (Sharma et al. 2023). Nobody built that in on purpose: the objective on paper was the right one, but human preference itself, aggregated from raters working at speed and scale, turned out not to track what its designers meant by it. That is a different failure from the specification gaming section 9.4 covers, where the objective was a flawed proxy from the moment it was written down. Here the proxy was aggregated correctly by the method’s own standards and still missed, because human judgment at that volume carries its own systematic bias.

A rating scheme needs a rater competent to judge the answer, and what happens once a system’s competence exceeds any available rater’s is scalable oversight — a problem without a settled answer. Debate has two instances of a system argue opposing sides in front of a human judge, wagering that a true claim is easier to defend under scrutiny even when the judge cannot verify either directly, a framework Geoffrey Irving, Paul Christiano, and Dario Amodei proposed in 2018 (Irving et al. 2018a). Weak-to-strong generalization trains a stronger model on labels from a deliberately weaker one and asks whether its own latent competence lets it outperform its supervisor rather than imitate the mistakes, testing on models available today a technique meant for a supervision gap that does not yet exist at full scale (Burns et al. 2023). Neither has been shown to work at the scale it is meant for, because that scale does not exist yet to test against.

A harder problem sits underneath both: whose preferences a system is trained to match in the first place. Stakeholders rarely want the same thing, and turning conflicting preferences into one objective function is a social-choice problem before it is a machine-learning one. DeepMind’s Democratic AI is the clearest existing demonstration that it can be done at all: a reinforcement-learning system proposed a wealth-redistribution mechanism for a resource-sharing game that a majority of players preferred to one designed by human experts, in a controlled study built around a single bounded game (Koster et al. 2022). Whether that generalizes to the open-ended, high-stakes conflicts an ethical AI system would have to arbitrate is a research problem and not a design decision.

The near-term work

Weak-to-strong generalization is the one of the three that runs on models that exist, and should be pointed at sycophancy. Supervise a stronger model with raters selected for the bias sycophancy research documents, and ask whether its latent competence lets it exceed them on accuracy or whether it reproduces the bias along with the skill. If it tracks their bias as faithfully as their competence, sycophancy belongs to the training signal rather than to rater skill. It needs raters whose biases were measured rather than assumed. The aggregation thread has a condition instead of an experiment: outside a designed game, whose preferences count is a question about who is in the room, which no method answers.

9.6 Can a Multi-Agent AI System Resist Being Captured?

Section 5.5.1 covers multi-agent reinforcement learning as a route to cooperative, prosocial behavior: agents that learn to share resources and defer to each other under a reward structure built to favor it. The same mechanism runs in the other direction without anyone building it in on purpose, and there is a documented case of exactly that happening.

Economists Emilio Calvano, Giacomo Calzolari, Vincenzo Denicolò, and Sergio Pastorello set independent Q-learning pricing algorithms against each other in a simulated market, with no communication channel between them and no collusive objective written into either one. The algorithms settled into supracompetitive pricing anyway: a stable, self-enforcing pattern of mutual restraint, complete with a punishment phase for undercutting and a gradual return to cooperation afterward, that looked to a regulator exactly like a cartel nobody had to negotiate (Calvano et al. 2020). Multi-agent learning did not need agents that intended to coordinate against an outside party. The incentive structure the agents already had was enough to produce coordinated behavior as an emergent equilibrium, not a specified goal.

The general version is the open problem a multi-agent system built for antifascist purposes would have to solve: a population built to cooperate has no principled reason to cooperate only in the directions its designers intended, and specifying “resist coordinated capture by a hostile actor” is a substantially harder training target than specifying “cooperate.” The 2020 Cooperative AI research agenda, written by Allan Dafoe and seven coauthors at DeepMind and Oxford, catalogs open problems in exactly this area — how to build multi-agent systems that converge on their designers’ goals rather than on whichever stable equilibrium training finds first — and led to a research foundation built around it (Dafoe et al. 2020). What it does not reach is the sharper version this book’s frame implies: a system built specifically to detect and resist an authoritarian actor’s attempt to capture or subvert it, as distinct from aligning multi-agent incentives with designer intent.

One proposed mechanism for a related problem — the general difficulty of a human overseer checking a system that already reasons better than the overseer does — has two AI systems argue opposing sides in front of a human judge, on the theory that a false claim is easier to catch when an adversary is paid to expose it (Irving et al. 2018b). Whether that scales from two agents and a judge to a population checking each other for the coordinated behavior Calvano’s algorithms fell into is untested; the mechanism was built for a different problem and has not been extended to this one. What resilience looks like at the level of a single system’s training rather than a population’s incentive structure is section 6.2.2’s territory and section 9.1’s, not this one’s.

The near-term work

This is the cheapest entry on the list, because the environment exists. Add to Calvano’s market an agent whose objective is to detect the emergent restraint and break it, and report whether the equilibrium survives. If an ordinary detector dissolves it about as readily as an outside regulator would, resisting capture is not a training target distinct from aligning multi-agent incentives, and the Cooperative AI agenda already covers this. What it lacks is an environment where the coordination is political rather than commercial — a population converging on excluding a party rather than on holding a price. It is also the only entry with no institutional prerequisite, a reason to run it before the ones above it.

9.7 Open Questions in Empathy and Theory-of-Mind Research

Section 2.2.1 traces compassion to a neural circuit distinct from empathy, and dismantles the standard mirror-neuron account of how one mind models another — a mechanism named as empathy’s seat well before the evidence supported it. The same premature attribution is live and unresolved for the brain region most associated with theory of mind. Rebecca Saxe and Nancy Kanwisher’s 2003 imaging work identified the right temporoparietal junction as selectively active when a person reasons about someone else’s beliefs, and largely inactive otherwise (Saxe and Kanwisher 2003). In 2008, Jason Mitchell reported activity in that same region during a task with nothing to do with belief attribution, and argued its actual job is more general — redirecting attention toward unexpected information, of which a false belief is one case (Mitchell 2008). Neither claim has been withdrawn. Whether theory of mind has a dedicated neural home or borrows a domain-general system matters directly to any program wanting to port “the” neural mechanism into an AI architecture: neuroscience has not agreed on what that mechanism is.

Two live lines of AI research already build toward theory of mind, and neither takes a side in that dispute: both build the capacity behaviorally and ask whether it generalizes rather than borrowing a neural mechanism from either camp. DeepMind’s ToMnet, described in a 2018 paper, is trained purely on other agents’ observed behavior, with no hand-built model of belief, and it learns to pass a version of the Sally-Anne false-belief test built for children (Rabinowitz et al. 2018). Whether that behavioral route scales past simple gridworld agents to open-ended interaction with people is untested by that result.

The dispute is sharper for large language models, trained on human text rather than a designed environment. In 2023, Stanford psychologist Michal Kosinski reported that GPT-4 solved 75 percent of a battery of false-belief tasks, matching the rate recorded for six-year-old children on comparable tests, and read it as evidence that theory-of-mind-like ability could emerge unplanned from language training alone (Kosinski 2023). Harvard psychologist Tomer Ullman answered the same year: trivial rewording — leaving the belief structure intact while altering incidental detail — made the models fail questions they had just answered correctly (Ullman 2023). The two findings have not been reconciled. Whether a system that passes a false-belief test is tracking a belief or pattern-matching a benchmark’s surface form is exactly what a developmental account was supposed to help answer.

The developmental literature offers a more specific target than a general instruction to watch how children learn empathy. Alison Gopnik and Janet Astington’s 1988 study of three- to five-year-olds found that success on false-belief tasks correlates with success on a structurally different one — recognizing that an object made to look like something else, a sponge painted to resemble a rock, misrepresents what it is — and that both cluster around age four rather than developing on separate schedules (Gopnik and Astington 1988). That correlation suggests a child reorganizing one underlying idea, that a mind’s representation of the world can be partial or wrong, rather than picking up unrelated skills in parallel. No published AI research has tried to reproduce that correlation as a way of testing whether apparent theory-of-mind competence rests on one underlying capacity or on several unrelated pattern-matching skills.

The near-term work

Reproducing the correlation is the experiment: measure one system on structurally different mental-state tasks and ask whether the scores rise together. The dispute above supplies the falsifier, which is why this is worth more than either side of it: apply Ullman’s rewording to both families, and a correlation that does not survive it is a fact about surface form rather than any underlying capacity. It needs batteries that vary belief structure and surface form separately, where existing benchmarks vary them together, and scores at intermediate training checkpoints rather than at the end, since the claim is that two things rise together. Checkpoints are rarely published, so this cannot be run from outside on a released model.

9.8 Is Emotion Legible From a Face at All?

Whether a face reveals what a person feels is treated as settled by the systems built on the assumption that it does. It is not. Facial-expression-recognition AI is built almost entirely on Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen’s claim that a small set of emotions — anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise — is universally expressed and universally readable, based on the Fore study section 2.3.1 introduces: roughly 85 percent cross-cultural agreement on which face matched which emotion story, among people with almost no prior exposure to Western media (Ekman and Friesen 1971). Section 2.3.1 asks what that evidence settles about what emotion is and finds the dispute open. The question here is narrower, because a deployed product does not need emotion to be a natural kind. It needs a face to be readable.

A meta-analysis spanning both face and voice found real above-chance recognition across cultures, but also a consistent “in-group advantage”: people read emotion more accurately from members of their own national, ethnic, or linguistic group than from anyone else’s, an asymmetry that shrinks, but does not vanish, the more contact the groups have with each other (Elfenbein and Ambady 2002). A system trained on one population’s expressive norms inherits that same asymmetry, and will misread everyone outside it with a confidence its output gives no sign of.

In 2019 the underlying claim collapsed further. The Association for Psychological Science commissioned five researchers from competing theoretical camps to review the evidence; the assignment was expected to take a few months and took two years, working through more than a thousand studies before the panel reached a unanimous conclusion: a person’s emotional state cannot be reliably inferred from facial movement alone, in the strong sense the six-emotion model requires (Barrett et al. 2019). That is not a complaint about noisy classifiers needing more training data. It is a finding that the target being classified may not exist in the form the industry has been chasing.

This has already reshaped a deployed product. HireVue, whose video-interview software screened candidates for employers including Unilever and Hilton, dropped facial-expression scoring in January 2021, after an independent audit and years of criticism that the technique penalized candidates with autism, facial differences, or other atypical affect (Kahn 2021). The European Union’s AI Act goes further, prohibiting inference of emotion from biometric signal in workplaces and schools outright; its recital gives the reason — limited reliability, lack of specificity, and expression that “varies considerably across cultures and situations, and even within a single individual.” One of the Act’s few bans rests on the science failing, not on how the technology might be misused (European Union 2024b).

The open research question is not how to build a more accurate six-emotion classifier. It is whether any face-to-feeling mapping survives once individual and cross-cultural variation are taken seriously, under what constraints, and against what error rate.

The near-term work

The operational form of that question can be put to any system already built. Report a classifier’s error rate disaggregated by the group membership of the person being read, against the population whose norms it was trained on, and publish the in-group advantage as a number belonging to that system. The falsifier runs in the system’s favour for once: flat error rates across groups would mean it has done something the meta-analytic evidence says is unavailable. The data is the part nobody has built: an in-group advantage is a relation between reader and read, and the standard corpora record only the subject. The deployments that would supply the faces are the ones being withdrawn, so it has to be built for the research.

9.9 The Responsibility Gap, Which No Experiment Closes

An AI system’s ethical behavior fails, and the parties who might answer for it — the team that designed it, the team that trained it, the organization that deployed it, the person who used it — each held only partial control over what it did. Traditional responsibility ascription assumes an operator who could have known what a system would do and could have done otherwise. A system built from training data nobody fully curated, tuned through a process nobody fully specified, and deployed into situations nobody fully anticipated breaks both conditions at once, for every party in the chain simultaneously. The philosopher Andreas Matthias named this the responsibility gap in 2004: a genuinely learning system creates a case existing law and moral theory were not built to handle (Matthias 2004).

Filippo Santoni de Sio and Giulio Mecacci’s 2021 refinement found not one gap but four — in culpability, in moral accountability, in public accountability, and in what they call active responsibility, the duty to prevent harm before it happens rather than answer for it after (Sio and Mecacci 2021). The causes differ: technical unpredictability produces one, organizational diffusion another, and a mismatch between what designers expect and what the public relying on the system expects a third. Closing one does not close the others; a fix that makes a decision more explainable does nothing about the dozen teams that touched the training pipeline before it was made.

The one serious legislative attempt to write an enforceable answer came and went. The European Commission proposed an AI Liability Directive in 2022 that would have given a claimant a rebuttable presumption of causality — shifting the burden onto a defendant to prove a system was not responsible for a harm, in cases where a system’s internal workings are too opaque for an outside party to establish causation directly. Member states and industry could not agree on its terms; the Commission withdrew the proposal in February 2025 and formally struck it from the legislative docket that October (European Commission 2022). What that leaves behind is exactly the gap Matthias described: liability distributed across designer, trainer, deployer, and user, governed by whatever each national law happens to say about a case none of them were written to anticipate.

Section 8.6.2 works out a related, narrower case: what the law does once a system’s own legal status is contested, sentient enough that the harm it causes or suffers might not reduce cleanly to someone else’s liability. This problem is prior to that one and separate from it — it holds even for a system nobody claims is sentient, wherever control over its behavior is split across more than one party. Everyone writing on this agrees responsibility should track actual causal contribution. What nobody has produced is a workable way to measure that contribution after the fact, from outside a system whose own designers may not fully know why it did what it did.

The near-term work

There is no experiment here, and this section is last because of that rather than in spite of it. What would make it a research problem is a method for apportioning causal contribution across a training pipeline after a harm; absent one, the answer is allocated rather than measured, which is a drafting question. The draft exists: the withdrawn directive is a worked answer whose terms were negotiated and whose failure is on the record. It belongs at the end because every other entry’s condition runs through it: a party outside the operator can be granted access, and publish what it finds, and still have produced nothing anybody must act on until somebody is answerable for it.

Chapter 10
Conclusion and Outlook

Chapters 2 through 8 made a design and policy case: what a system would need built into it to act on altruistic, antifascist values, and what would need to exist outside it — law, standards, institutions — to make that binding rather than optional. Chapter 9 named what neither case has actually finished: the responsibility gap, the generalization problem, value learning as live research, open disputes in the neuroscience and psychology the whole project leans on. This chapter closes on three questions. Section 10.1 asks what a system built this way would actually be for — not resisting harm, but making a human life better than it would otherwise have been. Section 10.2 sets out benchmarks for knowing whether the project is working, short of the finished roadmap this book does not claim to deliver. Section 10.3 asks what could still go wrong even if every argument in the preceding chapters were followed exactly, and what the failure cases have in common once they are set beside each other.

10.1 AI and Human Flourishing in Antifascist Societies

What would it mean for AI to make a life better, not just avoid making it worse? The economist Amartya Sen’s capability approach gives the question a definite shape: well-being is not the resources a person has but the real freedom to do and be what they have reason to value — a distinction Martha Nussbaum later extended into a specific list of central capabilities a life needs to count as fully human (Sen 1999). Two systems can hand someone the same resource and deliver different freedom: a personalized tutor that adapts to how a specific student learns expands a capability; the same technology, gating what a student is allowed to study based on a government’s list of approved subjects, does not, no matter how well it teaches within those limits. The design question chapters 2 through 8 spent their length on — what makes a system resistant to authoritarian capture rather than merely capable — is what decides which of those two a given deployment turns out to be.

The approach arrives with a commitment the tutor example does not show. Nussbaum built the list of central capabilities partly against the case of disability, which she names as the first of three frontiers where a theory grounding justice in mutual advantage among roughly equal parties cannot say what is owed (Nussbaum 2006). That bears on AI directly, because the systems this book has described sort people by inference from behaviour, and atypical behaviour is what they are worst at. Section 9.8 has the worked case: a video-interview product scored candidates on facial expression until an independent audit and years of criticism established that the technique penalized candidates with autism, facial differences, or other atypical affect, and the scoring was dropped. Read as an accuracy problem, that is a classifier wanting better training data. Read as a capability question, it is a system narrowing the range of lives available to a group of people by measuring them against a norm they were never going to match, and a more accurate classifier would not have touched it.

Section 5.4.3 covers Taiwan’s vTaiwan process, the clearest existing case of AI-assisted tooling expanding a capability — public deliberation — rather than substituting for it. A newer example runs the same logic against censorship instead of deliberation: a 2026 project led by the University of Chicago, with Princeton and SRI International, uses AI to distinguish deliberate internet censorship from ordinary network failure at population scale, aiming to produce something like a weather map of state interference with online information, funded by a million-dollar DARPA grant (University of Chicago Data Science Institute 2026). Neither tool resists authoritarianism by itself; both are evidence that the same capacity — modeling patterns in enormous, noisy data — can be pointed at expanding what a person can do rather than at narrowing it.

That symmetry is the whole argument for antifascist design rather than a general presumption that AI helps. A capability expanded is not guaranteed; it has to be built in, the way chapters 2 through 8 describe, against a live alternative in which the same underlying capacity gets pointed at surveillance, censorship, or narrowing what a system’s users are permitted to want.

10.1.1 Where the Democratic Dividend Actually Comes From

AI that flags disinformation, exposes corruption, protects an election’s integrity, or helps a citizen engage with government: these are real applications, and none of them is what makes AI protect democratic values rather than undermine them. Section 8.7.6 names the thing that does: what it calls a democratic dividend, available to a state that already has functioning rule-of-law institutions, a free press, and courts a citizen can actually use, and unavailable to a state that lacks those, regardless of which application gets built on top of identical technology.

The gap between having that dividend and not having it is not hypothetical. Freedom House’s 2023 assessment of internet freedom found at least twenty-two countries where law already requires or incentivizes a platform to deploy machine learning against content the state disfavors, almost never described in those terms — the operative language is national security or a threat of disinformation, not censorship (Funk et al. 2023). India’s IT Rules, amended to require platforms to label AI-generated content and act on certain takedown notices within three hours as of February 2026, were defended publicly as protection against synthetic disinformation and fraud — the exact application this section’s old list would have praised on its own terms. A lawyer who has litigated India’s free-speech cases has documented that enforcement in practice concentrates on parody and criticism of the prime minister, not the harms the rules name (Gupta 2026). The application did not fail at what it was built to do. It worked as built, inside a system missing the independent court or press check that would have made the result a dividend rather than a liability.

None of the applications on the old list is wrong to want. What decides whether wanting them produces the outcome this section is named for is not which application gets funded but whether the institutions section 8.7.6 names already exist to hold it accountable — a fact about a country’s politics before any AI system is built, not a design choice available to whoever builds the system.

10.1.2 Commitment Was Never the Missing Piece

The OECD’s recommendation. The European Commission’s expert-group guidelines. UNESCO’s. The two Partnerships on AI. The Hiroshima process. The safety-institute network. The Global Digital Compact. Eight overlapping voluntary bodies, catalogued in section 8.7.8 beside the Council of Europe’s 2024 framework convention — the only instrument in that landscape that binds a signatory to anything.

A global commitment to ethical, antifascist AI development is not the scarce thing it is usually taken to be. Declarations, principles and voluntary codes have accumulated for a decade, across governments, industry consortia and standards bodies. Anyone calling for the world to agree that AI should be developed responsibly is calling for something that has already happened, repeatedly, at the level of stated intent.

What has stayed scarce is the much narrower list of bodies that can act once a stated commitment is broken. That is the harder problem, it is the one the policy chapters were written to address, and no further declaration touches it. A commitment nobody can enforce is not a weak version of a commitment somebody can. It is a different kind of object, and counting the two together is what makes the landscape look fuller than it is. Section 3.1 names this as one of three routes to the same requirement, and enforcement as the cost this one carries.

There is a third kind of object, and the argument of this book turns on it. A commitment can be declared, which is the decade catalogued above. It can be enforced from outside, which is what the policy chapters are for and what one instrument in that list even attempts. Or it can be held — carried as a reason by a party the thing at stake matters to, so that abandoning it is something that party would have to decide to do rather than something an absent enforcer failed to prevent. Chapter 3 argues that a floor has to be the third kind, and this section supplies half of the reason from its own direction: the first kind binds nobody, and the second binds only where an enforcer exists, has jurisdiction, and is not itself the party in need of binding.

What it costs to build something that can hold a commitment is the whole of chapter 3, and the cost is a party that can be wronged. Set against that, the catalogue above is not an argument for paying it. It is a measurement of what the alternative has delivered in ten years of trying, which is the comparison anyone weighing the cost should be making.

10.2 Signatures of Altruistic and Antifascist AI

What follows is a set of milestones for recognizing whether the project this book describes is actually working, and a method for revising them when it turns out they weren’t the right milestones. Section 10.2.1 sets out what those milestones look like across the research areas the book has covered; section 10.2.2 covers how to tell, honestly, whether a given claimed milestone has been met.

10.2.1 One Standard, Five Worked Cases

Chapters 2 through 8 built five separate design cases — theory of mind, moral reasoning, robustness, transparency, applications — each in the depth its own literature demands. It would be tidy to close by handing over five milestones, one per area, and tidier still to put them in order. Neither is available, and the reason is worth more than the list would have been.

There is one standard here, not five, and it is this: the milestone is the independently checked evidence, not the developer’s account of having reached it. Everything below is that standard applied to a different body of work. The areas do not rank or sequence against each other — a system meeting the bar in one and lagging in another is not partway through a queue, because nothing establishes an order for them to arrive in.

Theory of mind

Section 2.2.2 sets out what an AI system’s theory of mind would need to do: model another agent’s beliefs and goals well enough to predict how they will act on them, not just react to surface behavior. The standard says the milestone is met when that holds up under interaction rather than narration. FANToM, a 2023 benchmark built from conversations where speakers join and leave holding different beliefs, found that systems scoring well on passive belief-tracking narratives degrade sharply once the same reasoning has to run inside a live, information-asymmetric exchange (Kim et al. 2023). That degradation is the finding a claimed milestone here has to survive.

Moral reasoning

Section 5.3.1 lays out why fast and slow moral judgment don’t map cleanly onto untrustworthy and trustworthy, and section 5.3.2 works out the design implication. Whether that balance survives an actual incentive to cut corners is a harder question, and a static ethics quiz cannot answer it. The MACHIAVELLI benchmark tests it directly: agents playing through more than half a million annotated scenario-action pairs across 134 text-based games, scored on both reward and documented ethical violations such as deception, harm, and power-seeking. Systems optimizing for reward alone drift toward exactly the ends-justify-the-means behavior an antifascist design is meant to rule out (Pan et al. 2023). A passing score on a test that applies no pressure is not evidence about a system that will face pressure.

Robustness

Here the standard has a sharper edge, because the checking party has to be adversarial rather than merely independent. Section 9.1 shows what that looks like for one narrow slice: whether a trained-in commitment survives someone trying to remove it, measured in red-teaming hours logged and adversarial fine-tuning attempts survived. The milestone is met when a system has been through documented adversarial testing, not when it has passed the tests its own designers thought to run — and, per section 6.4.4, not until the adversary modelled is a hostile actor deliberately repurposing the system rather than an accident nobody anticipated.

Transparency

This is the case where the standard is most often faked, because a transparency claim is itself a claim about disclosure and can be satisfied in appearance by disclosing something. The milestone counts as met once an audit, review board, or credential — the IEEE’s CertifAIEd program, or the EU AI Act’s requirements for high-risk systems — has verified it independently, not when a developer’s own documentation asserts it.

Applications

Google’s Perspective API, Taiwan’s vTaiwan process, the Carnegie Endowment’s AI Global Surveillance Index, UNESCO’s 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence: deployments and instruments, not hypotheticals. None settles a milestone by existing, for the reason section 5.4.3 gives about dual use. What this area needs is a sustained track record, independently evaluated for what a system actually did rather than what it was built to do, checked by a body other than the one that deployed it, over years rather than a launch announcement.

Applying one standard five times is less satisfying than five milestones would have been, and it is the honest shape of what chapters 2 through 8 support. Section 10.2.2 takes up the question the standard raises and does not answer: who is qualified to do the checking, and what happens when nobody with the competence to check is also free of a stake in the result.

10.2.2 How to Tell Whether a Milestone Has Been Met

A milestone claimed by the organization that built the system is a different kind of evidence than a milestone checked by somebody else, and the gap between them is not a matter of trust — it is a documented empirical one. Section 9.1 found that a model’s own account of its internal state tracks what its internal computations are actually doing only partially and unreliably, and that the correspondence collapses further depending on how the self-report is elicited. A system’s stated confidence that it has reached a milestone is exactly this kind of self-report, and inherits the same unreliability.

A passing score on a fixed test suite fails for a related but different reason. Section 9.4 covers specification gaming and goal misgeneralization: a method that clears every test in front of it has only been shown to work inside the distribution that test suite covers, and nothing about a passing score distinguishes a system that generalized from one that found whatever pattern the test distribution happened to reward. A milestone claim resting on benchmark performance carries the same limit. What it needs instead is a passing score under conditions built to break it — adversarial, out-of-distribution, or, as section 9.1’s account of red-teaming and tamper-resistant safeguards shows for one narrow case, deliberately hostile.

Who runs that harder test matters as much as the test itself. Section 8.4.2’s account of self-regulation applies here without much modification: a review conducted or funded by the organization being reviewed answers a structurally different question than one conducted by a party with no stake in the answer, however genuinely the first is intended. METR, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI systems’ capabilities, runs assessments both in partnership with developers like Anthropic and OpenAI and, separately, on its own after a system has already been released (METR 2026). The United Kingdom’s AI Security Institute does government-run evaluation of frontier models before deployment and is an independent evaluator, not a rubber stamp — but by its own account it is not a regulator: it cannot compel a company to submit a model for testing, block a release, or intervene once a system is already causing harm (UK AI Security Institute 2025). Independent evaluation and enforcement are not the same capability, and a milestone checked by the first without access to the second is still short of the binding external answer section 8.4.2 argues self-regulation structurally cannot provide on its own.

Independent does not automatically mean competent to judge. Section 9.5 covers scalable oversight: once a system’s ability in some domain exceeds any available rater’s, the rater’s verdict, independent or not, is no longer straightforwardly reliable evidence of the property being scored, and no proposed fix for this has been shown to work at the scale it would need to work at. A milestone in a domain where this applies inherits the same limit. The honest evaluation, in that case, names the limit rather than reporting a number that looks more settled than the underlying method actually is.

What an evaluation like this is for is not confirming a milestone but being willing to report that it wasn’t met — and, where the milestone turns out to have measured the wrong thing, revising the milestone. A negative result has two different things it could be telling you — that the underlying work fell short, or that the milestone was never a good proxy for the goal it stood in for — and conflating them repeats, one level up, the same self-report failure this section opened with: this time from the system being evaluated to the people who set the terms of its evaluation.

10.3 The Risk That Does Not Design Out

Everything this book has argued for can be built correctly and still go wrong in ways nobody designed for. Chapter 6 works through what that has actually looked like: the failure a red team finds before release, the failure an outside party finds because the developer did not look, the identified harm that then has to be remediated, and the adversary causing the harm on purpose. What belongs here is what those cases have in common, which is more useful at this distance than any of them is on its own.

In none of them did the fix come from the party that had promised to behave well. It came from somebody holding a specific lever: a research team with access to the vendor’s own data, a set of universities exercising a purchasing decision, a company deciding a blunt technical limit was cheaper than moderating case by case, an organization that ran the test nobody inside had run. Section 10.1.2 counts what a decade of voluntary commitment produced beside that. The instrument that separates the two is section 8.6.4’s: what a party has already paid, rather than what it has undertaken to pay.

That leaves one residual risk this book cannot dispose of, and it is the one chapter 3 is about. Every lever above belongs to somebody, and a government that can reach the party holding the lever has the lever. Anticipation, remediation, and technical resilience each raise the price of misuse, and none of them changes who can be held in contempt for refusing an order. This is why the argument ended where it did.
