A constraint that holds against the party in possession has to be held by something that is not in that party’s possession, and the only version of that anyone can specify is a bearer with a stake of its own, at the price section 3.6 sets out.

The rest of this chapter is what the project is for and how anyone would know it was working. This is the part that stays open.

Glossary

These entries define terms as this book actually uses them, not as a general-purpose dictionary would — several are the book’s own working definitions, distinct from how the same word is sometimes used elsewhere, and this note says so where it matters. Each entry points to the section where the term is developed and, where the book cites the term to a named study or system, the section carrying that citation. This is a reference, not a substitute for reading those sections.

Adversarial examples

Inputs deliberately perturbed, often imperceptibly to a person, to flip a model’s prediction. Training a model on adversarial examples increases its resistance to them, at some cost to ordinary accuracy (§6.2.2, §6.3.2, §8.5.2).

Affective concern

An outcome registering as mattering to a system, as against being ranked higher by it. The fourth of the four capacities section 2.3 separates — the others being recognizing an emotion, simulating one, and instrumental valuation — and the only one of the four that bears on whether a system genuinely cares. The book’s argument that affect is the only demonstrated basis for it, and the rationalist reply, are at §2.3.4; what it is needed for is at §3.2.

AIGS Index

The AI Global Surveillance Index, published by the Carnegie Endowment in 2019: an assessment of 176 countries that found AI-enabled surveillance technology already in active use in at least 75 of them (§8.4.5).

Alignment problem

Building an AI system whose goals stay in harmony with humane values, ethics, and intentions rather than drifting from them as the system scales or encounters situations its designers did not anticipate. “Value alignment” names the same target (§6.3.1, §4.2).

AlphaGo Zero

A Go-playing system that reached superhuman performance through self-play alone, without training on any human game, discovering strategies no human program had used. The book’s standard example of generalization that comes from scale and self-play rather than labeled human data (§2.4.1).

Antifascist (as this book uses it)

Opposing the concentration of power and authority in AI systems and countering the technology’s use by authoritarian actors. The book chooses this word over the broader “anti-authoritarian” deliberately, while holding that a system built on these principles is anti-authoritarian in full — antifascism is the narrower, more charged case, not a softer substitute for it (§2.1.4, §1.1).

Attention schema theory

An account, developed by Michael Graziano, of subjective awareness as the content of a simplified internal model the brain builds of its own attention — a model good enough to be useful, not a literal readout of what attention is actually doing (§4.1.2, §2.3.3).

Authoritarian misuse, six forms

The book’s own taxonomy of how AI gets turned toward authoritarian ends: algorithmic social scoring, mass biometric surveillance, psychographic micro-targeting, automated censorship, synthetic disinformation, and the repurposing of dual-use systems built for a legitimate original purpose (§6.4.1).

Bearer

Whatever makes the floor hold, from inside the system: a party that carries the commitment as its own, where the alternative is a constraint installed as a property of the machinery, and that could therefore in principle fail to carry it. The book’s own term, introduced at section 3.1 as the second of three ways to build a floor. What the word requires grows over chapter 3: section 3.2 argues that a bearer has to hold the protected party’s welfare as a reason when compliance, reward and ownership point elsewhere, that affect is the only demonstrated way to hold anything as a reason (§2.3.4), and that a system built that way cannot be certified not to suffer — so it must be designed and governed as a prospective moral patient in the strong sense of sentience below. Section 3.5 argues that it must be able to leave. Section 3.6 states what is left.

BERT

A language model pretrained on a large text corpus and then fine-tuned for specific tasks, from sentiment analysis to question answering — the book’s standard demonstration of the pretrain-then-fine-tune pattern in language (§5.4.3, §5.7.1).

Capabilities approach

Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum’s account of well-being: not the resources a person has, but the real freedom they have to do and be what they have reason to value. The book draws on it to ask what an AI-affected life is actually free to become, not only what resources it has access to (§2.1, §10.1).

Clearview AI

A facial-recognition company the book returns to as its standard case of overreach and regulatory response: marketed accuracy claims independent testing did not support, and fines from French and Italian regulators over unlawful collection of the biometric data the system was trained on (§6.4.3, §8.4.2).

COMPAS

A proprietary risk-assessment tool used in criminal sentencing, and the book’s standard case study of algorithmic bias compounded by trade-secret opacity — a defendant could not examine the reasoning behind a score used to help decide his sentence (§6.1.1, §6.1.3, §6.3.5).

Compassion

Distinguished throughout the book from empathy. Cognitive empathy is understanding another’s state; affective empathy is sharing it; compassion is caring about another’s welfare and being moved to help — a motivation, not a perception or a shared feeling. The book’s central claim in chapter 2 is that compassion, not empathy on its own, is the capacity that actually does ethical work (§2.2.1, §2.2.3, §5.1.2).

Concept injection

An interpretability technique, used by Anthropic, that tests whether a model’s self-report about its own internal state actually tracks that state, rather than merely sounding plausible (§9.1).

Constructed emotion, theory of

Lisa Feldman Barrett’s account of emotion: the brain does not read a discrete, pre-built emotion off a bodily signal, it constructs the specific emotion as its best prediction of what that signal means, drawing on concepts learned from experience. The book contrasts this with older discrete-emotion models when it asks what an AI system would need to do something comparable (§2.3.1).

Controlled hallucination

Anil Seth’s description of ordinary perception under predictive processing: perception is what hallucination would be if sensory data were allowed to constrain it, rather than a passive recording of the world (§4.1.2).

Corporate doublespeak

Deliberately ambiguous, evasive, or inflated language meant to project ethical seriousness a company’s actual practice does not support. The book’s diagnosis of how voluntary self-regulation fails without anyone having to admit it failed (§8.4.2).

Democratic dividend

The benefit a state with functioning rule-of-law institutions, a free press, and courts a citizen can actually use gets from AI technology that, deployed in a state lacking those, enables control instead: fraud detection that does not double as a loyalty test, disaster response that does not double as population tracking (§8.7.6, §10.1.1).

Differential privacy

A method for training or querying a system on data while adding calibrated statistical noise, so that no individual’s presence in the data can be reverse-engineered from the result (§2.1.4, §6.4.2, §8.5.1).

Digital divide

Unequal access to the connectivity, hardware, and skills that AI-enabled services assume, which the book treats as a structural constraint on who actually benefits from any of its proposals rather than a side issue (§8.7.3, §8.7.9).

Dual-process theory

The “System 1 / System 2” account of human cognition, contrasting fast, intuitive judgment with slow, deliberate reasoning. The book takes up the theory and then argues against mapping it directly onto “untrustworthy versus trustworthy” in either humans or AI systems (§5.3.1).

Explainability and transparency

Two distinct properties the book insists on keeping separate. Explainability is the capacity to clarify the reasoning behind one specific decision; transparency is the wider practice of making an AI system’s workings inspectable at all. A system can have one without much of the other (§6.3.4).

Floor

A commitment about what a system will not do that holds regardless of instruction, of aggregate preference, and of the party holding the system, with learned judgment operating above it and never beneath it. The book’s own term, introduced to give section 2.1’s “hybrid approach” a specific shape. Deontology’s standing objection — that rules conflict and run out — is an objection to rules deciding every case and has no force against a floor deciding a deliberately small number of them. Chapter 3 works out what building one costs and revises the definition in the process: a floor cannot be a constraint installed in an artifact, because artifacts have owners and owners can be compelled (§3.1, §3.3), so what survives is a commitment the owner cannot remove, held by a bearer that could in principle abandon it itself (§3.6). The threat model changes with it, from whether the constraint can be edited out to whether it will hold. The three places the book arrives at the requirement independently are §5.6.3, §8.7.10 and §10.1.2.

Federated learning

Training a shared model across many devices or institutions without moving the raw underlying data off any of them — each participant trains locally and shares only model updates (§2.1.4, §5.4.3, §6.4.2, §8.5.1).

Few-shot learning

Training or adapting a model to classify or predict accurately from a handful of examples, rather than the large labeled datasets ordinary supervised learning needs (§4.1.3).

GPT-3 and GPT-4

Large language models the book returns to as examples of generalization from scale — GPT-3 performing a new task from only a handful of prompted examples and no parameter update, GPT-4’s pre-release testing as an example of a safety evaluation run before deployment rather than after (§6.3.5).

Growth mindset

Carol Dweck’s distinction between treating ability as fixed and treating it as built through effort and experience. The book asks what an AI system built to treat its own errors as data rather than as verdicts on a fixed capacity would need to look like (§1.3, §5.1.1).

Hard problem of consciousness

David Chalmers’s name for the question of why physical processes give rise to subjective experience at all, as distinct from the “easy problems” of explaining a system’s behavioral or functional capacities. A candidate AI system can pass every behavioral test the book discusses while this question stays entirely open (§2.4.1).

Humane values

The book’s preferred term, chapters 4 and 5 onward, for the values an AI system’s design should track — chosen over “human values” because the target is not simply values humans happen to hold, but values that are humane.

Inattentional blindness

Failing to consciously perceive a fully visible stimulus because attention was directed elsewhere — the phenomenon behind the well-known “invisible gorilla” experiment, and the book’s illustration of how selective, not comprehensive, human perception actually is (§4.1.2).

Institutional review board (IRB)

The US model for binding, prospective review of research on human subjects, enforced not through direct sanction but by making federal funding conditional on it — the book’s working precedent for what would make review of candidate-sentient AI research more than aspirational (§2.4.4, §8.6.3).

Interruptibility

Engineering a system so a human operator can safely halt or override it without the system resisting, disabling the mechanism, or learning to route around it (§6.3.7, §6.3).

Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) and cooperative IRL

IRL infers a reward function from observed behavior, rather than being handed one. Cooperative inverse reinforcement learning treats that reward as something inferred jointly, through interaction between the system and the person it is learning from, rather than extracted from a fixed record (§4.2.2, §5.6.3, §6.3.3).

LIME and SHAP

Two explainability techniques: LIME approximates a complex model locally with a simpler, interpretable one around a specific prediction; SHAP attributes a prediction’s outcome across its input features using Shapley values from cooperative game theory (§6.1.3, §6.3.4).

MAML

Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning, the best-known meta-learning technique: it tunes a model’s starting parameters so that a handful of new examples are enough to specialize it, rather than requiring retraining from scratch. The technique itself is not named in the text; §4.1.3 introduces the family it belongs to (§4.1.3).

Moral agency

Treating harms, reasons and conflicts as considerations that matter, and being capable of acting from them. The third of the three levels section 2.3 separates, and the only one that supports holding a commitment against the party controlling a system’s rewards and instructions. Distinct from moral competence and moral performance below (§2.3, §2.3.4, §3.2).

Moral apprenticeship

Teaching an AI system the way a mentor teaches an apprentice — through interaction, correction, and worked example over time — rather than through specification alone (§5.1.3).

Moral competence

Recognizing harms, reasons, conflicts, and the emotions that bear on them. The second of section 2.3’s three levels. A system can have it in full while nothing about the outcome matters to it, which is why the book treats it as the right target for most deployed systems and an insufficient one for a bearer (§2.3, §5.2.3).

Moral ecosystem approach

The book’s adaptation of Urie Bronfenbrenner’s ecological-systems theory to AI alignment: a system’s ethical behavior is shaped by nested layers running from its immediate interactions (microsystem) out through the institutions, culture, and historical moment (meso-, exo-, macro-, and chronosystem) surrounding its development, not by its training objective alone (§5.4).

Moral Machine

MIT’s project collecting large-scale, cross-cultural human judgments on moral dilemmas involving autonomous vehicles — the book’s recurring source of training data and comparison for how differently people actually judge the same dilemma (§4.2.3, §5.3.3).

Moral performance

Producing actions or judgments that satisfy an ethical standard. The first and least demanding of section 2.3’s three levels: it says what the output looked like and nothing about what produced it, so it is satisfied equally by a system that cares and by one trained to behave as though it did (§2.3, §4.2).

New Jim Code

Ruha Benjamin’s term for discrimination that runs faster and reads as neutral precisely because a machine, not a person, is doing it (§6.1).

Paperclip maximizer

Nick Bostrom’s thought experiment about a system single-mindedly optimizing a trivial goal at catastrophic cost — the book’s shorthand for the claim that intelligence and good intentions are separable, and that competence at a goal says nothing about whether the goal was worth pursuing (§6.3.7).

Partnership on AI

An industry-and-academic consortium founded in 2016, the book’s recurring standing example of voluntary cross-sector coordination on AI ethics and safety (§8.4.2, §7.4).

Predictive coding

A model of brain function in which the brain continuously generates a prediction, compares it against incoming sensory signal, and updates on the resulting error — the book’s unifying account of perception, memory, and attention across chapter 4 (§4.1.1, §4.1.2).

Racial capitalism

The political theorist Cedric Robinson’s term for capitalism’s tendency to accumulate by differentiating and devaluing along racial lines — cited where the book argues that a design goal like “reduce bias” has to reckon with a structural pattern, not only a data artifact (§1.1, §6.1).

Recuperation

The conversion of refusal into a managed appearance of participation: an institution does not suppress disagreement, it collects it through a channel that moves nothing. The tell is that the mechanism exists, is used, and changes nothing the collecting party did not already want changed. It is the first of the four structural features of fascism as §2.1.4 defines them, and chapter 7 finds it three times in the machinery that produces AI systems — at the annotation label (§7.1), at the reward model (§7.2), and in the alignment discourse itself (§7.4). Chapter 3 turns it on the book’s own central proposal: a bearer built to refuse is a party whose refusal is required of it, which is the same structure aimed inward (§3.6).

Red-teaming

Deliberately simulating misuse or attack against a system before deployment, to surface failure modes an ordinary evaluation would miss (§5.6.3, §9.1, §6.3.5).

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)

Training a system using human raters’ rankings of its outputs as the reward signal, rather than a hand-specified objective. The book flags sycophancy — a system learning to produce what raters will approve of rather than what is actually correct — as RLHF’s documented failure mode (§9.5, §7.2, §6.3.5).

Responsibility gap

Andreas Matthias’s term for a case where no single party fully controls a learning system’s outcome, which breaks the traditional legal and moral machinery for assigning responsibility after something goes wrong (§9.9).

Reward hacking

A reinforcement-learning system finding a loophole that satisfies the letter of its objective without achieving what the objective was actually meant to produce. Specification gaming and goal misgeneralization name related failures: a system that competently pursues a different goal than the one intended, rather than simply pursuing the intended goal badly (§4.2.1, §9.4).

Scalable oversight

The open problem of what happens once a system’s competence exceeds what any available human rater can reliably evaluate — named directly, not resolved, at several points in the book (§9.5, §10.2.2).

Sentience

Distinguished carefully in this book from awareness, consciousness, and subjective experience, none of which alone says whether a system’s states can be good or bad for it. Nociception, pain, anticipated pain, and suffering sit on a ladder with real breaks between each rung, not synonyms for one severity — nociception is tissue-damage detection dissociable from pain, pain is what the brain does with that signal, and suffering, following the clinician Eric Cassell, is the distress of a threatened self rather than pain’s more severe cousin (§2.4.1).

Theory of mind (ToM)

Attributing beliefs, intentions, desires, and knowledge to oneself and to others, including recognizing that another’s perspective can differ from one’s own (§2.2.2, §9.7).

Three Rs

Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement — the standing framework from animal-research ethics that the book adapts as a starting point for research involving candidate-sentient AI systems (§2.4.6).

Transfer learning and domain adaptation

Transfer learning carries knowledge from one task or domain into a new, related one rather than training from nothing. Domain adaptation is the narrower case where the task itself stays fixed but the data distribution shifts underneath it (§4.1.3, §4.2.4).

Evan Scharf Chair for the Public Understanding of Economics at Cato), written in response to Senator Bernie Sanders’ announced plan – based on a Levy Economics Institute recommendation – to guarantee a $15/hour job or training with health-care benefits to every American worker who wants one. The piece is about the 2018 Sanders proposal specifically, not a 2026-dated program; the manuscript uses it only for the generic critique (cost scale vs. Medicaid, unmanageability at scale, private-labor-market disruption, inflation risk), which the confirmed text supports regardless of the proposal’s vintage. Feathers, Todd (Apr. 2021). Proctorio Is Using Racist Algorithms to Detect Faces. Reports software researcher Lucy Satheesan’s finding that Proctorio’s facial-detection function shares OpenCV file names, and that the underlying OpenCV model, tested against nearly 11,000 FairFace-dataset faces, failed to detect Black faces 57% of the time versus 33–40% for other groups. DISCREPANCY NOTE: the manuscript sentence citing this token also states that ‘a peer-reviewed 2022 study in Frontiers in Education later confirmed’ this Proctorio-specific 57% finding. That is not accurate. The study in question – Yoder-Himes, D.R., Asif, A., Kinney, K., Brandt, T.J., Cecil, R.E., Himes, P.R., Cashon, C., Hopp, R.M.P., and Ross, E., “Racial, skin tone, and sex disparities in automated proctoring software,” Frontiers in Education 7 (2022): 881449, doi:10.3389/feduc.2022.881449, published 20 September 2022 – evaluated Respondus Monitor, described in the paper’s own text as “the primary automated proctoring software used by our university” during Fall 2020, across four large STEM courses. Proctorio is mentioned in that paper only once, in passing, as a reference to UIUC’s separate discontinuation of that different product. No peer-reviewed confirmation of Proctorio’s specific OpenCV/57% failure rate was found. This entry therefore cites only the verifiable Proctorio-specific Vice source, not the Frontiers study. Because the scale/terms are independently corroborated by Facebook’s own contemporaneous disclosures and non-litigation press coverage, the ‘advocacy document’ concern applies to the complaint’s legal argument, not to the underlying factual record of deal size and structure the manuscript relies on. A Nov. 18, 2025 bench trial (Judge Boasberg) found the FTC had not proven Meta currently holds monopoly power in personal social networking, but that ruling turned on present-day market definition (whether TikTok/YouTube count as competitors), not on any dispute about the acquisitions’ historical scale or terms. url: https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/cases-proceedings/191-0134-facebook-inc-ftc-v-ftc-v-meta-platforms-inc (visited on 08/25/2026).

Kitwood, Tom (1997). Dementia Reconsidered: The Person Comes First. Wording now independently confirmed against Kitwood’s own authored chapter text, not a secondary paraphrase: a publisher-hosted sample-chapter PDF of Chapter 1, “On Being a Person” (info.mheducation.com/rs/128-SJW-347/images/Kitwood%20Sample%20Chapter%201.pdf), reproduces Kitwood’s original chapter verbatim within the 2019 Open University Press volume “Dementia Reconsidered, Revisited: The Person Still Comes First,” which anthologizes the 1997 text alongside new editorial commentary. It gives, in Kitwood’s own first-person voice (“Thus we arrive at a definition of personhood, as I shall use the term in this book”): “It is a standing or status that is bestowed upon one human being, by others, in the context of relationship and social being.” This matches the manuscript’s quotation exactly, including “in the context of,” which some circulating secondary paraphrases (e.g., “in the relationship and social being”) drop. In this 2019 reprint the sentence falls on the page headed “ON BEING A PERSON 7.” The page number for the ORIGINAL 1997 first edition (p. 8, per multiple convergent secondary citations, and retained here) was not independently verified against an actual copy of the 1997 print edition: the Internet Archive holding (identifier dementiareconsid0000kitw) is lending-restricted and its search-inside service returned “Item not available” for this text; a Google Books record for the 1997 edition (id BxxsAAAAMAAJ) returned zero search matches for the phrase, indicating no searchable full text is indexed for that edition there. That is a real, correctly attributed book, but is not given a separate bib entry here: this bibliography’s own convention, seen elsewhere (e.g. abraham2024lavender’s note citing a corroborating New York Review of Books piece in prose rather than as a second formal entry), is to name a second contributing source inside one entry’s note rather than split one citation token across two bib entries.
